entries.en: Xin replied, saying, "Your Majesty raised me from the alleys and let me face south as an independent ruler—this was my good fortune.
entries.literal: Xin replied, saying, "Your Majesty raised your servant from the alleys and let him face south as an independent ruler—this was my good fortune.

entries.zh: 滎陽之事，僕不能死，囚於項籍，此一罪也。
entries.en: At Xingyang I failed to die and was taken prisoner by Xiang Yu—this was my first crime.
entries.literal: At Xingyang I failed to die and was held prisoner by Xiang Ji—this was my first crime.

entries.zh: 寇攻馬邑，僕不能堅守，以城降之，此二罪也。
entries.en: When the enemy attacked Mayi I failed to hold firm and surrendered the city—this was my second crime.
entries.literal: When the enemy attacked Mayi I failed to hold firm and surrendered the city—this was my second crime.

entries.zh: 今為反寇，將兵與將軍爭一旦之命，此三罪也。
entries.en: Now, as a rebel leader leading troops to contend with the general for life and death in a single day—this is my third crime.
entries.literal: Now, as a rebel leader leading troops to contend with the general for life and death in a single day—this is my third crime.

entries.zh: 夫種、蠡無一罪，身死亡；
entries.en: Wen Zhong and Fan Li had committed no such crimes, yet they still perished.
entries.literal: Wen Zhong and Fan Li committed no such crimes, yet they died.

entries.zh: 僕有三罪，而欲求活，此伍子胥所以僨於吳世也。
entries.en: With three crimes of my own, to seek life would be like Wu Zixu's downfall in Wu.
entries.literal: With three crimes of my own, to seek life would be like Wu Zixu's ruin in Wu.

entries.zh: 今僕亡匿山谷間，旦暮乞貣蠻夷，僕之思歸，如痿人不忘起，盲者不忘視，勢不可耳。」
entries.en: Now I hide in mountain valleys, begging among the frontier tribes day and night. I long to return as a paralytic longs to stand and a blind man longs to see—but the circumstances make it impossible."
entries.literal: Now your servant hides in mountain valleys, begging among the frontier tribes day and night. Your servant longs to return as a paralytic longs to rise and a blind man longs to see—but the circumstances make it impossible."

entries.zh: 遂戰。
entries.en: So battle resumed.
entries.literal: So battle resumed.

entries.zh: 柴將軍屠參合，斬信。
entries.en: General Chai massacred Shenhe and beheaded Xin.
entries.literal: General Chai massacred Shenhe and beheaded Xin.

entries.zh: 信之入匈奴，與太子俱，及至頹當城，生子，因名曰頹當。
entries.en: Xin entered Xiongnu territory with his crown prince. When they reached Tuidang City, Xin had a son, whom he therefore named Tuidang.
entries.literal: When Xin entered Xiongnu territory, the crown prince went with him. When they reached Tuidang City, a son was born to Xin, and he therefore named him Tuidang.

entries.zh: 韓太子亦生子嬰。
entries.en: The Han crown prince also had a son, whom he named Ying.
entries.literal: The Han crown prince also had a son, whom he named Ying.

entries.zh: 至孝文時，頹當及嬰率其眾降。
entries.en: By the time of Emperor Wen, Tuidang and Ying led their followers to surrender.
entries.literal: By the time of Emperor Wen, Tuidang and Ying led their followers to surrender.

entries.zh: 漢封頹當為弓高侯，嬰為襄城侯。
entries.en: Han enfeoffed Tuidang as Marquis of Gonggao and Ying as Marquis of Xiangcheng.
entries.literal: Han enfeoffed Tuidang as Marquis of Gonggao and Ying as Marquis of Xiangcheng.

entries.zh: 吳楚反時，弓高侯功冠諸將。
entries.en: During the Rebellion of Wu and Chu, the Marquis of Gonggao's achievements surpassed those of all the other generals.
entries.literal: During the Rebellion of Wu and Chu, the Marquis of Gonggao's achievements surpassed those of all the other generals.

entries.zh: 傳子至孫，孫無子，國絕。
entries.en: The title passed through his son to his grandson; the grandson had no son, and the state was extinguished.
entries.literal: The title passed through his son to his grandson; the grandson had no son, and the state was extinguished.

entries.zh: 嬰孫以不敬失侯。
entries.en: Ying's grandson lost the marquisate for disrespect.
entries.literal: Ying's grandson lost the marquisate for disrespect.

entries.zh: 穨當孽孫嫣，貴幸，名顯當世。
entries.en: Tuidang's descendant through a concubine's line, Yan, was favored at court, and his name was renowned in his generation.
entries.literal: Tuidang's descendant through a concubine's line, Yan, was favored at court, and his name was renowned in his generation.

entries.zh: 嫣弟說，以校尉擊匈奴，封龍額侯。
entries.en: Yan's younger brother Shuo, serving as a captain against the Xiongnu, was enfeoffed as Marquis of Long'e.
entries.literal: Yan's younger brother Shuo, serving as a captain against the Xiongnu, was enfeoffed as Marquis of Long'e.

entries.zh: 後坐酎金失侯，復以待詔為橫海將軍，擊破東越，封按道侯。
entries.en: Later he lost his marquisate because of the tribute-gold offense, but was again summoned to await imperial command and was made General Who Crosses the Seas. He attacked and defeated Dongyue and was enfeoffed as Marquis of Andao.
entries.literal: Later he lost the marquisate in the tribute-gold affair, but was again summoned to await imperial command and made General Who Crosses the Seas; he defeated Dongyue and was enfeoffed as Marquis of Andao.

entries.zh: 太初中，為游擊將軍屯五原外列城，還為光祿勳，掘蠱太子宮，為太子所殺。
entries.en: During the Taichu period, he served as General of Mobile Cavalry and was stationed at the outer line of forts beyond Wuyuan. On his return he became Chamberlain for Attendants, dug for witchcraft evidence in the crown prince's palace, and was killed by the crown prince.
entries.literal: During the Taichu period, he served as raiding general stationed at the outer bastions of Wuyuan, then returned as Director of Splendid Happiness, investigated witchcraft in the crown prince's palace, and was killed by the crown prince.

entries.zh: 子興嗣，坐巫蠱誅。
entries.en: His son Xing succeeded him but was executed for witchcraft.
entries.literal: His son Xing succeeded him but was executed for witchcraft.

entries.zh: 上曰：「游擊將軍死事，無論坐者。」
entries.en: The emperor said, "The raiding general died in the line of duty; do not implicate anyone for his crimes."
entries.literal: The emperor said, "The raiding general died in the line of duty; do not implicate anyone for his crimes."

entries.zh: 乃復封興弟增為龍額侯。
entries.en: Han then re-enfeoffed Xing's younger brother Zeng as Marquis of Long'e.
entries.literal: Han then re-enfeoffed Xing's younger brother Zeng as Marquis of Long'e.

entries.zh: 增少為郎，諸曹侍中光祿大夫，昭帝時至前將軍，與大將軍霍光定策立宣帝，益封千戶。
entries.en: Zeng entered palace service as a young man and served in the various bureaus, as Palace Attendant, and as Grandee of Splendid Light. Under Emperor Zhao he rose to Front General. Together with Grand General Huo Guang, he settled the succession and enthroned Emperor Xuan, for which his fief was increased by one thousand households.
entries.literal: Zeng entered palace service as a young man and served in the various bureaus, as Palace Attendant, and as Grandee of Splendid Light. Under Emperor Zhao he rose to Front General. Together with Grand General Huo Guang, he settled the succession and enthroned Emperor Xuan, for which his fief was increased by one thousand households.

entries.zh: 本始二年，五將征匈奴，增將三萬騎出雲中，斬首百餘級，至期而還。
entries.en: In the second year of Benshi, when the five generals campaigned against the Xiongnu, Zeng led thirty thousand cavalry out from Yunzhong, took more than a hundred heads, and returned at the appointed time.
entries.literal: In the second year of Benshi, when five generals campaigned against the Xiongnu, Zeng led thirty thousand cavalry out of Yunzhong, beheaded more than a hundred, and returned on schedule.

entries.zh: 神爵元年，代張安世為大司馬車騎將軍，領尚書事。
entries.en: In the first year of Shenjue, he replaced Zhang Anshi as grand marshal and chariot-and-cavalry general, and headed the Secretariat.
entries.literal: In the first year of Shenjue, he replaced Zhang Anshi as grand marshal and chariot-and-cavalry general, and headed the Secretariat.

entries.zh: 增世貴，幼為忠臣，事三主，重於朝廷。
entries.en: Zeng came from an illustrious family, was a loyal minister from youth, served three sovereigns, and was highly regarded at court.
entries.literal: Zeng came from an illustrious family, was a loyal minister from youth, served three sovereigns, and was highly regarded at court.

entries.zh: 為人寬和自守，以溫顏遜辭承上接下，無所失意，保身固寵，不能有所建明。
entries.en: By nature he was mild, harmonious, and self-controlled. With a warm expression and deferential words he served those above and dealt with those below, never disappointing anyone, preserving himself and keeping favor secure, but he was unable to offer any notable proposals.
entries.literal: By nature mild and self-restrained, he used a warm countenance and deferential speech with superiors and subordinates alike, never causing offense, preserving himself and securing imperial favor without achieving notable distinction.

entries.zh: 五鳳二年薨，諡曰安侯。
entries.en: In the second year of Wufeng he died, and was posthumously titled Marquis An.
entries.literal: In the second year of Wufeng he died, and was posthumously titled Marquis An.

entries.zh: 子寶嗣，亡子，國除。
entries.en: His son Bao succeeded him, but had no son, and the state was abolished.
entries.literal: His son Bao succeeded him, but had no son, and the state was abolished.

entries.zh: 成帝時，繼功臣後，封增兄子岑為龍額侯。
entries.en: During Emperor Cheng's reign, to continue the line of meritorious officials, Han enfeoffed Zeng's elder brother's son Cen as Marquis of Long'e.
entries.literal: During Emperor Cheng's reign, to continue the line of meritorious officials, Han enfeoffed Zeng's elder brother's son Cen as Marquis of Long'e.

entries.zh: 薨，子持弓嗣。
entries.en: When Cen died, his son Chigong succeeded.
entries.literal: When Cen died, his son Chigong succeeded.

entries.zh: 王莽敗，乃絕。
entries.en: When Wang Mang fell, the line was extinguished.
entries.literal: When Wang Mang fell, the line was extinguished.

entries.zh: 魏豹，故魏諸公子也。
entries.en: Wei Bao was a former prince of Wei.
entries.literal: Wei Bao was a former prince of Wei.

entries.zh: 其兄魏咎，故魏時封為甯陵君，秦滅魏，為庶人。
entries.en: His elder brother Wei Jiu had been enfeoffed in the former Wei as Lord of Ningling, but when Qin destroyed Wei he was reduced to commoner status.
entries.literal: His elder brother Wei Jiu had once held the title Lord of Ningling in old Wei, but after Qin destroyed Wei he became a commoner.

entries.zh: 陳勝之王也，咎往從之。
entries.en: When Chen Sheng made himself king, Wei Jiu went to follow him.
entries.literal: When Chen Sheng made himself king, Wei Jiu went to follow him.

entries.zh: 勝使魏人周市徇魏地，魏地已下，欲立周市為魏王。
entries.en: Chen Sheng sent Zhou Shi, a man of Wei, to bring Wei territory over. After Wei territory had submitted, the people wished to make Zhou Shi king of Wei.
entries.literal: Chen Sheng sent the Wei man Zhou Shi to pacify Wei territory. Once Wei lands were subdued, they wanted to make Zhou Shi king of Wei.

entries.zh: 市曰：「天下昏亂，忠臣乃見。
entries.en: Zhou Shi said, "In a chaotic age, loyal ministers come to the fore.
entries.literal: Zhou Shi said: "When all under Heaven is dark and chaotic, true loyal ministers appear.

entries.zh: 今天下共畔秦，其誼必立魏王後乃可。」
entries.en: Now the whole empire has turned against Qin; propriety demands that we first set up a scion of the house of Wei."
entries.literal: Now all under Heaven jointly rebels against Qin; by right we must enthrone a descendant of the kings of Wei first."

entries.zh: 齊、趙使車各五十乘，立市為王。
entries.en: Qi and Zhao each sent fifty chariots to support installing Zhou Shi as king.
entries.literal: Qi and Zhao each sent fifty chariots to support installing Zhou Shi as king.

entries.zh: 市不受，迎魏咎於陳，五反，陳王乃遣立咎為魏王。
entries.en: Zhou Shi refused the title. He went to Chen to bring Wei Jiu back, and after he asked five times, the King of Chen finally sent Wei Jiu and installed him as king of Wei.
entries.literal: Zhou Shi refused. He went to Chen to bring back Wei Jiu; after repeated requests, the King of Chen finally sent Wei Jiu back and enthroned him as king of Wei.

entries.zh: 賈既有功，而高祖子弱，昆弟少，又不賢，欲王同姓以填天下，乃下詔曰：「將軍劉賈有功，及擇子弟可以為王者。」
entries.en: Liu Jia had earned great merit, yet Gaozu’s sons were young, his brothers few, and none of them fit to hold the frontier. Gaozu meant to plant Liu kinsmen as kings to steady the empire, and proclaimed: “General Liu Jia has distinguished himself; choose from among the younger generation of the house one worthy to receive a kingdom.”
entries.literal: Liu Jia had already earned great merit, but Gaozu’s sons were still young, his brothers were few, and none showed real talent, so he wished to invest princes of his own surname to secure the realm. He therefore issued an edict: “General Liu Jia has rendered outstanding service; now select from among the younger members of the house one fit to be king.”

entries.zh: 群臣皆曰：「立劉賈為荊王，王淮東。」
entries.en: The ministers replied in one voice: “Make Liu Jia king of Jing with his seat east of the Huai.”
entries.literal: The assembled ministers all said, “Establish Liu Jia as King of Jing, ruling the territory east of the Huai.”

entries.zh: 立六年而淮南王黥布反，東擊荊。
entries.en: In the sixth year of his reign Qing Bu, the tattooed king of Huainan, rose in revolt and drove east into Jing.
entries.literal: Six years after his enthronement, Qing Bu, king of Huainan, rebelled and marched east against Jing.

entries.zh: 賈與戰，弗勝，走富陵，為布軍所殺。
entries.en: Liu Jia engaged him but could not prevail. He retreated to Fuling, where Qing Bu’s troops cut him down.
entries.literal: Liu Jia gave battle but was defeated, fled to Fuling, and was killed by Qing Bu’s army.

entries.zh: 燕王劉澤，高祖從祖昆弟也。
entries.en: Liu Ze, king of Yan, was Gaozu’s second cousin on the male line.
entries.literal: King Liu Ze of Yan was a second cousin of Gaozu on the male line (they shared the same great-grandfather).

entries.zh: 高祖三年，澤為郎中。
entries.en: In the third year of Gaozu’s reign Liu Ze was appointed gentleman of the palace.
entries.literal: In Gaozu’s third year, Liu Ze served as gentleman of the palace.

entries.zh: 十一年，以將軍擊陳豨將王黃，封為營陵侯。
entries.en: In the eleventh year he campaigned as a general against Wang Huang, one of Chen Xi’s officers, and received the marquisate of Yingling.
entries.literal: In the eleventh year, as a general he attacked Wang Huang, a commander under Chen Xi, and was enfeoffed marquis of Yingling.

entries.zh: 吳王濞，高帝兄仲之子也。
entries.en: Liu Bi, king of Wu, was the son of Liu Zhong, the founder’s elder brother.
entries.literal: Liu Bi, prince of Wu, was the son of Liu Zhong, elder brother to Gaozu.

entries.zh: 高帝立仲為代王。
entries.en: The founder first made Liu Zhong king of Dai.
entries.literal: Gaozu had first enfeoffed Liu Zhong as king of Dai.

entries.zh: 匈奴攻代，仲不能堅守，棄國間行，走雒陽，自歸，天子不忍致法，廢為合陽侯。
entries.en: The nomads struck Dai; Liu Zhong failed to defend it. He slipped away to Luoyang and gave himself up. The emperor spared him the full penalty and reduced him to marquis of Heyang.
entries.literal: When the Xiongnu attacked Dai, Liu Zhong could not hold his ground. He abandoned his kingdom, traveled in secret to Luoyang, and surrendered himself. The Son of Heaven could not bear to punish him harshly, so he was demoted to marquis of Heyang.

entries.zh: 子濞，封為沛侯。
entries.en: His son Liu Bi received the marquisate of Pei.
entries.literal: His son Liu Bi was enfeoffed marquis of Pei.

entries.zh: 黥布反，高祖自將往誅之。
entries.en: When Qing Bu rose, Gaozu marched in person to crush the revolt.
entries.literal: When Qing Bu rebelled, Gaozu took the field in person to destroy him.

entries.zh: 濞年二十，以騎將從破布軍。
entries.en: At twenty Liu Bi rode as a cavalry general in the host that broke Qing Bu.
entries.literal: Twenty-year-old Liu Bi served as a cavalry commander in the army that defeated Qing Bu.

entries.zh: 荊王劉賈為布所殺，無後。
entries.en: Liu Jia, king of Jing, had fallen to Qing Bu and had no successor.
entries.literal: King Liu Jia of Jing had been killed by Qing Bu and left no heir.

entries.zh: 上患吳會稽輕悍，無壯王填之，諸子少，乃立濞於沛，為吳王，王三郡五十三城。
entries.en: The throne feared the martial temper of Wu and Kuaiji and wanted a mature prince to hold them, yet the imperial sons were young. Liu Bi was therefore elevated from Pei to king of Wu with three commanderies and fifty-three towns.
entries.literal: The emperor worried that the people of Wu and Kuaiji were light and fierce and needed a strong prince to govern them; his own sons were still young, so he raised Liu Bi from Pei to be king of Wu over three commanderies and fifty-three cities.

entries.zh: 已拜受印，高祖召濞相之，曰：「若狀有反相。」
entries.en: When the seal had been delivered Gaozu studied his face and said, “You have the look of a rebel.”
entries.literal: After the investiture rites Gaozu examined Liu Bi’s face and said, “Your features carry the mark of one who would revolt.”

entries.zh: 獨悔，業已拜，因拊其背，曰：「漢後五十年東南有亂，豈若邪？
entries.en: He repented immediately, yet the appointment stood, so he patted Liu Bi’s back and said, “Within fifty years the southeast will rise in strife—will it be you?
entries.literal: He regretted it at once, but the patent had already been granted, so he clapped Liu Bi on the back and said, “Fifty years hence there will be turmoil in the southeast of the Han realm—will that be your doing?

entries.zh: 然天下同姓一家，慎無反！」
entries.en: Still, the realm is one Liu clan; do not dare revolt!”
entries.literal: Yet the empire is one house of the Liu name; see that you never think of rebellion!”

entries.zh: 濞頓首曰：「不敢。」
entries.en: Liu Bi kowtowed and said, “I would not dare.”
entries.literal: Liu Bi kowtowed and said, “I would not dare.”

entries.zh: 荊王劉賈，高帝從父兄也，不知其初起時。
entries.en: Liu Jia, king of Jing, was Gaozu's patrilateral cousin; nothing is known of his earliest career.
entries.literal: King Liu Jia of Jing was Gaozu's patrilateral cousin; nothing is known of his earliest career.

entries.zh: 漢元年，還定三秦，賈為將軍，定塞地，從東擊項籍。
entries.en: In the first year of Han, after the pacification of the Three Qins, Liu Jia served as a general, secured Sai territory, and marched east against Xiang Yu.
entries.literal: In Han year 1, when the Three Qins were pacified, Jia served as a general, secured Sai territory, and marched east against Xiang Ji.

entries.zh: 漢王敗成皋，北度河，得張耳、韓信軍，軍脩武，深溝高壘，使賈將二萬人，騎數百，擊楚，度白馬津入楚地，燒其積聚，以破其業，無以給項王軍食。
entries.en: After his defeat at Chenggao, the King of Han withdrew north across the river and joined the forces of Zhang Er and Han Xin. They made camp at Xiuwu behind deep moats and high walls. He dispatched Liu Jia with twenty thousand foot soldiers and several hundred cavalry to hit Chu from the flank. Liu Jia crossed the Baima Ford into Chu lands and torched their depots, shattering their logistics so that King Xiang’s troops went hungry.
entries.literal: When the King of Han was defeated at Chenggao, he crossed the Yellow River to the north, took command of the armies of Zhang Er and Han Xin, and encamped at Xiuwu, digging deep moats and raising high ramparts. He sent Liu Jia with twenty thousand infantry and several hundred horsemen to strike Chu. Liu Jia crossed the Baima Ford into Chu territory and burned their accumulated stores, wrecking their supply lines so that nothing could be fed to King Xiang’s army.

entries.zh: 已而楚兵擊之，賈輒避不肯與戰，而與彭越相保。
entries.en: When Chu forces moved against him, Liu Jia repeatedly avoided battle and held his ground in concert with Peng Yue.
entries.literal: Soon afterward Chu troops attacked him; Liu Jia repeatedly avoided them and refused battle, while maintaining a joint defense with Peng Yue.

entries.zh: 高后時，齊人田生游乏資，以畫奸澤。
entries.en: Under Empress Dowager Lü, the Qi native Tian Sheng wandered the capital in want of money and approached Liu Ze with a subtle plan.
entries.literal: During the reign of Empress Gao, a man of Qi named Tian Sheng traveled in reduced circumstances and, short of funds, importuned Liu Ze with a crafty scheme.

entries.zh: 澤大說之，用金二百斤為田生壽。
entries.en: Delighted, Liu Ze gave him two hundred catties of gold to toast his longevity.
entries.literal: Liu Ze was delighted and presented him with two hundred catties of gold as a birthday gift.

entries.zh: 田生已得金，即歸齊。
entries.en: Tian Sheng pocketed the gold and went home to Qi.
entries.literal: Tian Sheng took the gold and returned to Qi.

entries.zh: 二歲，澤使人謂田生曰：「弗與矣。」
entries.en: Two years later Liu Ze sent Tian Sheng word: “There will be no more gifts.”
entries.literal: Two years later Liu Ze sent Tian Sheng word: “There will be no more gifts.”

entries.zh: 田生如長安，不見澤，而假大宅，令其子求事呂后所幸大謁者張卿。
entries.en: Tian Sheng traveled to Chang’an, never called on Liu Ze, rented a large house, and arranged for his son to enter service under Zhang Qing, the great usher in the empress dowager’s intimate circle.
entries.literal: Tian Sheng went to Chang’an but avoided Liu Ze. Instead he leased a grand mansion and had his son seek a post under Zhang Qing, the chief usher whom Empress Dowager Lü favored.

entries.zh: 居數月，田生子請張卿臨，親脩具。
entries.en: Months later the son invited Zhang Qing to dinner and oversaw every detail of the banquet himself.
entries.literal: Several months later Tian Sheng’s son invited Zhang Qing to visit and personally prepared the feast.

entries.zh: 張卿往，見田生帷帳具置如列侯。
entries.en: When Zhang Qing arrived he found hangings and service fit for a marquis of the first rank.
entries.literal: Zhang Qing came and saw curtains and vessels arrayed as for a full marquis.

entries.zh: 張卿驚。
entries.en: Zhang Qing was taken aback.
entries.literal: Zhang Qing was startled.

entries.zh: 酒酣，乃屏人說張卿曰：「臣觀諸侯邸第百餘，皆高帝一切功臣。
entries.en: When they were deep in their cups, Tian Sheng sent the servants away and said, “I have walked the lanes of over a hundred noble houses. Every one belongs to the merit ministers whom Gaozu enfeoffed wholesale at the founding.
entries.literal: When the wine had flowed freely, Tian Sheng dismissed the attendants and said to Zhang Qing, “I have inspected the mansions of more than a hundred nobles; all belong to Gaozu’s founding ministers enfeoffed in a single stroke at the empire’s beginning.

entries.zh: 今呂氏雅故本推轂高帝就天下，功至大，又有親戚太后之重。
entries.en: The Lüs helped Gaozu win the realm from the outset; their merit is unmatched, and they are the empress dowager’s own kin besides.
entries.literal: The Lü clan from the outset turned the wheels for Gaozu in winning the realm; their service is unmatched, and they also hold the empress dowager’s blood ties.

entries.zh: 太后春秋長，諸呂弱，太后欲立呂產為呂王，王代。
entries.en: The empress dowager is old, her Lü nephews still young in power, and she means to raise Lü Chan as king of the Lü line with the territory of Dai.
entries.literal: The empress dowager is advanced in years, the Lü men are still weak, and she wishes to make Lü Chan king of the Lü domain and invest him with Dai.

entries.zh: 呂后又重發之，恐大臣不聽。
entries.en: She dare not press it openly for fear the great ministers will balk.
entries.literal: Yet she hesitates to bring the matter forward, fearing the high ministers will not consent.

entries.zh: 今卿最幸，大臣所敬，何不風大臣以聞太后，太后必喜。
entries.en: You enjoy her deepest trust and the ministers’ deference. Hint to the ministers that they should memorialize the throne—she will rejoice at it.
entries.literal: You stand highest in her favor and are respected at court. Why not prompt the ministers to memorialize her? She will be pleased.

entries.zh: 諸呂以王，萬戶侯亦卿之有。
entries.en: When the Lü princes are enthroned, a ten-thousand-household marquisate will be yours as well.
entries.literal: Once the Lü are kings, you may expect to be raised to marquis over ten thousand households yourself.

entries.zh: 太后心欲之，而卿為內臣，不急發，恐過及身矣。」
entries.en: This is what she longs for, and you are her inside man. If you delay, misfortune may fall on you first.”
entries.literal: Her heart is set on this; as her intimate courtier, if you do not move quickly, disaster may reach your own person.”

entries.zh: 張卿大然之，乃風大臣語太后。
entries.en: Zhang Qing was convinced and privately coached the high ministers to approach the empress dowager.
entries.literal: Zhang Qing agreed wholeheartedly and quietly urged the leading ministers to speak to the empress dowager.

entries.zh: 太后朝，因問大臣。
entries.en: When she held court she put the question to them directly.
entries.literal: At the next court audience she questioned the ministers on the point.

entries.zh: 大臣請立呂產為呂王。
entries.en: They asked that Lü Chan be established as king of the Lü domain.
entries.literal: The ministers requested that Lü Chan be made king of the Lü line.

entries.zh: 太后賜張卿千金，張卿以其半進田生。
entries.en: She bestowed a thousand catties of gold on Zhang Qing, who forwarded half to Tian Sheng.
entries.literal: The empress dowager rewarded Zhang Qing with a thousand catties of gold, and he gave half of it to Tian Sheng.

entries.zh: 田生弗受，因說之曰：「呂產王也，諸大臣未大服。
entries.en: Tian Sheng declined the gold and argued, “Lü Chan’s kingship will not yet win the full submission of the great ministers.
entries.literal: Tian Sheng refused the gift and offered further counsel: “Even after Lü Chan is made king, many ministers will still be only half persuaded.

entries.zh: 今營陵侯澤，諸劉長，為大將軍，獨此尚觖望。
entries.en: Liu Ze, marquis of Yingling, is the senior member of the Liu clan and serves as grand general; he alone still feels slighted.
entries.literal: Marquis Liu Ze of Yingling is the senior member of the Liu clan and serves as grand general; he alone still nurses disappointment and resentment.

entries.zh: 今卿言太后，裂十餘縣王之，彼得王喜，於諸呂王益固矣。」
entries.en: Urge her to carve out a dozen counties and enfeoff him as king. Once he is satisfied, the Lü kingships will stand on firmer ground.”
entries.literal: If you tell the empress dowager to carve out more than ten counties and make him king, once he is pleased with his kingdom the Lü kings will be all the more secure.”

entries.zh: 張卿入言之。
entries.en: Zhang Qing carried the plea inward.
entries.literal: Zhang Qing relayed this to the throne.

entries.zh: 又太后女弟呂須女亦為營陵侯妻，故遂立營陵侯澤為琅邪王。
entries.en: The empress dowager’s younger sister Lü Xu had given her daughter in marriage to Marquis Liu Ze of Yingling, which is why Liu Ze was finally raised to king of Langye.
entries.literal: Moreover the empress dowager’s younger sister Lü Xu’s daughter was also wife to Marquis Liu Ze of Yingling; therefore Liu Ze of Yingling was at last established as king of Langye.

entries.zh: 琅邪王與田生之國，急行毋留。
entries.en: The king of Langye and Tian Sheng galloped for their fief and did not linger.
entries.literal: The new king of Langye and Tian Sheng set out for their domain at full speed and did not linger.

entries.zh: 出關，太后果使人追之。
entries.en: They cleared the barrier; she sent riders after them all the same.
entries.literal: When they had left the pass, the empress dowager still sent men in pursuit.

entries.zh: 已出，即還。
entries.en: Once they had cleared the pass, the pursuers turned back.
entries.literal: Once they were already out, the pursuers turned back.

entries.zh: 朝錯為太子家令，得幸皇太子，數從容言吳過可削。
entries.en: Chao Cuo was serving as household steward to the crown prince and had won his favor. He repeatedly said in private that Wu's offenses gave grounds for reducing its territory.
entries.literal: Chao Cuo served as household steward to the crown prince. Favored by the crown prince, he repeatedly said in private that Wu's offenses could be grounds for reducing its territory.

entries.zh: 數上書說之，文帝寬，不忍罰，以此吳王日益橫。
entries.en: He submitted memorial after memorial urging this course, but Emperor Wen was lenient and could not bear to punish Wu. As a result, the King of Wu became more overbearing by the day.
entries.literal: He submitted memorials urging this repeatedly. Emperor Wen was lenient and unwilling to punish; because of this the King of Wu grew more arrogant by the day.

entries.zh: 及景帝即位，錯為御史大夫，說上曰：「昔高帝初定天下，昆弟少，諸子弱，大封同姓，故孽子悼惠王王齊七十二城，庶弟元王王楚四十城，兄子王吳五十餘城。
entries.en: When Emperor Jing came to the throne, Chao Cuo became Imperial Counselor. He urged the emperor, "When Gaozu first settled the realm, he had few brothers and his sons were young, so he gave large fiefs to men of his own surname. Thus King Daohui, his son by a concubine, ruled Qi with seventy-two cities; King Yuan, his younger half-brother, ruled Chu with forty cities; and his nephew ruled Wu with more than fifty cities.
entries.literal: When Emperor Jing took the throne, Cuo became Grandee Secretary. He urged the emperor, "When Gaozu first settled the realm, his brothers were few and his sons were young, so he made large grants to men of his own surname. Thus King Daohui, his son by a concubine, ruled Qi with seventy-two cities; King Yuan, his younger half-brother, ruled Chu with forty cities; and his elder brother's son ruled Wu with more than fifty cities.

entries.zh: 封三庶孽，分天下半。
entries.en: These three junior or collateral branches received half the realm between them.
entries.literal: By enfeoffing these three junior or collateral kinsmen, he divided away half the realm.

entries.zh: 今吳王前有太子之隙，詐稱病不朝，於古法當誅。
entries.en: Now the King of Wu already had a grievance over the crown prince, then falsely claimed illness and failed to attend court. Under the ancient laws, this deserved execution.
entries.literal: Now the King of Wu, having earlier had a falling-out over the crown prince, feigned illness and failed to attend court—in ancient law this was punishable by death.

entries.zh: 文帝不忍，因賜几杖，德至厚也。
entries.en: Emperor Wen could not bear it and therefore granted him an armrest and staff—a kindness of the utmost depth.
entries.literal: Emperor Wen could not bear it and therefore granted him an armrest and staff—a kindness of the utmost depth.

entries.zh: 不改過自新，乃益驕恣，公即山鑄錢，煮海為鹽，誘天下亡人謀作亂逆。
entries.en: Instead of correcting his faults and making a new start, he became still more arrogant and unrestrained. He openly minted coins in the mountains, boiled seawater for salt, and lured fugitives from throughout the realm into plotting rebellion.
entries.literal: Rather than reform and renew himself, he grew all the more arrogant and overbearing: he openly minted coin at the mountains and boiled sea water for salt, enticing fugitives throughout the realm to plot rebellion.

entries.zh: 今削之亦反，不削亦反。
entries.en: If we reduce him now, he will rebel; if we do not reduce him, he will rebel too.
entries.literal: If we reduce him now, he will rebel; if we do not reduce him, he will rebel too.

entries.zh: 削之，其反亟，禍小；
entries.en: If we reduce him, his rebellion will come quickly and the calamity will be small;
entries.literal: If we reduce him, his rebellion will come quickly and the calamity will be small;

entries.zh: 不削之，其反遲，禍大。」
entries.en: if we do not reduce him, his rebellion will come late and the calamity will be great."
entries.literal: if we do not reduce him, his rebellion will come late and the calamity will be great."

entries.zh: 三年冬，楚王來朝，錯因言楚王戊往年為薄太后服，私姦服舍，請誅之。
entries.en: In the winter of the third year, the King of Chu came to court. Chao Cuo then reported that in earlier years, while observing mourning for Empress Dowager Bo, the King of Chu, Wu, had had illicit relations in the mourning quarters, and he requested that Wu be executed.
entries.literal: In the third year, winter, the King of Chu came to court. Cuo therefore reported that the King of Chu, Wu, in earlier years while in mourning for Empress Dowager Bo, had had illicit relations in the mourning quarters, and asked that he be executed.

entries.zh: 詔赦，削東海郡。
entries.en: An edict pardoned him but stripped the Donghai commandery.
entries.literal: An edict pardoned him but stripped the Donghai commandery.

entries.zh: 及前二年，趙王有罪，削其常山郡。
entries.en: In the year before last, the King of Zhao was found guilty and his Changshan commandery was stripped.
entries.literal: In the year before last, the King of Zhao was found guilty and his Changshan commandery was stripped.

entries.zh: 膠西王卬以賣爵事有姦，削其六縣。
entries.en: The King of Jiaoxi, Ang, had improprieties in the sale of noble ranks; six counties were stripped from him.
entries.literal: The King of Jiaoxi, Ang, had improprieties in the sale of noble ranks; six counties were stripped from him.

entries.zh: 漢王追項籍至固陵，使賈南度淮圍壽春。
entries.en: Pursuing Xiang Yu as far as Guling, the King of Han ordered Liu Jia south across the Huai to invest Shouchun.
entries.literal: The King of Han pursued Xiang Ji to Guling and sent Liu Jia south across the Huai to besiege Shouchun.

entries.zh: 還至，使人間招楚大司馬周殷。
entries.en: When he came back he dispatched agents to sound out Zhou Yin, Chu’s grand marshal, in private.
entries.literal: On his return he sent men in secret to win over Zhou Yin, the Great Marshal of Chu.

entries.zh: 周殷反楚，佐賈舉九江，迎英布兵，皆會垓下，誅項籍。
entries.en: Zhou Yin rebelled against Chu, helped Liu Jia secure Jiujiang, joined with Ying Bu’s army, and the allied hosts met at Gaixia to destroy Xiang Yu.
entries.literal: Zhou Yin turned against Chu, aided Liu Jia in raising Jiujiang, welcomed Ying Bu’s troops, and they all converged at Gaixia, where Xiang Ji was executed.

entries.zh: 漢王因使賈將九江兵，與太尉盧綰西南擊臨江王共尉，尉死，以臨江為南郡。
entries.en: The King of Han then put Liu Jia in command of the Jiujiang forces. With Grand Commandant Lu Wan he struck southwest at Gong Wei, king of Linjiang. Gong Wei fell, and his domain was converted into Nan Commandery.
entries.literal: The King of Han therefore ordered Liu Jia to lead the Jiujiang troops. Together with Grand Commandant Lu Wan he attacked King Gong Wei of Linjiang from the southwest. Gong Wei died, and Linjiang was reorganized as Nan Commandery.

entries.zh: 二月，吳王兵既破，敗走，於是天子制詔將軍：「蓋聞為善者天報以福，為非者天報以殃。
entries.en: In the second month Wu’s army was shattered; the emperor told his generals: “Heaven crowns virtue with fortune and strikes evil with woe.
entries.literal: In the second month the King of Wu's army had already been broken and fled in defeat; the Son of Heaven then issued an edict to the generals: “We have heard that Heaven rewards the good with blessing and the wicked with calamity.

entries.zh: 高皇帝親垂功德，建立諸侯，幽王、悼惠王絕無後，孝文皇帝哀憐加惠，王幽王子遂，悼惠王子卬等，令奉其先王宗廟，為漢藩國，德配天地，明並日月。
entries.en: Gaozu established the kingdoms. When the lines of King You of Zhao and King Daohui of Qi had been cut off, Emperor Wen compassionately made You’s son Sui, Daohui’s son Ang, and others kings so that they could tend their forefathers’ shrines and serve as Han’s outer bulwarks. His virtue matched Heaven and Earth, and his brilliance equaled the sun and moon.
entries.literal: The August Emperor Gaozu personally bestowed merit and virtue by establishing the princes. When the lines of King You of Zhao and King Daohui of Qi had been cut off without successors, Emperor Xiaowen took pity and extended his grace, making King You's son Sui, King Daohui's son Ang, and others kings so that they could maintain their forefathers' ancestral temples and serve as Han's outer bulwarks—his virtue matched Heaven and Earth, and his brilliance equaled the sun and moon.

entries.zh: 而吳王濞背德反義，誘受天下亡命罪人，亂天下幣，稱疾不朝二十餘年。
entries.en: Yet Liu Bi spurned virtue, drew in fugitives, disrupted the currency, and for more than twenty years pleaded illness and stayed away from court.
entries.literal: Yet the King of Wu Liu Bi turned his back on virtue and violated righteousness, enticed and harbored fugitive criminals from the realm, threw the realm's currency into confusion, and for more than twenty years claimed illness and did not attend court.

entries.zh: 有司數請濞罪，孝文皇帝寬之，欲其改行為善。
entries.en: Officials begged his head; Wendi spared him, hoping he would mend his ways.
entries.literal: The authorities repeatedly requested Bi's punishment; Emperor Xiaowen was lenient and wished him to change his conduct for the good.

entries.zh: 今乃與楚王戊、趙王遂、膠西王卬、濟南王辟光、菑川王賢、膠東王雄渠約從謀反，為逆無道，起兵以危宗廟，賊殺大臣及漢使者，迫劫萬民，伐殺無罪，燒殘民家，掘其丘壟，甚為虐暴。
entries.en: Now he has allied with Liu Wu of Chu, Liu Sui of Zhao, Liu Ang of Jiaoxi, Liu Piguang of Jinan, Liu Xian of Zichuan, and Liu Xiongqu of Jiaodong to plot rebellion. These lawless traitors menace the temples, murder ministers and envoys, coerce the people, kill the innocent, burn their homes, and dig open their graves. Their cruelty is monstrous.
entries.literal: Now he has joined with Liu Wu, king of Chu, Liu Sui, king of Zhao, Liu Ang, king of Jiaoxi, Liu Piguang, king of Jinan, Liu Xian, king of Zichuan, and Liu Xiongqu, king of Jiaodong, in an alliance to plot rebellion. Lawless in their treason, they raised troops to endanger the ancestral temples, murdered great ministers and Han envoys, coerced the people, slaughtered the innocent, burned commoners' homes, and dug open their tombs—utterly cruel and violent.

entries.zh: 而卬等又重逆無道，燒宗廟，鹵御物，朕甚痛之。
entries.en: Ang’s crew have burned the shrines and plundered the palace stores—Our heart is torn.
entries.literal: Yet Ang and the others have again been utterly lawless, burned the temples, looted the imperial gear—the pain of this is great in Us.

entries.zh: 朕素服避正殿，將軍其勸士大夫擊反虜。
entries.en: We wear mourning and quit the main hall—generals, drive your men at the traitors.
entries.literal: We have donned plain dress and avoided the main hall; generals, urge your officers to strike the rebels.

entries.zh: 擊反虜者，深入多殺為功，斬首捕虜比三百石以上皆殺，無有所置。
entries.en: Advance deep and kill many to earn merit; execute every captured rebel of three-hundred-picul rank or higher, sparing none.
entries.literal: Those who strike the rebels shall take deep advances and heavy killing as merit; every captured rebel of the three-hundred-picul rank or above shall be put to death, with none spared.

entries.zh: 敢有議詔及不如詔者，皆要斬。」
entries.en: Debate the decree or disobey it—death by waist chop.”
entries.literal: Whoever dares debate the edict or fail to match the edict—waist cut in two.”

entries.zh: 三王之圍齊臨菑也，三月不能下。
entries.en: The three kings besieged Linzi for three months and could not take it.
entries.literal: When the three kings besieged Qi’s capital Linzi, they could not take it in three months.

entries.zh: 漢兵至，膠西、膠東、菑川王各引兵歸國。
entries.en: Imperial columns approached; the kings of Jiaoxi, Jiaodong, and Zichuan peeled off and raced for home.
entries.literal: When Han troops arrived, the kings of Jiaoxi, Jiaodong, and Zichuan each led their armies back to their kingdoms.

entries.zh: 膠西王徒跣，席稿，飲水，謝太后。
entries.en: Liu Ang shed shoes, sat on rough straw, drank nothing but water, and begged his mother’s pardon.
entries.literal: The King of Jiaoxi went barefoot, sat on straw matting, drank only water, and apologized to the queen dowager.

entries.zh: 王太子德曰：「漢兵還，臣觀之以罷，可襲，願收王餘兵擊之，不勝而逃入海，未晚也。」
entries.en: Prince De urged: “The Han host is spent from the march; strike now with what is left. If we lose, we can still run to the sea.”
entries.literal: The king's heir De said, “The Han army has returned; in my observation they are exhausted—we may strike. I beg to gather Your Majesty's remaining troops and attack them; if we do not prevail we can still flee to the sea—it will not be too late.”

entries.zh: 王曰：「吾士卒皆已壞，不可用。」
entries.en: The king answered, “My men are shattered—useless.”
entries.literal: The king said, “My soldiers are already broken and cannot be used.”

entries.zh: 不聽。
entries.en: He refused.
entries.literal: He would not listen.

entries.zh: 漢將弓高侯頹當遺王書曰：「奉詔誅不義，降者赦，除其罪，復故；
entries.en: Han Tuidang, marquis of Gonggao, wrote: “The throne punishes treason; yield and you are forgiven, your guilt wiped away, and your former standing restored;
entries.literal: Han general Han Tuidang, marquis of Gonggao, sent the king a letter saying, “By edict We punish the unrighteous; those who surrender shall be pardoned, their crimes removed, and their former status restored;

entries.zh: 不降者滅之。
entries.en: refuse and you are wiped out.
entries.literal: those who do not submit shall be destroyed.

entries.zh: 王何處？
entries.en: What will you do?
entries.literal: What will the king do?

entries.zh: 須以從事。」
entries.en: Answer, and we shall proceed accordingly.”
entries.literal: We await your word and will act accordingly.”

entries.zh: 王肉袒叩頭漢軍壁，謁曰：「臣卬奉法不謹，驚駭百姓，乃苦將軍遠道至于窮國，敢請葅醢之罪。」
entries.en: Ang stripped to the chest, kowtowed at the Han lines, and said, “I broke the law, frightened the people, and dragged you to this poor corner—I deserve dismemberment.”
entries.literal: The king bared his breast, knocked his head at the Han army rampart, and declared in audience, “Your servant Ang has not been careful in observing the law; I have terrified the common people and thus caused the general to come far to this exhausted state—I dare beg the crime of being minced for pickle.”

entries.zh: 弓高侯執金鼓見之，曰：「王苦軍事，願聞王發兵狀。」
entries.en: Han Tuidang received him holding the gong and drum of command and said, “You have suffered through this war; tell me how you came to raise troops.”
entries.literal: The marquis of Gonggao, holding the gong and drum that symbolized military command, received him and said, “The king has suffered through military affairs; I wish to hear how the king raised troops.”

entries.zh: 王頓首膝行對曰：「今者，朝錯天子用事臣，變更高皇帝法令，侵奪諸侯地。
entries.en: On his knees Ang said, “Chao Cuo rules the court, rewrites Gaozu’s statutes, and gnaws at princely fiefs.
entries.literal: The king, knocking his head and crawling on his knees, replied, “At present Chao Cuo is the minister in charge at the Son of Heaven's side; he has altered the laws of the August Emperor Gaozu and seized the princes' lands.

entries.zh: 卬等以為不義，恐其敗亂天下，七國發兵，且以誅錯。
entries.en: We judged that wicked and feared he would wreck the realm; the seven kingdoms rose chiefly to kill Cuo.
entries.literal: Ang and the others deemed this unrighteous and feared he would ruin and disorder the realm; therefore the seven states raised troops, intending for the time being to execute Chao Cuo.

entries.zh: 今聞錯已誅，卬等謹已罷兵歸。」
entries.en: Word came that Cuo is dead; we have stood down and gone home.”
entries.literal: Now we hear Chao Cuo has already been executed; Ang and the others respectfully have already disbanded the army and returned.”

entries.zh: 將軍曰：「王苟以錯為不善，何不以聞？
entries.en: The general answered, “If Cuo was vile, why not memorialize the throne?
entries.literal: The general said, “If the king truly thought Chao Cuo unworthy, why did you not report it?

entries.zh: 及未有詔虎符，擅發兵擊義國。
entries.en: You had no rescript, no tally, yet you mobilized and struck loyal states.
entries.literal: Moreover, before there was an edict or tiger tally, you on your own raised troops and attacked loyal principalities.

entries.zh: 以此觀之，意非徒欲誅錯也。」
entries.en: That was never only about Cuo.”
entries.literal: Judging by this, your intent was not merely to execute Chao Cuo.”

entries.zh: 乃出詔書為王讀之，曰：「王其自圖之。」
entries.en: He drew out the imperial order and read it: “Decide your own fate.”
entries.literal: He then produced the edict and read it to the king, saying, “The king must decide for himself.”

entries.zh: 王曰：「如卬等死有餘罪。」
entries.en: Ang said, “Men like me deserve more than one death.”
entries.literal: The king said, “For men like Ang death still leaves surplus guilt.”

entries.zh: 遂自殺。
entries.en: He took his own life.
entries.literal: He then took his own life.

entries.zh: 太后、太子皆死。
entries.en: His mother and heir died with him.
entries.literal: The queen dowager and the heir both died.

entries.zh: 膠東、菑川、濟南王皆伏誅。
entries.en: Jiaodong, Zichuan, and Jinan were put to the sword.
entries.literal: The kings of Jiaodong, Zichuan, and Jinan were all executed according to law.

entries.zh: 酈將軍攻趙，十月而下之，趙王自殺。
entries.en: General Li took Zhao after a ten-month campaign, and the king of Zhao killed himself.
entries.literal: General Li attacked Zhao and took it after ten months; the King of Zhao committed suicide.

entries.zh: 濟北王以劫故，不誅。
entries.en: The King of Jibei was spared because he had been coerced.
entries.literal: The King of Jibei, on account of having been coerced, was not executed.

entries.zh: 孝景前三年正月甲子，初起兵於廣陵。
entries.en: On jiǎzǐ in the first month of Xiaojing’s third year the rebellion opened at Guangling.
entries.literal: On the jiǎzǐ day of the first month in the third year of Emperor Xiaojing, he first raised troops at Guangling.

entries.zh: 西涉淮，因并楚兵。
entries.en: He crossed the Huai westward and merged his columns with Chu’s host.
entries.literal: Westward he crossed the Huai and absorbed the Chu army.

entries.zh: 發使遺諸侯書曰：「吳王劉濞敬問膠西王、膠東王、菑川王、濟南王、趙王、楚王、淮南王、衡山王、廬江王、故長沙王子：幸教！
entries.en: His messengers carried a manifesto: “The king of Wu Liu Bi greets the kings of Jiaoxi, Jiaodong, Zichuan, Jinan, Zhao, Chu, Huainan, Hengshan, Lujiang, and the heir of old Changsha—may you instruct me!
entries.literal: He sent envoys bearing a letter to the princes: “Liu Bi, King of Wu, respectfully inquires of the kings of Jiaoxi, Jiaodong, Zichuan, Jinan, Zhao, Chu, Huainan, Hengshan, Lujiang, and the son of the former King of Changsha: I beg your counsel!

entries.zh: 以漢有賊臣錯，無功天下，侵奪諸侯之地，使吏劾繫訊治，以侵辱之為故，不以諸侯人君禮遇劉氏骨肉，絕先帝功臣，進任姦人，誑亂天下，欲危社稷。
entries.en: Han is ridden by the traitor Chao Cuo, a man without service to the empire who gnaws at princely fiefs, hounds nobles with indictments and chains, insults them by design, dishonors the Liu kin, casts aside Gaozu’s old ministers, elevates scoundrels, and would overturn the state.
entries.literal: Because Han harbors the traitorous minister Chao Cuo, who has won no merit for the realm yet seizes the princes' lands, sends officers to impeach, bind, and interrogate them, and makes deliberate humiliation his constant practice—he does not treat the Liu flesh and blood with the courtesy due princes, cuts off the founding emperor's meritorious servants, promotes villains, throws the realm into confusion, and would endanger the altars of soil and grain.

entries.zh: 陛下多病志逸，不能省察。
entries.en: The Son of Heaven is sick in body and distracted in will; he cannot see through the plot.
entries.literal: The sovereign is often ill in mind and body and cannot look into these matters.

entries.zh: 欲舉兵誅之，謹聞教。
entries.en: We mean to take up arms to put Cuo to the sword and await your orders.
entries.literal: We intend to raise arms to execute him and respectfully await your teaching.

entries.zh: 敝國雖狹，地方三千里；
entries.en: Wu is small, yet its territory runs three thousand li;
entries.literal: Our poor state though narrow still covers three thousand li of ground;

entries.zh: 人民雖少，精兵可具五十萬。
entries.en: its people are not numerous, yet half a million sharp soldiers can be armed.
entries.literal: our people though few can still equip five hundred thousand picked troops.

entries.zh: 寡人素事南越三十餘年，其王諸君皆不辭分其兵以隨寡人，又可得三十萬。
entries.en: I have dealt with Southern Yue for thirty years; its rulers will gladly detach troops to march with me and add another three hundred thousand blades.
entries.literal: For more than thirty years I have cultivated ties with Southern Yue; its kings and lords will not refuse to divide their forces and follow me—I can gain another three hundred thousand.

entries.zh: 寡人雖不肖，願以身從諸王。
entries.en: Unworthy as I am, I will take the field at your side.
entries.literal: Though I am unworthy, I would follow the kings in person.

entries.zh: 南越直長沙者，因王子定長沙以北，西走蜀、漢中。
entries.en: Southern Yue lies directly opposite Changsha; with its support, the son of the former king can secure the country north of Changsha and advance west into Shu and Hanzhong.
entries.literal: Southern Yue lies directly opposite Changsha; with its support, the son of the former king can secure the country north of Changsha and advance west into Shu and Hanzhong.

entries.zh: 告越、楚王、淮南三王，與寡人西面；
entries.en: Tell Yue, the king of Chu, and the three Huainan kings to wheel west with me;
entries.literal: Inform Yue, the King of Chu, and the three Huainan kings to march west with me;

entries.zh: 齊諸王與趙王定河間、河內，或入臨晉關，或與寡人會雒陽；
entries.en: let the Qi princes and the king of Zhao take Hejian and Henei—some to force Linjin Pass, others to meet me at Luoyang;
entries.literal: the kings of Qi with the King of Zhao shall secure Hejian and Henei, either enter Linjin Pass or rendezvous with me at Luoyang;

entries.zh: 燕王、趙王故與胡王有約，燕王北定代、雲中，轉胡眾入蕭關，走長安，匡正天下，以安高廟。
entries.en: Yan and Zhao long ago pledged the steppe lords: Yan shall pacify Dai and Yunzhong in the north, swing the nomad horse through Xiaoguan toward Chang’an, set the realm right, and guard Gaozu’s shrine.
entries.literal: the Kings of Yan and Zhao formerly had covenants with the Hu king—the King of Yan shall secure north Dai and Yunzhong, wheel the Hu hosts through Xiaoguan toward Chang'an, rectify the realm, and settle the Founder Temple.

entries.zh: 願王勉之。
entries.en: I urge every king to bend his utmost.
entries.literal: I pray the kings will exert themselves.

entries.zh: 楚元王子、淮南三王或不沐洗十餘年，怨入骨髓，欲壹有所出久矣，寡人未得諸王之意，未敢聽。
entries.en: Among the sons of King Yuan of Chu and the three kings of Huainan, some have gone more than ten years without washing or bathing. Resentment runs to their marrow, and they have long wanted one chance to vent it; I have not yet learned the princes’ intentions and have not dared heed them.
entries.literal: Among the sons of King Yuan of Chu and the three kings of Huainan, some have gone more than ten years without washing or bathing; resentment runs to their marrow, and they have long wanted a single chance to let it out. I have not yet learned the princes' intentions and have not dared heed them.

entries.zh: 今諸王苟能存亡繼絕，振弱伐暴，以安劉氏，社稷所願也。
entries.en: If you can preserve those facing destruction, restore broken lines, aid the weak, and punish the violent so as to secure the Liu house, you will fulfill the desire of the state.
entries.literal: If the princes can preserve those facing destruction, continue broken lines, aid the weak, and punish the violent, thereby securing the Liu house, that is what the altars of state desire.

entries.zh: 吳國雖貧，寡人節衣食用，積金錢，脩兵革，聚糧食，夜以繼日，三十餘年矣。
entries.en: Wu is poor, yet thirty years I have pinched my table and wardrobe, piled gold, forged arms, stored grain, and toiled from dusk to dawn.
entries.literal: Wu though poor—for thirty years I have stinted my dress and food, hoarded gold and cash, readied armor and weapons, gathered grain, worked night into day.

entries.zh: 凡皆為此，願諸王勉之。
entries.en: Everything I have done aims at this hour—again, I beg you to strive.
entries.literal: All of it has been for this; I pray the kings will exert themselves.

entries.zh: 能斬捕大將者，賜金五千斤，封萬戶；
entries.en: Strike down an enemy commander-in-chief and you take five thousand catties of gold and a ten-thousand-household marquisate;
entries.literal: Whoever beheads or captures a grand general shall receive five thousand catties of gold and a fief of ten thousand households;

entries.zh: 列將，三千斤，封五千戶；
entries.en: a corps commander earns three thousand catties and five thousand households;
entries.literal: a column commander, three thousand catties and a fief of five thousand households;

entries.zh: 裨將，二千斤，封二千戶；
entries.en: a lieutenant-general earns two thousand catties and two thousand households;
entries.literal: a deputy commander, two thousand catties and a fief of two thousand households;

entries.zh: 二千石，千斤，封千戶：皆為列侯。
entries.en: any two-thousand-picul officer brings a thousand catties and a thousand-household fief—all such men become full marquises.
entries.literal: an official of two thousand piculs, one thousand catties and a fief of one thousand households—all shall be full marquises.

entries.zh: 其以軍若城邑降者，卒萬人，邑萬戶，如得大將；
entries.en: Surrender a host or a city: ten thousand soldiers and ten thousand households earn the reward for capturing a commander-in-chief;
entries.literal: Those who surrender with an army or a walled city: for ten thousand soldiers and a town of ten thousand households, reward as for capturing a grand general;

entries.zh: 人戶五千，如得列將；
entries.en: five thousand households earn a corps commander’s reward;
entries.literal: five thousand households as for capturing a column commander;

entries.zh: 人戶三千，如得裨將；
entries.en: three thousand households earn a lieutenant-general’s reward;
entries.literal: three thousand households as for capturing a deputy commander;

entries.zh: 人戶千，如得二千石；
entries.en: one thousand households matches the reward for a two-thousand-picul captive;
entries.literal: one thousand households as for capturing an official of two thousand piculs;

entries.zh: 其小吏皆以差次受爵金。
entries.en: junior ranks receive titles and gold by graded steps.
entries.literal: lesser officers shall receive rank and gold in graduated order.

entries.zh: 它封賜皆倍軍法。
entries.en: Every other bounty runs at twice the usual army scale.
entries.literal: All other enfeoffments and gifts shall double the military ordinance scale.

entries.zh: 其有故爵邑者，更益勿因。
entries.en: Men who already hold rank or fiefs will receive further rewards without limit from their existing holdings.
entries.literal: Those who already hold noble rank or fiefs shall receive additional grants without being restricted by their existing holdings.

entries.zh: 願諸王明以令士大夫，不敢欺也。
entries.en: Publish these terms plainly to your officers and men; I would not deceive them.
entries.literal: I pray the kings will clearly publish these terms to their officers and men; I would not deceive them.

entries.zh: 寡人金錢在天下者往往而有，非必取於吳，諸王日夜用之不能盡。
entries.en: My treasure lies everywhere under heaven, not only in Wu; spend it night and day—you cannot empty it.
entries.literal: My gold and cash are scattered throughout the realm and need not be drawn only from Wu; the kings may spend them day and night without exhausting them.

entries.zh: 有當賜者告寡人，寡人且往遺之。
entries.en: Name the worthy and I will ride to hand them their share.
entries.literal: When any are due reward, inform me and I will go in person to bestow it.

entries.zh: 敬以聞。」
entries.en: So I report, with respect.”
entries.literal: Respectfully submitted for your hearing.”

entries.zh: 澤王琅邪二年，而太后崩，澤乃曰：「帝少，諸呂用事，諸劉孤弱。」
entries.en: In Liu Ze's second year as king of Langye, the empress dowager died. Ze said, "The emperor is young, the Lü clan controls affairs, and the Liu house is isolated and weak."
entries.literal: In the second year of Liu Ze's reign as king of Langye, the empress dowager died. Ze said, "The emperor is young, the Lü clan holds power, and the Liu are isolated and weak."

entries.zh: 引兵與齊王合謀西，欲誅諸呂。
entries.en: He led his troops to join the King of Qi in plotting a westward march to execute the Lü.
entries.literal: He led his troops to join the King of Qi in plotting a westward march to execute the Lü.

entries.zh: 至梁，聞漢灌將軍屯滎陽，澤還兵備西界，遂跳驅至長安。
entries.en: When he reached Liang, he heard that the Han general Guan Ying was encamped at Xingyang. Ze turned his troops back to guard the western border and then hurried on to Chang'an.
entries.literal: Reaching Liang, he heard that General Guan Ying of Han was encamped at Xingyang. Ze turned his army to guard the western frontier and dashed post-haste to Chang'an.

entries.zh: 代王亦從代至。
entries.en: The King of Dai also came from Dai.
entries.literal: The King of Dai also came from Dai.

entries.zh: 諸將相與琅邪王共立代王，是為孝文帝。
entries.en: The generals and ministers together with the king of Langye enthroned the King of Dai, who became Emperor Wen of Han.
entries.literal: The generals and ministers together with the king of Langye enthroned the King of Dai, who became Emperor Wen of Han.

entries.zh: 文帝元年，徙澤為燕王，而復以琅邪歸齊。
entries.en: In the first year of Emperor Wen, Ze was transferred to be king of Yan, and Langye was returned to Qi.
entries.literal: In the first year of Emperor Wen, Ze was transferred to be king of Yan, and Langye was returned to Qi.

entries.zh: 澤王燕二年，薨，諡曰敬王。
entries.en: In the second year of Ze's reign as king of Yan, he died; his posthumous title was King Jing.
entries.literal: In the second year of Ze's reign as king of Yan, he died; his posthumous title was King Jing.

entries.zh: 子康王嘉嗣，九年薨。
entries.en: His son King Kang Jia succeeded him; after nine years he died.
entries.literal: His son King Kang Jia succeeded him; after nine years he died.

entries.zh: 子定國嗣。
entries.en: His son Dingguo succeeded.
entries.literal: His son Dingguo succeeded.

entries.zh: 定國與父康王姬姦，生子男一人。
entries.en: Dingguo committed incest with his father King Kang's concubine and had one male child.
entries.literal: Dingguo committed incest with his father King Kang's concubine and had one male child.

entries.zh: 奪弟妻為姬。
entries.en: He seized his younger brother's wife as a concubine.
entries.literal: He seized his younger brother's wife as a concubine.

entries.zh: 與子女三人姦。
entries.en: He committed incest with three of his children.
entries.literal: He committed incest with three of his children.

entries.zh: 定國有所欲誅殺臣肥如令郢人，郢人等告定國。
entries.en: Dingguo wished to execute his minister Yingren, the magistrate of Feiru. Yingren and others reported Dingguo.
entries.literal: Dingguo wished to execute his minister Yingren, the magistrate of Feiru. Yingren and others reported Dingguo.

entries.zh: 定國使謁者以它法劾捕格殺郢人滅口。
entries.en: Dingguo sent an usher to impeach and arrest Yingren on another charge and beat him to death to silence him.
entries.literal: Dingguo sent an usher to impeach and arrest Yingren on another charge and beat him to death to silence him.

entries.zh: 至元朔中，郢人昆弟復上書具言定國事。
entries.en: In the Yuanshuo era, Yingren's brothers again submitted a memorial detailing Dingguo's crimes.
entries.literal: In the Yuanshuo era, Yingren's brothers again submitted a memorial detailing Dingguo's crimes.

entries.zh: 下公卿，皆議曰：「定國禽獸行，亂人倫，逆天道，當誅。」
entries.en: The matter was sent down to the dukes and ministers, and they all judged, "Dingguo behaves like a beast. He has thrown human relations into disorder and gone against the Way of Heaven; he should be executed."
entries.literal: The case went to the lords and ministers, who all deliberated: "Dingguo's conduct is that of a beast; he disorders human relations, violates Heaven's Way, and should be executed."

entries.zh: 上許之。
entries.en: The emperor approved it.
entries.literal: The emperor approved it.

entries.zh: 定國自殺，立四十二年，國除。
entries.en: Dingguo killed himself. The state had stood forty-two years and was abolished.
entries.literal: Dingguo killed himself. The state had stood forty-two years and was abolished.

entries.zh: 哀帝時繼絕世，乃封敬王澤玄孫之孫無終公士歸生為營陵侯，更始中為兵所殺。
entries.en: In Emperor Ai's time, the court continued the broken line by enfeoffing Guisheng of Wuzhong, a holder of the Gongshi rank and grandson of a great-great-grandson of King Jing Liu Ze, as marquis of Yingling. He was killed by soldiers during the Gengshi era.
entries.literal: In Emperor Ai's time, to continue the broken line, Guisheng of Wuzhong, who held the rank of Gongshi and was the grandson of a great-great-grandson of King Jing Liu Ze, was enfeoffed as marquis of Yingling; during the Gengshi era he was killed by soldiers.

entries.zh: 會孝惠、高后時天下初定，郡國諸侯各務自拊循其民。
entries.en: In the Xiaohui and Empress Gao years, with the realm just settled, each regional lord strove to win the goodwill of his subjects.
entries.literal: During the reigns of Emperor Xiaohui and Empress Gao, when the land was newly pacified, every prince and marquis devoted himself to comforting his people.

entries.zh: 吳有豫章郡銅山，即招致天下亡命者盜鑄錢，東煮海水為鹽，以故無賦，國用饒足。
entries.en: Wu held the Yuzhang copper pits and drew runaways from every quarter to cast money illicitly; along the coast it boiled brine for salt. On that income it waived ordinary levies and the kingdom grew fabulously rich.
entries.literal: Wu controlled the copper mountains of Yuzhang and summoned fugitives from across the realm to mint coin in secret; eastward it boiled seawater for salt. It therefore levied no grain tax, and the royal treasury overflowed.

entries.zh: 孝文時，吳太子入見，得侍皇太子飲博。
entries.en: In Emperor Wen’s reign the crown prince of Wu attended court and was allowed to drink and play liubo with the imperial heir.
entries.literal: Under Emperor Xiaowen the Wu heir came to court and was admitted to drink and play liubo with the heir apparent.

entries.zh: 吳太子師傅皆楚人，輕悍，又素驕。
entries.en: The Wu heir’s tutors were all men of Chu, rash and fierce, while the heir himself had long been arrogant.
entries.literal: The Wu heir’s tutors were all men of Chu, rash and fierce, and the heir himself had long been arrogant.

entries.zh: 博爭道，不恭，皇太子引博局提吳太子，殺之。
entries.en: They quarreled over the rules; the Wu heir showed disrespect, and the crown prince seized the heavy board and struck him dead.
entries.literal: A dispute over a move in the game turned disrespectful; the imperial heir snatched up the gaming board and dashed it against the Wu prince, killing him.

entries.zh: 於是遣其喪歸葬吳。
entries.en: The court had the body sent home to Wu for burial.
entries.literal: The court therefore sent the corpse back to Wu for burial.

entries.zh: 吳王慍曰：「天下一宗，死長安即葬長安，何必來葬！」
entries.en: The king of Wu growled, “All under heaven are one clan; if he died in Chang’an he should lie in Chang’an—why drag him back to Wu?”
entries.literal: The king of Wu said bitterly, “The realm is one family; if he died in Chang’an, let him be buried in Chang’an—why send him back here?”

entries.zh: 復遣喪之長安葬。
entries.en: The remains were forwarded to Chang’an for interment.
entries.literal: They sent the remains back to Chang’an for burial after all.

entries.zh: 吳王由是怨望，稍失藩臣禮，稱疾不朝。
entries.en: From then on Liu Bi harbored resentment, slackened the ritual due from a vassal, pleaded sickness, and stayed away from audience.
entries.literal: From that day Liu Bi nursed a grudge. He gradually neglected the courtesies owed a vassal, feigned illness, and stopped coming to court.

entries.zh: 京師知其以子故，驗問實不病，諸吳使來，輒繫責治之。
entries.en: The court understood the slight was about his son; investigations showed he was not ill, and Wu envoys were routinely seized and chastised.
entries.literal: The capital knew it was about his son; inquiries proved he was not sick, so whenever envoys arrived from Wu they were detained and punished.

entries.zh: 吳王恐，所謀滋甚。
entries.en: Fear drove him, and his plotting grew wilder.
entries.literal: The king grew afraid, and his schemes grew more desperate.

entries.zh: 及後使人為秋請，上復責問吳使者。
entries.en: Later, when Wu sent an envoy for the autumn audience, the emperor again questioned and rebuked him.
entries.literal: Later, when Wu sent a man for the autumn audience, the emperor again questioned and rebuked the Wu envoy.

entries.zh: 使者曰：「察見淵中魚，不祥。
entries.en: The messenger answered, “There is a saying: it is unlucky to see every fish in a clear pool.
entries.literal: The envoy replied, “It is ill luck to spy out every fish in a clear pool.

entries.zh: 今吳王始詐疾，反覺，見責急，愈益閉，恐上誅之，計乃無聊。
entries.en: Our king feigned illness; when that was seen through and blame piled on, he withdrew further, fearing the axe and finding no way out.
entries.literal: Our king first pretended sickness; once exposed, he was pressed so hard that he shut himself away all the more, dreading execution and seeing no honorable course left.

entries.zh: 唯上與更始。」
entries.en: We beg you to grant him a new beginning.”
entries.literal: We beg Your Majesty to give him a fresh start.”

entries.zh: 於是天子皆赦吳使者歸之，而賜吳王几杖，老，不朝。
entries.en: The Son of Heaven pardoned the envoys and sent them back, then gave the king of Wu a folding stool and staff in token of old age, freeing him from court calls.
entries.literal: The emperor pardoned Wu’s envoys and sent them home, then bestowed on the king of Wu an arm-rest and staff as tokens of age, exempting him from court attendance.

entries.zh: 吳得釋，其謀亦益解。
entries.en: With the pressure off, Wu relaxed, and the plot lost its edge.
entries.literal: With that pressure lifted, the king’s rebellious planning also eased.

entries.zh: 然其居國以銅鹽故，百姓無賦。
entries.en: Within his borders copper and salt still paid the bills, so the commoners owed no land tax.
entries.literal: Still, inside his kingdom the profits of coinage and salt meant that ordinary households paid no grain tax.

entries.zh: 卒踐更，輒予平賈。
entries.en: When militia duty fell due, he paid them the fair market rate.
entries.literal: Whenever commoners owed their annual labor service, he paid them the standard wage in cash.

entries.zh: 歲時存問茂材，賞賜閭里。
entries.en: At New Year and other seasons he looked in on promising men and scattered largesse through the neighborhoods.
entries.literal: At the festivals he visited local talent and showered gifts on whole villages.

entries.zh: 它郡國吏欲來捕亡人者，頌共禁不與。
entries.en: If officers from other commanderies came to seize fugitives, Wu authorities shielded them together and would not hand them over.
entries.literal: If officers from other jurisdictions came to arrest fugitives, the Wu authorities shielded them and refused cooperation.

entries.zh: 如此者三十餘年，以故能使其眾。
entries.en: He did this for over thirty years, and so won the hearts of his people.
entries.literal: For more than three decades he managed his people in this way, which is why he could command their loyalty.

entries.zh: 七國反書聞，天子乃遣太尉條侯周亞夫將三十六將軍往擊吳楚；
entries.en: News of the seven kingdoms’ revolt reached court; the emperor sent Grand Commandant Zhou Yafu of Tiaohou with thirty-six generals against Wu and Chu;
entries.literal: When word of the seven states' rebellion reached the throne, the Son of Heaven dispatched Grand Commandant Marquis of Tiaohou Zhou Yafu with thirty-six generals to strike Wu and Chu;

entries.zh: 遣曲周侯酈寄擊趙，將軍欒布擊齊，大將軍竇嬰屯滎陽監齊趙兵。
entries.en: he sent Li Ji, marquis of Quzhou, against Zhao and Luan Bu against Qi, while Grand General Dou Ying encamped at Xingyang to keep watch over the armies of Qi and Zhao.
entries.literal: he sent Marquis Li Ji of Quzhou against Zhao and General Luan Bu against Qi; Grand General Dou Ying encamped at Xingyang to keep watch over the Qi and Zhao armies.

entries.zh: 初，吳王之度淮，與楚王遂西敗棘壁，乘勝而前，銳甚。
entries.en: When Liu Bi crossed the Huai he and the king of Chu drove west, stormed the Han strongpoint at Ji, and swept on while their momentum was white-hot.
entries.literal: Earlier, when the King of Wu crossed the Huai, he and the King of Chu advanced west together, broke the Han fort at Ji, and pressed forward in the flush of victory—their edge was keen.

entries.zh: 梁孝王恐，遣將軍擊之，又敗梁兩軍，士卒皆還走。
entries.en: King Xiao of Liang sent a general; Wu-Chu broke two Liang hosts and the men fled.
entries.literal: King Xiao of Liang was afraid and sent a general against them; they again defeated two Liang armies and the soldiers all ran back.

entries.zh: 梁數使使條侯求救，條侯不許。
entries.en: Liang begged Zhou Yafu again and again; he refused.
entries.literal: Liang repeatedly sent envoys begging Zhou Yafu of Tiaohou for rescue; Zhou Yafu would not consent.

entries.zh: 又使使愬條侯於上，上使告條侯救梁，又守便宜不行。
entries.en: They complained to the throne; the emperor told him to relieve Liang, yet he clung to his plan and stayed put.
entries.literal: They also sent envoys to denounce Zhou Yafu to the emperor; the emperor ordered him to save Liang, yet he still held to tactical advantage and did not move.

entries.zh: 梁使韓安國及楚死事相弟張羽為將軍，乃得頗敗吳兵。
entries.en: Only when Liang made Han Anguo and Zhang Yu—the younger brother of Chu’s chancellor, who had died in service—generals could it begin to defeat Wu’s troops.
entries.literal: Liang then made Han Anguo and Zhang Yu, younger brother of Chu's chancellor who had died in service, generals; only then were they able to inflict some defeats on the Wu army.

entries.zh: 吳兵欲西，梁城守，不敢西，即走條侯軍，會下邑。
entries.en: Wu meant to drive west, but Liang held its cities and blocked the way. The rebels dared not push on, so they turned toward Zhou Yafu’s army and met it at Xiayi.
entries.literal: The Wu army wished to go west, but Liang defended its cities and they dared not advance; they therefore turned toward Zhou Yafu’s army and met it at Xiayi.

entries.zh: 欲戰，條侯壁，不肯戰。
entries.en: They clamored for a fight; Zhou Yafu stayed behind his walls and refused.
entries.literal: They wished to fight, but Zhou Yafu held fast behind his ramparts and would not give battle.

entries.zh: 吳糧絕，卒飢，數挑戰，遂夜奔條侯壁，驚東南。
entries.en: With supplies gone and the men starving, Wu repeatedly challenged Yafu to battle, then rushed his ramparts by night and feinted against the southeast.
entries.literal: Wu’s grain was cut off and its soldiers starved. They repeatedly challenged to battle, then rushed Zhou Yafu’s ramparts by night, making a feint against the southeast.

entries.zh: 條侯使備西北，果從西北。
entries.en: He had stacked his defense on the northwest; the feint failed and the real blow came there.
entries.literal: Zhou Yafu had prepared the northwest; they indeed came from the northwest.

entries.zh: 不得入，吳大敗，士卒多飢死叛散。
entries.en: They never breached the wall. Wu’s host collapsed; thousands starved or melted away.
entries.literal: They could not break in; Wu suffered great defeat, and many soldiers starved to death or deserted.

entries.zh: 於是吳王乃與其戲下壯士千人夜亡去，度淮走丹徒，保東越。
entries.en: Liu Bi slipped away at night with a thousand picked warriors from under his banner, crossed the Huai, made for Dantu, and took refuge with Eastern Yue.
entries.literal: The King of Wu then fled by night with a thousand picked warriors from under his banner, crossed the Huai, made his way to Dantu, and took refuge with Eastern Yue.

entries.zh: 東越兵可萬餘人，使人收聚亡卒。
entries.en: Eastern Yue could field more than ten thousand men, and Liu Bi sent agents to gather the remnants of his army.
entries.literal: Eastern Yue had perhaps more than ten thousand troops, and Liu Bi sent men to gather his scattered soldiers.

entries.zh: 漢使人以利啗東越，東越即紿吳王，吳王出勞軍，使人鏦殺吳王，盛其頭，馳傳以聞。
entries.en: Han bribed Eastern Yue, which then deceived Liu Bi. When he came out to address and reward the troops, assassins ran him through, packed up his head, and sent it by relay to the capital.
entries.literal: Han sent men to tempt Eastern Yue with rewards, and Eastern Yue then deceived the King of Wu. When he came out to comfort and reward the troops, they had him speared to death, placed his head in a container, and sent it by relay to report the news.

entries.zh: 吳王太子駒亡走閩越。
entries.en: Crown prince Ju fled into Minyue.
entries.literal: The Wu heir Ju fled to Minyue.

entries.zh: 吳王之棄軍亡也，軍遂潰，往往稍降太尉條侯及梁軍。
entries.en: Once the king bolted, his army unraveled; bands here and there gave themselves up to Zhou Yafu or to Liang.
entries.literal: When the King of Wu abandoned his army and fled, the army collapsed; in many places men gradually surrendered to Grand Commandant Zhou Yafu of Tiaohou and to Liang’s forces.

entries.zh: 楚王戊軍敗，自殺。
entries.en: Liu Wu, king of Chu, was broken in the field and took his own life.
entries.literal: King Wu of Chu, Liu Wu, was defeated in battle and committed suicide.

entries.zh: 初，吳楚反書聞，兵未發，竇嬰言故吳相爰盎。
entries.en: At first, when word of the Wu-Chu revolt arrived but troops had not yet marched, Dou Ying mentioned the former chancellor of Wu, Yuan Ang.
entries.literal: At first, when word of the Wu-Chu revolt arrived but troops had not yet been dispatched, Dou Ying spoke of the former chancellor of Wu, Yuan Ang.

entries.zh: 召入見，上問以吳楚之計，盎對曰：「吳楚相遺書，曰『賊臣朝錯擅適諸侯，削奪之地』，以故反，名為西共誅錯，復故地而罷。
entries.en: Yuan Ang was summoned to audience, and the emperor asked him about the plans of Wu and Chu. Ang replied, "Wu and Chu have exchanged letters saying, 'The wicked minister Chao Cuo has arbitrarily punished the feudal lords and stripped away their lands.' That is why they have rebelled. Their stated aim is to march west together, execute Chao Cuo, restore their former territories, and then disband.
entries.literal: Ang was summoned to audience. The emperor asked him about the Wu-Chu situation. Ang replied, "Wu and Chu have sent each other messages saying, 'The wicked minister Chao Cuo has wantonly punished the feudal lords and seized their lands.' For this reason they have rebelled, claiming to execute Chao Cuo together from the west and then restore their former territories and disband.

entries.zh: 方今計獨斬錯，發使赦七國，復其故地，則兵可毋血刃而俱罷。」
entries.en: The plan now is simply to execute Chao Cuo, send envoys to pardon the Seven States, and restore their former territories. Then the armies can all stand down without bloodying a blade."
entries.literal: At present the plan is simply to execute Chao Cuo, send envoys to pardon the Seven States, and restore their former territories—then the armies can both stand down without bloodshed."

entries.zh: 上從其議，遂斬錯。
entries.en: The emperor accepted his counsel and had Chao Cuo executed.
entries.literal: The emperor accepted his counsel and had Chao Cuo executed.

entries.zh: 語具在盎傳。
entries.en: The full account is given in Ang's biography.
entries.literal: The full account is given in Ang's biography.

entries.zh: 以盎為泰常，奉宗廟，使吳王，吳王弟子德侯為宗正，輔親戚。
entries.en: Yuan Ang was appointed Grand Master of Ceremonies, in charge of the ancestral temples, and sent as envoy to the King of Wu. The king's nephew, the Marquis of De, was made Director of the Imperial Clan to support the imperial relatives.
entries.literal: Ang was appointed Grand Master of Ceremonies to oversee the ancestral temples and was sent as envoy to the King of Wu. The King of Wu's nephew, the Marquis of De, was made Director of the Imperial Clan to assist the imperial kin.

entries.zh: 使至吳，吳楚兵已攻梁壁矣。
entries.en: When the envoy reached Wu, the Wu-Chu armies had already attacked the walls of Liang.
entries.literal: When the envoy reached Wu, the Wu-Chu armies had already attacked the walls of Liang.

entries.zh: 宗正以親故，先入見，諭吳王拜受詔。
entries.en: Because the Director of the Imperial Clan was a royal relative, he entered first to see the king and instructed him to bow and receive the edict.
entries.literal: As Director of the Imperial Clan and a royal kinsman, he entered first to see the king and instruct him to bow and receive the edict.

entries.zh: 吳王聞盎來，亦知其欲說，笑而應曰：「我已為東帝，尚誰拜？」
entries.en: When the King of Wu heard that Yuan Ang had arrived, he knew Ang intended to persuade him. He laughed and replied, "I have already become the Eastern Emperor. To whom else should I bow?"
entries.literal: When the King of Wu heard Ang had come, he knew he meant to persuade him. Laughing, he replied, "I have already become Eastern Emperor—whom else should I bow to?"

entries.zh: 不肯見盎而留軍中，欲劫使將。
entries.en: He refused to see Ang and kept him in the army camp, intending to coerce the envoy into becoming his general.
entries.literal: He refused to see Ang and kept him in the army camp, intending to coerce the envoy into becoming his general.

entries.zh: 盎不肯，使人圍守，且殺之。
entries.en: Ang refused. The king had men surround and guard him, about to kill him.
entries.literal: Ang refused. The king had men surround and guard him, about to kill him.

entries.zh: 盎得夜亡走梁，遂歸報。
entries.en: Ang fled by night to Liang and returned to report.
entries.literal: Ang fled by night to Liang and returned to report.

entries.zh: 漢廷臣方議削吳，吳王恐削地無已，因欲發謀舉事。
entries.en: As the Han court debated carving up Wu, the king dreaded endless reductions and meant to launch his plot.
entries.literal: When Han ministers debated stripping Wu of land, Liu Bi feared endless confiscations and resolved to act on his conspiracy.

entries.zh: 念諸侯無足與計者，聞膠西王勇，好兵，諸侯皆畏憚之，於是乃使中大夫應高口說膠西王曰：「吳王不肖，有夙夜之憂，不敢自外，使使臣諭其愚心。」
entries.en: He found no other prince fit to conspire with, but heard that the king of Jiaoxi was brave and warlike and that the other lords all feared him. He therefore sent Palace Counsellor Ying Gao with an oral message: “The king of Wu, unworthy as he is, lies awake at night with worry; he dares not keep you at arm’s length and sends me to voice his humble heart.”
entries.literal: He saw no peer among the other princes with whom to conspire. Learning that the king of Jiaoxi was bold and loved war, and that the other lords all stood in awe of him, he dispatched Palace Counsellor Ying Gao to sound him out without a written memorial. Ying Gao said on the Wu king’s behalf, “Our unworthy sovereign carries a constant anxiety and cannot treat you as a stranger; he sends me to lay his humble thoughts before you.”

entries.zh: 王曰：「何以教之？」
entries.en: The king said, “What would you teach me?”
entries.literal: The king asked, “What counsel do you bring?”

entries.zh: 高曰：「今者主上任用邪臣，聽信讒賊，變更律令，侵削諸侯，徵求滋多，誅罰良重，日以益甚。
entries.en: Ying Gao said, “The sovereign now trusts wicked ministers, heeds slanderers, alters laws and orders, gnaws at the kingdoms, heaps new demands, and punishes with growing severity—worse every day.
entries.literal: Gao said, “The throne now rests in the hands of treacherous ministers who spread slander, who endlessly revise statutes, whittle away the princely domains, multiply exactions, and pile cruel punishments upon good men—each day worse than the last.

entries.zh: 語有之曰：「舐糠及米。」
entries.en: There is a proverb: ‘Lick the chaff and you reach the grain.’
entries.literal: There is an old saying: ‘Lick the bran off the grain and you will taste the rice.’

entries.zh: 吳與膠西，知名諸侯也，一時見察，不得安肆矣。
entries.en: Wu and Jiaoxi are famous states; once we fall under close scrutiny we can never again live at ease.
entries.literal: Wu and Jiaoxi are celebrated kingdoms; the moment the court turns a harsh eye on us, we shall no longer live at ease.

entries.zh: 吳王身有內疾，不能朝請二十餘年，常患見疑，無以自白，脅肩絫足，猶懼不見釋。
entries.en: For more than twenty years the king of Wu has suffered from an internal ailment and been unable to attend court. He has always feared suspicion, with no way to clear his name; even as he shrinks and cringes, he still fears he will not be forgiven.
entries.literal: For more than twenty years our king has suffered from an internal ailment and been unable to attend court; he has long dreaded suspicion with no way to clear himself. Even hunched in fear, he still dreads that he may not be pardoned.

entries.zh: 竊聞大王以爵事有過，所聞諸侯削地，罪不至此，此恐不止削地而已。」
entries.en: I hear Your Majesty committed an offense in the sale of noble ranks. The territorial reductions imposed on the princes go beyond what their crimes warrant; I fear the court will not stop at taking land.”
entries.literal: I hear Your Majesty committed an offense in the matter of selling noble ranks. The territorial reductions imposed on other princes exceed what their crimes warrant; I fear this will not stop with land alone.”

entries.zh: 王曰：「有之，子將柰何？」
entries.en: The king said, “That is true. What then?”
entries.literal: The king replied, “It is so. What would you have me do?”

entries.zh: 高曰：「同惡相助，同好相留，同情相求，同欲相趨，同利相死。
entries.en: “Those who hate the same foe help one another; those who love the same ends keep one another; those who feel the same seek one another; those who desire the same flock together; those who profit together die for one another.
entries.literal: “Shared hatred brings mutual aid, shared likes mutual shelter, shared sentiment mutual pursuit, shared appetite mutual rush, shared gain brings men to die for one another.

entries.zh: 今吳王自以與大王同憂，願因時循理，棄軀以除患於天下，意亦可乎？」
entries.en: The king of Wu thinks he shares your danger and wishes to seize the hour in good order—to stake his life and wipe this evil from the realm. Would that suit you?”
entries.literal: Now the King of Wu believes he shares your peril and wishes to seize the moment in good order—to hazard himself and rid the realm of this scourge. Would that suit your mind?”

entries.zh: 膠西王瞿然駭曰：「寡人何敢如是？
entries.en: The king of Jiaoxi started, aghast: “How should I dare such a thing?
entries.literal: The King of Jiaoxi started in alarm: “How could I presume to anything of the kind?

entries.zh: 主上雖急，固有死耳，安得不事？」
entries.en: The sovereign may drive me hard, but there is still only death at the end—how could I fail to serve him?”
entries.literal: The Son of Heaven may press me hard, but at worst there is always death; how could I refuse to serve him?”

entries.zh: 高曰：「御史大夫朝錯熒惑天子，侵奪諸侯，蔽忠塞賢，朝廷疾怨，諸侯皆有背叛之意，人事極矣。
entries.en: Ying Gao said, “Grandee Secretary Chao Cuo dazzles the Son of Heaven, strips the feudatories, blocks the loyal and worthy, so that the court boils with anger and every prince nurses rebellion. The crisis is complete.
entries.literal: Gao answered, “Grandee Secretary Chao Cuo dazzles the sovereign, carves up the princes, silences loyal men and worthy advisors, until both court and kingdoms seethe with resentment and every prince harbors thoughts of revolt. Human patience is stretched to the limit.
