entries.zh: 彗星出，蝗蟲起，此萬世一時，而愁勞，聖人所以起也。
entries.en: Comets appear and locusts swarm—a moment that comes once in ten thousand generations; when the realm is full of grief and toil, that is when a man of worth rises up.
entries.literal: Comets streak the sky and locust clouds rise—such a conjunction comes once in an age; when the people are vexed and weary, that is when a sage-hero rises.

entries.zh: 吳王內以朝錯為誅，外從大王後車，方洋天下，所向者降，所指者下，莫敢不服。
entries.en: The king of Wu will move first against Chao Cuo under the banner of clearing the court; abroad he would march in your wake, sweeping the realm until every place you face surrenders and every host you point at falls—none would dare resist.
entries.literal: The King of Wu will take the execution of Chao Cuo as his opening demand in the heartland; in the field he would follow at Your Majesty’s chariot-wheel, roaming the realm so that every city that faces him yields and every army he points at kneels. Who would dare refuse?

entries.zh: 大王誠幸而許之一言，則吳王率楚王略函谷關，守滎陽敖倉之粟，距漢兵，治次舍，須大王。
entries.en: If you will but nod once, the king of Wu will lead the king of Chu to seize Hangu Pass, guard the grain at Ao Granary by Xingyang, hold the Han armies at bay, pitch camp, and wait for you.
entries.literal: If Your Majesty will but pledge a single word, the King of Wu will march with the King of Chu to seize Hangu Pass, hold the grain of Ao Granary at Xingyang, block the imperial armies, prepare encampments, and await your arrival.

entries.zh: 大王幸而臨之，則天下可并，兩主分割，不亦可乎？」
entries.en: If you then join him in person, the world may be shared and the two thrones split—would that not be well?”
entries.literal: If you then ride to join him, the empire can be seized and the two of you might divide it between yourselves—would that not serve?”

entries.zh: 王曰：「善。」
entries.en: The king said, “Good.”
entries.literal: “Good!” said the king.

entries.zh: 歸報吳王，猶恐其不果，乃身自為使者，至膠西面約之。
entries.en: Ying Gao reported back, but the king of Wu still feared that the king of Jiaoxi might waver, so he traveled there himself to seal the agreement face to face.
entries.literal: Ying Gao returned his report, yet the Wu king still doubted his commitment and went in person as envoy to Jiaoxi to conclude the pact face to face.

entries.zh: 諸侯既新削罰，震恐，多怨錯。
entries.en: The princes, newly shorn by edict, were shaken and for the most part hated Chao Cuo.
entries.literal: The princes, fresh from punitive confiscations, trembled with fear and for the most part blamed Chao Cuo.

entries.zh: 乃削吳會稽、豫章郡書至，則吳王先起兵，誅漢吏二千石以下。
entries.en: When the rescript arrived stripping Wu of Kuaiji and Yuzhang, the king of Wu was the first to raise troops and execute every Han officer from two-thousand-picul rank downward.
entries.literal: When the edict ordering Wu to surrender the commanderies of Kuaiji and Yuzhang reached him, the King of Wu was first to rise in arms and put every Han official of two-thousand-picul rank and below to the sword.

entries.zh: 膠西、膠東、菑川、濟南、楚、趙亦皆反，發兵西。
entries.en: Jiaoxi, Jiaodong, Zichuan, Jinan, Chu, and Zhao rose as well, each sending armies toward the west.
entries.literal: Jiaoxi, Jiaodong, Zichuan, Jinan, Chu, and Zhao likewise rebelled and raised troops westward.

entries.zh: 齊王後悔，背約城守。
entries.en: The king of Qi had second thoughts, abandoned the pact, and shut himself behind his walls.
entries.literal: The King of Qi repented, broke the covenant, and defended his city.

entries.zh: 濟北王城壞未完，其郎中令劫守王，不得發兵。
entries.en: Jibei’s ramparts were still in ruins; his gentleman of the palace took him hostage, and no troops could be raised.
entries.literal: The King of Jibei's walls were damaged and not yet finished; his chief of the gentlemen-of-the-palace seized and held the king, so he could not mobilize.

entries.zh: 膠西王、膠東王為渠率，與菑川、濟南共攻圍臨菑。
entries.en: The kings of Jiaoxi and Jiaodong led the host, and with Zichuan and Jinan jointly invested Linzi.
entries.literal: The kings of Jiaoxi and Jiaodong served as commanders-in-chief and, with Zichuan and Jinan together, attacked and besieged Linzi.

entries.zh: 趙王遂亦陰使匈奴與連兵。
entries.en: King Zhao Sui likewise sent secret word to the Xiongnu to join forces.
entries.literal: King Zhao Sui also secretly sent to the Xiongnu to link armies.

entries.zh: 季布，楚人也，為任俠有名。
entries.en: Ji Bu was a native of Chu who had won renown as a knight-errant.
entries.literal: Ji Bu was a man of Chu; as a knight-errant he had a reputation.

entries.zh: 項籍使將兵，數窘漢王。
entries.en: Xiang Yu put him in command of troops, and time and again he cornered the King of Han.
entries.literal: Xiang Ji had him lead troops, and he repeatedly embarrassed the King of Han.

entries.zh: 項籍滅，高祖購求布千金，敢有舍匿，罪三族。
entries.en: After Xiang Yu fell, Gaozu posted a reward of a thousand pounds of gold for Ji Bu, with death for three generations of kin for anyone who dared hide him.
entries.literal: When Xiang Ji was destroyed, Gaozu offered a thousand catties of gold for Ji Bu; whoever dared shelter or conceal him would suffer punishment extending to three kin groups.

entries.zh: 布匿濮陽周氏，周氏曰：「漢求將軍急，跡且至臣家，能聽臣，臣敢進計；
entries.en: Ji Bu took refuge with the Zhou clan of Puyang. They told him, "The Han are hunting you relentlessly; their agents will soon be at my door. If you will trust me, I have a plan to propose;
entries.literal: Bu hid with the Zhou family of Puyang. The Zhou family said, "The Han search for the general is urgent; the trail will soon reach my house. If you can heed me, I dare advance a plan;

entries.zh: 即否，願先自剄。」
entries.en: if not, I would rather slit my own throat first."
entries.literal: if not, I wish first to cut my own throat."

entries.zh: 布許之。
entries.en: Ji Bu agreed.
entries.literal: Bu assented to it.

entries.zh: 乃髡鉗布，衣褐，置廣柳車中，并與其家僮數十人，之魯朱家所賣之。
entries.en: They shaved his head, clamped him in the convict's collar, dressed him in a laborer's hemp, stowed him in a funeral cart with several dozen household servants, and drove him to Zhu Jia of Lu to be sold off as a slave.
entries.literal: Thereupon they shaved his head and put the iron collar on Bu, clothed him in coarse cloth, placed him in a broad-willow cart, together with several tens of his household slaves, and went to the place of Zhu Jia of Lu to sell him.

entries.zh: 朱家心知其季布也，買置田舍。
entries.en: Zhu Jia recognized him at once as Ji Bu, bought him, and lodged him on a country estate.
entries.literal: Zhu Jia in his heart knew he was Ji Bu; he bought him and placed him in a field house.

entries.zh: 乃之雒陽見汝陰侯滕公，說曰：「季布何罪？
entries.en: Then he traveled to Luoyang to see Xiahou Ying, the Marquis of Ru-yin, and argued, "What wrong has Ji Bu done?
entries.literal: Thereupon he went to Luoyang to see the Marquis of Ru-yin, Lord Teng, and urged him, saying, "What crime has Ji Bu committed?

entries.zh: 臣各為其主用，職耳。
entries.en: Ministers serve their own lords—that is simply what duty requires.
entries.literal: Ministers each for their lord are employed; it is duty only.

entries.zh: 項氏臣豈可盡誅邪？
entries.en: Are we to execute every man who once served the house of Xiang?
entries.literal: The Xiang clan's ministers—how can they all be executed?

entries.zh: 今上始得天下，而以私怨求一人，何示不廣也！
entries.en: The Son of Heaven has only just won the realm; to hound one man out of personal spite shows a narrowness ill befitting his position.
entries.literal: Now the sovereign has just obtained the empire, yet by private resentment seeks one man—what a narrow show this makes!

entries.zh: 且以季布之賢，漢求之急如此，此不北走胡，南走越耳。
entries.en: A man of Ji Bu's caliber, pressed this hard, will flee north to the Xiongnu or south to Nanyue.
entries.literal: Moreover, by Ji Bu's worthiness, the Han's search for him being so urgent—this is nothing but fleeing north to the Hu or fleeing south to Yue.

entries.zh: 夫忌壯士以資敵國，此伍子胥所以鞭荊平之墓也。
entries.en: To drive a brave man into the arms of a rival is the sort of blunder that made Wu Zixu flog the grave of King Ping of Chu.
entries.literal: As for driving away a brave man so as to aid an enemy state—this is why Wu Zixu whipped the tomb of King Ping of Chu.

entries.zh: 君何不從容為上言之？」
entries.en: Why not find a tactful moment and put this to the emperor yourself?"
entries.literal: Why do you not speak of this to the sovereign at your leisure?"

entries.zh: 滕公心知朱家大俠，意布匿其所，乃許諾。
entries.en: Xiahou Ying knew Zhu Jia for a famous man of chivalry and guessed Ji Bu lay hidden with him; he agreed to speak.
entries.literal: Lord Teng in his heart knew Zhu Jia was a great knight-errant; he suspected Bu was hidden at his place; thereupon he promised.

entries.zh: 侍間，果言如朱家指。
entries.en: When a suitable occasion came, he repeated Zhu Jia's argument to the throne.
entries.literal: Waiting for an interval, he indeed spoke as Zhu Jia had indicated.

entries.zh: 上乃赦布。
entries.en: The emperor then granted Ji Bu a full pardon.
entries.literal: The sovereign thereupon pardoned Bu.

entries.zh: 當是時，諸公皆多布能摧剛為柔，朱家亦以此名聞當世。
entries.en: Men of rank admired Ji Bu for bending unyielding pride into survival, and Zhu Jia's name rang through the age for it.
entries.literal: At this time, the various lords all praised Bu for being able to break hardness and make softness; Zhu Jia also by this had his name heard in that age.

entries.zh: 布召見，謝，拜郎中。
entries.en: Ji Bu was summoned to court, thanked the emperor, and was appointed a gentleman of the palace.
entries.literal: Bu was summoned and seen; he thanked; he was appointed gentleman of the palace.

entries.zh: 布母弟丁公，為項羽將，逐窘高祖彭城西。
entries.en: Ji Bu's maternal uncle Ding Gong, a general under Xiang Yu, had pressed Gaozu hard west of Pengcheng.
entries.literal: Ji Bu's maternal uncle Ding Gong, being Xiang Yu's general, pursued and cornered Gaozu west of Pengcheng.

entries.zh: 短兵接，漢王急，顧謂丁公曰：「兩賢豈相厄哉！」
entries.en: In close combat the King of Han was desperate; turning to Ding Gong he cried, "Must two able men try to destroy each other?"
entries.literal: Short weapons met; the King of Han was in straits; looking back he said to Ding Gong, "Two worthies—how could they mutually obstruct!"

entries.zh: 丁公引兵而還。
entries.en: Ding Gong withdrew his troops.
entries.literal: Ding Gong led the troops and returned.

entries.zh: 及項王滅，丁公謁見高祖，以丁公徇軍中，曰：「丁公為項王臣不忠，使項王失天下者也。」
entries.en: After Xiang Yu fell, Ding Gong came to pay his respects; Gaozu had him paraded before the host and declared, "Ding Gong was a faithless servant to his king; he helped cost Xiang Yu the empire."
entries.literal: When King Xiang was destroyed, Ding Gong had audience with Gaozu; Gaozu had Ding Gong paraded before the army, saying, "Ding Gong as King Xiang's minister was not loyal; he is one who made King Xiang lose the empire."

entries.zh: 遂斬之，曰：「使後為人臣無傚丁公也！」
entries.en: He had him executed, saying, "Let no future minister take Ding Gong as his model!"
entries.literal: Thereupon he beheaded him, saying, "Cause those after who are people's ministers not to imitate Ding Gong!"

entries.zh: 孝惠時，為中郎將。
entries.en: Under Emperor Hui he rose to general of the palace gentlemen.
entries.literal: In the time of Emperor Xiaohui, he was general of the gentlemen of the palace.

entries.zh: 單于嘗為書嫚呂太后，太后怒，召諸將議之。
entries.en: The Chanyu had once sent a letter that insulted Empress Dowager Lü; enraged, she called her generals in council.
entries.literal: The Chanyu once made a letter insulting Empress Dowager Lü; the empress dowager was angry and summoned the various generals to deliberate on it.

entries.zh: 上將軍樊噲曰：「臣願得十萬眾，橫行匈奴中。」
entries.en: Fan Kuai, the senior general, declared, "Give me a hundred thousand men and I will sweep through the heart of the Xiongnu steppe."
entries.literal: Senior General Fan Kuai said, "Your servant wishes to obtain a hundred thousand men and rampage through the middle of the Xiongnu."

entries.zh: 諸將皆阿呂太后，以噲言為然。
entries.en: The generals, eager to please the empress dowager, pronounced Fan Kuai right.
entries.literal: The various generals all fawned on Empress Dowager Lü and took Kuai's words as correct.

entries.zh: 布曰：「樊噲可斬也。
entries.en: Ji Bu said, "Fan Kuai deserves execution.
entries.literal: Bu said, "Fan Kuai can be beheaded.

entries.zh: 夫以高帝兵三十餘萬，困於平城，噲時亦在其中。
entries.en: Gaozu himself led over three hundred thousand men and was trapped at Pingcheng—and Fan Kuai was in that army.
entries.literal: As for by Gaozu's troops of more than three hundred thousand being trapped at Pingcheng, at that time Kuai also was within them.

entries.zh: 今噲奈何以十萬眾橫行匈奴中，面謾！
entries.en: How dare he now boast that a mere hundred thousand could ride roughshod over the Xiongnu? He is lying to your faces!
entries.literal: Now how can Kuai with a hundred thousand men rampage through the middle of the Xiongnu—lying to your faces!

entries.zh: 且秦以事胡，陳勝等起。
entries.en: Moreover, the Qin empire crumbled in part because it exhausted itself on the northern frontier, and Chen Sheng rose in rebellion.
entries.literal: Moreover, because Qin exhausted itself on affairs with the Hu, Chen Sheng and others rose in rebellion.

entries.zh: 今瘡痍未瘳，噲又面諛，欲搖動天下。」
entries.en: The realm is still bleeding from those wars, and Fan Kuai flatters you to your face and would unsettle the whole empire again."
entries.literal: Now the wounds are not yet healed, and Kuai again to the face flatters, wishing to shake and move the empire."

entries.zh: 是時殿上皆恐，太后罷朝，遂不復議擊匈奴事。
entries.en: A chill fell over the hall; the empress dowager adjourned court and never again brought up war on the Xiongnu.
entries.literal: At this time everyone in the hall was fearful; the empress dowager dismissed court and thereupon no longer deliberated on attacking the Xiongnu.

entries.zh: 孝文帝初立，召叔問曰：「公知天下長者乎？」
entries.en: Soon after Emperor Wen took the throne, he summoned Tian Shu and asked, "Sir, can you name the worthiest men in the realm?"
entries.literal: When Emperor Xiaowen first was established, he summoned Shu and asked, saying, "Sir, do you know the empire's venerable elders?"

entries.zh: 對曰：「臣何足以知之！」
entries.en: He replied, "I am hardly fit to judge such matters."
entries.literal: He replied, saying, "Your servant how could be sufficient to know them!"

entries.zh: 上曰：「公長者，宜知之。」
entries.en: The emperor said, "You are a man of weight yourself; you must have an opinion."
entries.literal: The sovereign said, "You are a venerable elder; you ought to know."

entries.zh: 叔頓首曰：「故雲中守孟舒，長者也。」
entries.en: Tian Shu kowtowed and said, "The former governor of Yunzhong, Meng Shu, is such a man."
entries.literal: Shu knocked his head and said, "The former Yunzhong governor Meng Shu is a venerable elder."

entries.zh: 是時孟舒坐虜大入雲中免。
entries.en: Meng Shu had just been dismissed because the Xiongnu had overrun Yunzhong in force.
entries.literal: At this time Meng Shu was dismissed because the barbarians had overrun Yunzhong in force.

entries.zh: 上曰：「先帝置孟舒雲中十餘年矣，虜常一入，孟舒不能堅守，無故士卒戰死者數百人。
entries.en: The emperor said, "The late emperor kept Meng Shu at Yunzhong for more than ten years, yet when the raiders broke in he failed to hold the line, and hundreds of soldiers died for no good reason.
entries.literal: The sovereign said, "The late emperor placed Meng Shu in Yunzhong more than ten years already; barbarians often once entered, Meng Shu could not firmly defend; without reason soldiers who died in battle were several hundred.

entries.zh: 長者固殺人乎？」
entries.en: Is that the conduct of a 'worthy elder'?"
entries.literal: Do venerable elders thus kill people?"

entries.zh: 叔叩頭曰：「夫貫高等謀反，天子下明詔，趙有敢隨張王者罪三族，然孟舒自髡鉗，隨張王，以身死之，豈自知為雲中守哉！
entries.en: Tian Shu kowtowed and said, "When Guan Gao and his fellow plotters rose against the throne, the Son of Heaven decreed death for three generations of any Zhao official who followed King Zhang—yet Meng Shu shaved his head, took the collar, and followed his lord to the grave. How could he have dreamed he would one day govern Yunzhong?
entries.literal: Shu knocked his head and said, "As for Guan Gao and others plotting rebellion, the Son of Heaven issued a clear edict that in Zhao whoever dared follow King Zhang would be guilty to three clans, yet Meng Shu himself shaved head and collar, followed King Zhang, with body would die for him—how could he have known he would become Yunzhong governor!

entries.zh: 漢與楚相距，士卒罷敝，而匈奴冒頓新服北夷，來為邊寇，孟舒知士卒罷敝，不忍出言，士爭臨城死敵，如子為父，以故死者數百人，孟舒豈敺之哉！
entries.en: Han and Chu were deadlocked and the army was on its last legs, while Modun had just bent the northern tribes to his will and unleashed them on the frontier. Meng Shu knew his men were too spent to bear another order to battle—yet they stormed the walls like sons defending a father, and hundreds died. That was not Meng Shu driving them to their deaths.
entries.literal: Han and Chu faced each other in stalemate; the troops were worn out, while the Xiongnu Modun had newly subdued the northern tribes and sent them raiding the border. Meng Shu knew his soldiers were exhausted and could not bring himself to order them out; yet the men vied to man the walls and die facing the foe, like sons for a father—so several hundred perished. How could Meng Shu have driven them to it!

entries.zh: 是乃孟舒所以為長者。」
entries.en: That is precisely the mark of a true elder statesman."
entries.literal: This then is why Meng Shu is what is called a venerable elder."

entries.zh: 於是上曰：「賢哉孟舒！」
entries.en: The emperor exclaimed, "Meng Shu is a remarkable man!"
entries.literal: Thereupon the sovereign said, "How worthy is Meng Shu!"

entries.zh: 復召以為雲中守。
entries.en: He was summoned back and reappointed governor of Yunzhong.
entries.literal: Again he was summoned and made Yunzhong governor.

entries.zh: 欒布，梁人也。
entries.en: Luan Bu came from Liang.
entries.literal: Luan Bu was a man of Liang.

entries.zh: 彭越為家人時，嘗與布游，窮困，賣庸於齊，為酒家保。
entries.en: When Peng Yue was still a commoner, he and Luan Bu had been companions; broke, they hired out as laborers in Qi and Luan tended a tavern.
entries.literal: When Peng Yue was a commoner family man, he once roamed with Bu; in poverty and straits, they hired out labor in Qi, and Bu was a wine-shop guarantor.

entries.zh: 數歲別去，而布為人所略，賣為奴於燕。
entries.en: They parted for some years; then Luan Bu was kidnapped and sold into slavery in Yan.
entries.literal: Several years they parted and went away, but Bu by people was abducted and sold as a slave in Yan.

entries.zh: 為其主家報仇，燕將臧荼舉以為都尉。
entries.en: He avenged his master's family on their enemies; the Yan general Zang Tu, impressed, appointed him a commandant.
entries.literal: For his master's household he avenged a wrong; the Yan general Zang Tu raised him and made him commandant.

entries.zh: 荼為燕王，布為將。
entries.en: When Zang Tu became king of Yan, Luan Bu served as his general.
entries.literal: When Tu became Yan king, Bu was general.

entries.zh: 及荼反，漢擊燕，虜布。
entries.en: When Zang Tu rebelled, the Han attacked Yan and took Luan Bu prisoner.
entries.literal: When Tu rebelled, Han struck Yan and captured Bu.

entries.zh: 梁王彭越聞之，乃言上，請贖布為梁大夫。
entries.en: King Peng Yue of Liang heard of it and petitioned the emperor to ransom him and appoint him a grandee of Liang.
entries.literal: King of Liang Peng Yue heard it; thereupon he spoke to the sovereign, requesting to ransom Bu and make him Liang grandee.

entries.zh: 使於齊，未反，漢召彭越責以謀反，夷三族，梟首雒陽，下詔有收視者輒捕之。
entries.en: Luan Bu was on embassy to Qi when, before he could return, the court summoned Peng Yue on a charge of treason, wiped out three generations of his kin, exposed his head in Luoyang, and decreed arrest for anyone who dared mourn or look upon him.
entries.literal: He was sent on mission to Qi; before returning, Han summoned Peng Yue and reproached him with plotting rebellion, exterminated three clans, displayed the head at Luoyang, and issued an edict that whoever gathered or came to look upon it would immediately be arrested.

entries.zh: 布還，奏事彭越頭下，祠而哭之。
entries.en: Luan Bu returned, laid his report beneath Peng Yue's severed head, and offered sacrifice and tears.
entries.literal: Bu returned, reported affairs beneath Peng Yue's head, sacrificed and wept for him.

entries.zh: 吏捕以聞。
entries.en: The officials seized him and reported to the throne.
entries.literal: The clerks arrested and reported.

entries.zh: 上召布罵曰：「若與彭越反邪？
entries.en: The emperor summoned Luan Bu and shouted, "Were you in league with Peng Yue?
entries.literal: The sovereign summoned Bu and reviled, saying, "You with Peng Yue rebelled, yes?

entries.zh: 吾禁人勿收，若獨祠而哭之，與反明矣。
entries.en: I forbade anyone to claim his body or mourn him; you alone offered sacrifice and wept—your guilt is as plain as open rebellion.
entries.literal: I forbade anyone to gather his remains or mourn him; you alone held sacrifice and wept for him—with rebellion the matter is already clear.

entries.zh: 趣亨之。」
entries.en: Boil him at once."
entries.literal: Hasten boil him."

entries.zh: 方提趨湯，顧曰：「願一言而死。」
entries.en: As they dragged him toward the cauldron, he turned and said, "Let me speak one sentence before I die."
entries.literal: Just as being lifted and hurried to the soup, looking back he said, "I wish one word then die."

entries.zh: 上曰：「何言？」
entries.en: The emperor asked, "What is it?"
entries.literal: The sovereign said, "What words?"

entries.zh: 布曰：「方上之困彭城，敗滎陽、成皋間，項王所以不能遂西，徒以彭王居梁地，與漢合從苦楚也。
entries.en: Luan Bu said, "When you were besieged at Pengcheng and driven from Xingyang to Chenggao, the only reason Xiang Yu could not push west was that King Peng held Liang and kept Han and Chu locked in a stalemate that wore Chu down.
entries.literal: Bu said, "When Your Majesty was trapped at Pengcheng, defeated between Xingyang and Chenggao, the reason King Xiang could not thereupon proceed west was solely because King Peng held Liang territory, allied with Han in vertical alliance, and tormented Chu.

entries.zh: 當是之時，彭王壹顧，與楚則漢破，與漢則楚破。
entries.en: At that moment a single shift of Peng Yue's weight—if he had thrown in with Chu, Han would have shattered; if with Han, Chu would have shattered.
entries.literal: At this time, if King Peng had shifted his allegiance once—if with Chu then Han would have been broken, if with Han then Chu would have been broken.

entries.zh: 且垓下之會，微彭王，項氏不亡。
entries.en: And at Gaixia, without King Peng, the house of Xiang would never have fallen.
entries.literal: Moreover, at the Gaixia assembly, without King Peng, the Xiang clan would not have perished.

entries.zh: 天下已定，彭王剖符受封，亦欲傳之萬世。
entries.en: After peace was won, King Peng received his bronze tally like any other vassal king and hoped to pass his line down for ages.
entries.literal: The empire already settled, Peng Wang split tallies and received investiture; he also wished to transmit it ten thousand generations.

entries.zh: 今漢壹徵兵於梁，彭王病不行，而疑以為反。
entries.en: Now a single levy of troops from Liang, and because King Peng was too ill to march, you suspect him of treason.
entries.literal: Now Han once called up troops at Liang; Peng Wang was ill and did not go, yet was suspected and taken as rebellion.

entries.zh: 反形未見，以苛細誅之，臣恐功臣人人自危也。
entries.en: No sign of revolt appeared; to kill him on petty pretexts will make every man who helped you win the throne look over his shoulder.
entries.literal: Rebellion form not yet seen, by harsh minuteness executing him—your servant fears the merit ministers each will self-fear.

entries.zh: 今彭王已死，臣生不如死，請就亨。」
entries.en: King Peng is dead; I would rather join him in the cauldron than live on—throw me in."
entries.literal: Now Peng Wang is already dead; your servant alive is not as good as dead; I request to approach the boil."

entries.zh: 上乃釋布，拜為都尉。
entries.en: The emperor spared him and appointed him a commandant.
entries.literal: The sovereign thereupon released Bu and appointed him commandant.

entries.zh: 贊曰：以項羽之氣，而季布以勇顯名楚，身履軍搴旗者數矣，可謂壯士。
entries.en: The historian's verdict: In an age dominated by Xiang Yu's fury, Ji Bu won fame in Chu for raw courage; he repeatedly charged into battle and tore enemy banners from their poles—a true fighting man.
entries.literal: The appraisal says: By Xiang Yu's fierce spirit, yet Ji Bu by bravery displayed name in Chu; personally in the army seizing banners—several times—can be called a brave warrior.

entries.zh: 及至困厄奴僇，苟活而不變，何也？
entries.en: Yet when he was broken, enslaved, and humiliated, he clung to life without yielding his purpose—why was that?
entries.literal: When it came to straits and humiliation as a slave, living ignobly yet not changing—why?

entries.zh: 彼自負其材，受辱不羞，欲有所用其未足也，故終為漢名將。
entries.en: He trusted his own abilities; shame did not break him because he still meant to put his gifts to use. In the end he became one of the Han's celebrated generals.
entries.literal: He himself bore his talents; receiving humiliation he was not ashamed, wishing to have something to use of what was not yet sufficient; therefore in the end he became a Han famous general.

entries.zh: 賢者誠重其死。
entries.en: A worthy man weighs his death with utmost care.
entries.literal: The worthy truly value their death.

entries.zh: 夫婢妾賤人，感概而自殺，非能勇也，其畫無俚之至耳。
entries.en: Maids and common folk who work themselves into a passion and take their own lives show no courage—only the shallowest recklessness.
entries.literal: As for maidservants and mean persons, stirred in feeling and killing themselves—it is not able to be courage; their plan crude reaches the utmost only.

entries.zh: 欒布哭彭越，田叔隨張敖，赴死如歸，彼誠知所處，雖古烈士，何以加哉！
entries.en: Luan Bu mourned Peng Yue at the risk of his life; Tian Shu followed Zhang Ao into chains as if going home. They knew exactly where they stood; the steadfast heroes of old could scarcely have surpassed them.
entries.literal: Luan Bu wept for Peng Yue; Tian Shu followed Zhang Ao; they went to death like returning home—they truly knew their place; even ancient steadfast martyrs—how could one add more!

entries.zh: 布薨，子賁嗣侯，孝武時坐為太常犧牲不如令，國除。
entries.en: When Luan Bu died, his son Ben inherited the title; under Emperor Wu the fief was stripped after Ben, as Grand Master of Ceremonies, supplied defective sacrificial beasts.
entries.literal: Bu died; his son Ben inherited the marquisate; in the time of Emperor Xiaowu, sitting for as Grand Master of Ceremonies the sacrificial victims not according to ordinance, the state was removed.

entries.zh: 後數歲，叔坐法失官。
entries.en: Some years later Tian Shu lost his post for a legal infraction.
entries.literal: After several years, Shu lost office for a legal offense.

entries.zh: 梁孝王使人殺漢議臣爰盎，景帝召叔案梁，具得其事。
entries.en: When King Xiao of Liang had the Han adviser Yuan Ang murdered, Emperor Jing sent Tian Shu to investigate the kingdom of Liang; he uncovered the full truth.
entries.literal: King Xiao of Liang sent men to kill Han councillor Yuan Ang; Emperor Jing summoned Shu to investigate Liang, completely obtained the affair.

entries.zh: 還報，上曰：「梁有之乎？」
entries.en: On his return he was asked, "Did Liang do it?"
entries.literal: Returning he reported; the sovereign said, "Did Liang have it?"

entries.zh: 對曰：「有之。」
entries.en: He answered, "Yes."
entries.literal: He replied, "There was it."

entries.zh: 「事安在？」
entries.en: "Where is the proof?"
entries.literal: "Where is the affair?"

entries.zh: 叔曰：「上無以梁事為問也。
entries.en: Tian Shu said, "Your Majesty should not press the matter of Liang.
entries.literal: Shu said, "Your Majesty should not inquire further into the affair of Liang.

entries.zh: 今梁王不伏誅，是廢漢法也；
entries.en: If the king of Liang goes unpunished, the law of the Han is void;
entries.literal: Now if the King of Liang does not submit to execution, this is abandoning Han law;

entries.zh: 如其伏誅，太后食不甘味，臥不安席，此憂在陛下。」
entries.en: if he is executed, the empress dowager will eat without relish and sleep without rest—and that grief will be yours to bear."
entries.literal: if he submits to execution, the empress dowager will not find food sweet in eating, will not find peace in sleeping on mat—this worry is on Your Majesty."

entries.zh: 於是上大賢之，以為魯相。
entries.en: The emperor admired his judgment and appointed him chancellor to the king of Lu.
entries.literal: Thereupon the sovereign greatly deemed him worthy and made him Lu chancellor.

entries.zh: 趙共王恢。
entries.en: Liu Hui, the Joint Prince of Zhao.
entries.literal: Prince Hui of Zhao, Hui.

entries.zh: 十一年，梁王彭越誅，立恢為梁王。
entries.en: In the eleventh year of Gaozu's reign, after Peng Yue, king of Liang, was put to death, Liu Hui was transferred to Liang and invested there.
entries.literal: In the eleventh year, King Peng Yue of Liang was executed, and Hui was established as king of Liang.

entries.zh: 十六年，趙幽王死，呂后徙恢王趙，恢心不樂。
entries.en: In the sixteenth year, when Prince You of Zhao died, Empress Lü reassigned Liu Hui to Zhao. He went unwillingly, his heart heavy at the move.
entries.literal: In the sixteenth year, Prince You of Zhao the Obscure died; Empress Lü moved Hui to be king of Zhao; Hui's heart was not glad.

entries.zh: 太后以呂產女為趙王后，王后從官皆諸呂也，內擅權，微司趙王，王不得自恣。
entries.en: She married him to a daughter of Lü Chan, whose entire household staff were Lü partisans. They seized the inner court, spied on the king at every turn, and left him unable to live as he pleased.
entries.literal: The empress dowager took Lü Chan's daughter as queen of Zhao; the queen's attendants were all of the Lü clan; within they monopolized power, secretly watched the king of Zhao, and the king could not follow his own will.

entries.zh: 王有愛姬，王后鴆殺之。
entries.en: When he favored another woman, his Lü queen poisoned her.
entries.literal: The king had a beloved concubine; the queen killed her with poisoned wine.

entries.zh: 王乃為歌詩四章，令樂人歌之。
entries.en: In his grief he wrote four songs and had the court musicians perform them.
entries.literal: The king then composed four stanzas of song-poetry and ordered musicians to sing them.

entries.zh: 王悲思，六月自殺。
entries.en: Brokenhearted, he took his own life in the sixth month.
entries.literal: The king was sorrowful and brooding; in the sixth month he killed himself.

entries.zh: 太后聞之，以為用婦人故自殺，無思奉宗廟禮，廢其嗣。
entries.en: The empress dowager dismissed his death as the act of a man who had killed himself over a woman and showed no regard for his duty to the imperial ancestors; she struck his line from the succession.
entries.literal: When the empress dowager heard of it, she thought that because of a woman he had killed himself, without thought for the rites owed the ancestral temple; she abolished his posterity.

entries.zh: 趙王遂立二十六年，孝景時晁錯以過削趙常山郡，諸侯怨，吳楚反，遂與合謀起兵。
entries.en: Liu Sui had been king of Zhao for twenty-six years when, under Emperor Jing, Chao Cuo seized the Changshan commandery from Zhao as punishment for alleged wrongdoing. The kingdoms were already smoldering with resentment; when Wu and Chu rose in revolt, Liu Sui conspired with them and mobilized his own forces.
entries.literal: King Liu Sui of Zhao had reigned twenty-six years. In the time of Emperor Xiaojing, Chao Cuo, citing faults, stripped Zhao of the Changshan commandery; the feudal lords resented it; Wu and Chu rebelled, and Sui joined them in plotting to raise troops.

entries.zh: 其相建德、內史王悍諫，不聽。
entries.en: His chancellor Jiande and interior secretary Wang Han urged him to reconsider, but he refused to heed them.
entries.literal: His chancellor Jiande and his interior secretary Wang Han remonstrated; he would not listen.

entries.zh: 遂燒殺德、悍，發兵住其西界，欲待吳楚俱進，北使匈奴與連和。
entries.en: He had Jiande and Wang Han executed by fire, deployed troops along his western border to await a joint advance with Wu and Chu, and sent a mission north to court an alliance with the Xiongnu.
entries.literal: Sui then had Jiande and Han burned to death, sent troops to hold his western frontier, wished to wait until Wu and Chu advanced together, and sent envoys north to the Xiongnu to conclude an alliance.

entries.zh: 漢使曲周侯酈寄擊之，趙王城守邯鄲，相距七月。
entries.en: The court sent Marquis of Quzhou Li Ji against him. The king of Zhao shut himself inside Handan, and the siege lasted seven months.
entries.literal: The Han dispatched Marquis of Quzhou Li Ji to attack him; the King of Zhao defended Handan; they faced each other seven months.

entries.zh: 吳楚敗，匈奴聞之，亦不肯入邊。
entries.en: After Wu and Chu collapsed, the Xiongnu, learning the outcome, likewise declined to cross the frontier.
entries.literal: When Wu and Chu were defeated, the Xiongnu heard of it and would not enter the border either.

entries.zh: 欒布自破齊還，并兵引水灌趙城。
entries.en: Luan Bu, returning from the campaign that had broken Qi, joined his command with others, diverted a river, and inundated the Zhao capital.
entries.literal: Luan Bu, returning from having crushed Qi, combined forces, led water in, and flooded the Zhao city.

entries.zh: 城壞，王遂自殺，國除。
entries.en: The ramparts failed; Liu Sui took his own life, and the kingdom was abolished.
entries.literal: The walls gave way; King Sui killed himself; the state was abolished.

entries.zh: 景帝憐趙相、內史守正死，皆封其子為列侯。
entries.en: Touched by the loyalty of the Zhao chancellor and interior secretary who had died for their principles, Emperor Jing made each man's son a full marquis.
entries.literal: Emperor Jing pitied the Zhao chancellor and interior secretary who had died upholding what was right, and enfeoffed both their sons as full marquises.

entries.zh: 漢聞之，相國呂產等遣大將軍潁陰侯灌嬰將兵擊之。
entries.en: The court learned of the rising and ordered Grand General Guan Ying, Marquis of Yingyin, to take the field against Qi.
entries.literal: When the Han heard of it, Chancellor Lü Chan and others dispatched Grand General Marquis of Yingyin Guan Ying to lead troops and attack him.

entries.zh: 嬰至滎陽，乃謀曰：「諸呂舉兵關中，欲危劉氏而自立，今我破齊還報，是益呂氏資也。」
entries.en: At Xingyang he halted and reasoned with his officers: "The Lü hold Guanzhong and mean to supplant the Liu. If I crush Qi and march home, I only strengthen their hand."
entries.literal: When Guan Ying reached Xingyang, he plotted, saying: "The Lü have raised troops within the passes, wishing to endanger the Liu and establish themselves; now if I break Qi and return to report, this increases the Lü's resources."

entries.zh: 乃留兵屯滎陽，使人諭齊王及諸侯，與連和，以待呂氏之變而共誅之。
entries.en: He camped at Xingyang, sent envoys to the king of Qi and the other kings, and forged a common front to wait for the Lü to move, then strike them down together.
entries.literal: Then he left troops garrisoned at Xingyang, sent men to instruct the king of Qi and the feudal lords, joined in alliance with them, and waited for the Lü's coup in order together to execute them.

entries.zh: 齊王聞之，乃屯兵西界待約。
entries.en: The king of Qi drew up his army on his western frontier to await the signal.
entries.literal: The king of Qi heard it, then garrisoned troops on the western border awaiting the agreement.

entries.zh: 灌嬰在滎陽，聞魏勃本教齊王反，既誅呂氏，罷齊兵，使使召責問魏勃。
entries.en: Guan Ying, still at Xingyang, had heard that Wei Bo had instigated the king of Qi's revolt. Once the Lü were gone and Qi's army sent home, he summoned Wei Bo to account for himself.
entries.literal: Guan Ying was at Xingyang; he heard that Wei Bo had originally instructed the king of Qi to rebel; after the Lü had been executed and Qi troops disbanded, he sent envoys to summon and rebuke Wei Bo.

entries.zh: 勃曰：「失火之家，豈暇先言丈人後救火乎！」
entries.en: "When the roof is burning," Wei Bo replied, "do you first bow to your elders or grab a bucket?"
entries.literal: Bo said: "In a house on fire, how is there leisure first to speak to the elders and afterward fight the fire!"

entries.zh: 因退立，股戰而栗。
entries.en: He stepped back, legs trembling, unable to steady himself.
entries.literal: Thereupon he withdrew and stood; his thighs trembled and he shivered.

entries.zh: 恐不能言者，終無他語。
entries.en: Too frightened to say more, he offered no further defense.
entries.literal: Fearing he could not speak, in the end he had no other words.

entries.zh: 灌將軍孰視，笑曰：「人謂魏勃勇，妄庸人耳，何能為乎！」
entries.en: Guan Ying studied him a long moment, then laughed. "They say Wei Bo is bold. The man is a panicky fool—harmless."
entries.literal: General Guan stared long, laughed, and said: "People call Wei Bo brave—he is merely a foolish common fellow; what can he do!"

entries.zh: 乃罷勃。
entries.en: He let Wei Bo go.
entries.literal: Thereupon he dismissed Bo.

entries.zh: 勃父以善鼓琴見秦皇帝。
entries.en: Wei Bo's father had won an audience with the First Emperor of Qin by his skill on the zither.
entries.literal: Bo's father, by being good at drumming the zither, was received by the Qin August Emperor.

entries.zh: 及勃少時，欲求見齊相曹參，家貧無以自通，乃常獨早埽齊相舍人門外。
entries.en: In his youth, wanting to meet Chancellor Cao Shen of Qi but too poor for an introduction, he rose before dawn day after day to sweep the doorstep of one of the chancellor's retainers.
entries.literal: When Bo was young, he wished to seek an audience with Chancellor Cao Shen of Qi; his family was poor and had no means to introduce himself; therefore he often alone early swept outside the gate of the chancellor of Qi's retainer.

entries.zh: 舍人怪之，以為物而司之，得勃。
entries.en: The retainer thought some ghost was at work and lay in wait until he caught Wei Bo in the act.
entries.literal: The retainer thought it strange, thought it a spirit and watched for it, and caught Bo.

entries.zh: 勃曰：「願見相君，無因，故為子埽，欲以求見。」
entries.en: Wei Bo said, "I beg an audience with the chancellor, but I have no way in. That is why I have been sweeping your doorstep—to earn a chance to meet him."
entries.literal: Bo said: "I wish to see the chancellor; having no means of access, therefore I sweep for you, wishing thereby to seek an audience."

entries.zh: 城陽景王章，孝文二年以朱虛侯與東牟侯興居俱立，二年薨。
entries.en: Liu Zhang, Prince Jing of Chengyang, was enfeoffed in the second year of Emperor Wen together with his brother Xingju, Marquis of Dongmou; he died two years later.
entries.literal: Prince Jing of Chengyang, Zhang, in the second year of Xiaowen, together with Marquis of Zhuxu and Marquis of Dongmou Xingju was established; in the second year he died.

entries.zh: 子共王喜嗣。
entries.en: His son Liu Xi, Prince Gong of Chengyang, succeeded him.
entries.literal: The son, Prince Gong Xi, succeeded.

entries.zh: 孝文十二年，徙王淮南，五年，復還王城陽，凡立三十三年薨。
entries.en: In the twelfth year of Emperor Wen he was transferred to Huainan; five years after that he was brought back to Chengyang. He reigned thirty-three years in all before he died.
entries.literal: In the twelfth year of Xiaowen, he was moved to be king of Huainan; in the fifth year, again returned to be king of Chengyang; in all he reigned thirty-three years and died.

entries.zh: 子頃王延嗣，二十六年薨。
entries.en: His son Liu Yan, Prince Qing of Chengyang, reigned twenty-six years.
entries.literal: The son, Prince Qing Yan, succeeded; in twenty-six years he died.

entries.zh: 子敬王義嗣，九年薨。
entries.en: Liu Yi, Prince Jing, followed and reigned nine years.
entries.literal: The son, Prince Jing Yi, succeeded; in nine years he died.

entries.zh: 子惠王武嗣，十一年薨。
entries.en: Liu Wu, Prince Hui, held the throne eleven years.
entries.literal: The son, Prince Hui Wu, succeeded; in eleven years he died.

entries.zh: 子荒王順嗣，四十六年薨。
entries.en: Liu Shun, Prince Huang, ruled forty-six years.
entries.literal: The son, Prince Huang Shun, succeeded; in forty-six years he died.

entries.zh: 子戴王恢嗣，八年薨。
entries.en: Liu Hui, Prince Dai, succeeded him and died after eight years.
entries.literal: The son, Prince Dai Hui, succeeded; in eight years he died.

entries.zh: 子孝王景嗣，二十四年薨。
entries.en: His son Liu Jing, Prince Xiao of Chengyang, reigned twenty-four years.
entries.literal: The son, Prince Xiao Jing, succeeded; in twenty-four years he died.

entries.zh: 子哀王雲嗣，一年薨，無子，國絕。
entries.en: Liu Yun, Prince Ai, lasted only a year and left no heir; the kingdom lapsed.
entries.literal: The son, Prince Ai Yun, succeeded; in one year he died; he had no sons; the state was cut off.

entries.zh: 成帝復立雲兄俚為城陽王，王莽時絕。
entries.en: Emperor Cheng revived the title for Liu Li, Prince Yun's elder brother, but the line died out under Wang Mang.
entries.literal: Emperor Cheng again established Yun's elder brother Li as king of Chengyang; in Wang Mang's time it was cut off.

entries.zh: 文帝元年，盡以高后時所割齊之城陽、琅邪、濟南郡復予齊，而徙琅邪王王燕。
entries.en: In the first year of Emperor Wen's reign, Chengyang, Langye, and Jinan—the commanderies carved from Qi under Empress Dowager Lü—were all restored to Qi, and the king of Langye was transferred to rule Yan.
entries.literal: In the first year of Emperor Wen, all the territories cut from Qi during Empress Gao's time—Chengyang, Langye, and Jinan commanderies—were restored to Qi, and the king of Langye was moved to rule Yan.

entries.zh: 益封朱虛侯、東牟侯各二千戶，黃金千斤。
entries.en: The Marquis of Zhuxu and the Marquis of Dongmou each received an additional two thousand households and a thousand jin of gold.
entries.literal: Additional fiefs of two thousand households and a thousand jin of gold were granted to the Marquis of Zhuxu and the Marquis of Dongmou.

entries.zh: 是歲，齊哀王薨，子文王則嗣。
entries.en: That year Prince Ai of Qi died, and his son Liu Ze, Prince Wen of Qi, succeeded him.
entries.literal: That year Prince Ai of Qi died; his son Ze, Prince Wen, succeeded.

entries.zh: 十四年薨，無子，國除。
entries.en: He ruled fourteen years, left no heir, and the kingdom was abolished.
entries.literal: After fourteen years he died; he had no sons, and the state was abolished.

entries.zh: 始誅諸呂時，朱虛侯章功尤大，大臣許盡以趙地王章，盡以梁地王興居。
entries.en: When the Lü clan was first being destroyed, Liu Zhang, Marquis of Zhuxu, had done the greatest service; the great ministers agreed to make Zhang king of Zhao and Xingju king of Liang.
entries.literal: At the beginning, when the Lü clan was being executed, Zhang, Marquis of Zhuxu, had merit above all others; the great ministers agreed to make Zhang king of all Zhao and Xingju king of all Liang.

entries.zh: 及文帝立，聞朱虛、東牟之初欲立齊王，故黜其功。
entries.en: When Emperor Wen took the throne, he learned that the Marquis of Zhuxu and the Marquis of Dongmou had at first wished to make the king of Qi emperor, and therefore diminished their rewards.
entries.literal: When Emperor Wen was established, he heard that the Marquis of Zhuxu and the Marquis of Dongmou had at first wished to set up the king of Qi, and therefore reduced their merit.

entries.zh: 二年，王諸子，乃割齊二郡以王章、興居。
entries.en: In the second year, when imperial sons were invested as kings, two commanderies were carved from Qi to enfeoff Zhang and Xingju.
entries.literal: In the second year, when imperial sons were enfeoffed as kings, two commanderies were cut from Qi to make Zhang and Xingju kings.

entries.zh: 章、興居意自以失職奪功。
entries.en: Zhang and Xingju both felt they had been stripped of deserved rank and robbed of their merit.
entries.literal: Zhang and Xingju inwardly thought themselves deprived of office and robbed of merit.

entries.zh: 歲餘，章薨，而匈奴大入邊，漢多發兵，丞相灌嬰將擊之，文帝親幸太原。
entries.en: A little more than a year later Zhang died. The Xiongnu raided deeply along the frontier; the Han mobilized large forces; Chancellor Guan Ying took command; and Emperor Wen personally went to Taiyuan.
entries.literal: After a little more than a year Zhang died. The Xiongnu made a major incursion on the border; the Han mobilized many troops; Chancellor Guan Ying led the attack; Emperor Wen personally visited Taiyuan.

entries.zh: 興居以為天子自擊胡，遂發兵反。
entries.en: Xingju assumed the emperor had left the capital to fight the barbarians in person and therefore raised troops in rebellion.
entries.literal: Xingju thought the Son of Heaven was personally striking the barbarians and therefore raised troops in rebellion.

entries.zh: 上聞之，罷兵歸長安，使棘蒲侯柴將軍擊破，虜濟北王。
entries.en: When the emperor heard of it, he recalled his forces to Chang'an and sent General Chai, Marquis of Jipo, to defeat him and capture the king of Jibei.
entries.literal: When the emperor heard of it, he recalled the troops and returned to Chang'an, sent Chai the general, Marquis of Jipo, to defeat him, and captured the king of Jibei.

entries.zh: 王自殺，國除。
entries.en: The king killed himself, and the kingdom was abolished.
entries.literal: The king killed himself; the state was abolished.

entries.zh: 文帝憫濟北王逆亂以自滅，明年，盡封悼惠王諸子罷軍等七人為列侯。
entries.en: Pitying the king of Jibei for destroying himself through rebellion, the next year Emperor Wen enfeoffed seven sons of Prince Daohui, including Liu Bagun, as ranked marquises.
entries.literal: Emperor Wen pitied the king of Jibei for bringing ruin on himself through rebellion; the next year he enfeoffed seven sons of Prince Daohui, including Bagun, as ranked marquises.

entries.zh: 至十五年，齊文王又薨，無子。
entries.en: By the fifteenth year Prince Wen of Qi had died again, leaving no heir.
entries.literal: By the fifteenth year Prince Wen of Qi again died and had no sons.

entries.zh: 時悼惠王後尚有城陽王在，文帝憐悼惠王適嗣之絕，於是乃分齊為六國，盡立前所封悼惠王子列侯見在者六人為王。
entries.en: The king of Chengyang still survived among Prince Daohui's descendants; pitying the extinction of the legitimate Qi succession, Emperor Wen divided Qi into six kingdoms and invested all six of Prince Daohui's living sons who had previously held marquisates as kings.
entries.literal: At that time among Prince Daohui's descendants the king of Chengyang still survived; Emperor Wen pitied the extinction of Prince Daohui's legitimate succession, and therefore divided Qi into six states and established as kings all six of Prince Daohui's sons then living who had previously been enfeoffed as ranked marquises.

entries.zh: 齊孝王將閭以楊虛侯立，濟北王志以安都侯立，菑川王賢以武成侯立，膠東王雄渠以白石侯立，膠西王卬以平昌侯立，濟南王辟光以扐侯立。
entries.en: Liu Jianglü became Prince Xiao of Qi from the Marquisate of Yangxu; Liu Zhi, king of Jibei, from Andu; Liu Xian of Zichuan from Wucheng; Liu Xiongqu of Jiaodong from Baishi; Liu Ang of Jiaoxi from Pingchang; and Liu Piguang of Jinan from Zhi.
entries.literal: Prince Xiao of Qi, Jianglü, was established from Marquis of Yangxu; Prince Zhi of Jibei from Marquis of Andu; Prince Xian of Zichuan from Marquis of Wucheng; Prince Xiongqu of Jiaodong from Marquis of Baishi; Prince Ang of Jiaoxi from Marquis of Pingchang; and Prince Piguang of Jinan from Marquis of Zhi.

entries.zh: 孝文十六年，六王同日俱立。
entries.en: In the sixteenth year of Emperor Wen all six were invested on the same day.
entries.literal: In the sixteenth year of Xiaowen the six kings were all established on the same day.

entries.zh: 高皇帝八男：呂后生孝惠帝，曹夫人生齊悼惠王肥，薄姬生孝文帝，戚夫人生趙隱王如意，趙姬生淮南厲王長，諸姬生趙幽王友、趙共王恢、燕靈王建。
entries.en: Emperor Gao fathered eight sons: Empress Lü gave him Emperor Xiaohui; Lady Cao gave him Prince Daohui of Qi, Liu Fei; Consort Bo bore the future Emperor Wen; Lady Qi bore Liu Ruyi, later titled the Hidden Prince of Zhao; Lady Zhao bore Liu Chang, the Fierce Prince of Huainan; and lesser consorts bore Liu You, Liu Hui, and Liu Jian, the Obscure Prince of Zhao, the Joint Prince of Zhao, and the Numinous Prince of Yan respectively.
entries.literal: The August Emperor Gao had eight sons: Empress Lü bore Emperor Xiaohui; Lady Cao bore Prince Daohui of Qi, Fei; Consort Bo bore Emperor Xiaowen; Lady Qi bore the Hidden Prince of Zhao, Ruyi; Lady Zhao bore the Fierce Prince of Huainan, Chang; other ladies bore Prince You of Zhao the Obscure, Prince Hui of Zhao the Joint, and the Numinous Prince of Yan, Jian.

entries.zh: 淮南厲王長自有傳。
entries.en: Liu Chang, the Fierce Prince of Huainan, is treated in a separate biography.
entries.literal: The Fierce Prince of Huainan, Chang, has his own biography.

entries.zh: 蕭何，沛人也。
entries.en: Xiao He came from Pei.
entries.literal: Xiao He was a man of Pei.

entries.zh: 以文毋害為沛主吏掾。
entries.en: Because his paperwork was impeccable, he was appointed chief clerk to Pei’s chief administrator.
entries.literal: By being flawless in documents he became chief clerk of the chief administrator of Pei.

entries.zh: 高祖為布衣時，數以吏事護高祖。
entries.en: While Liu Bang was still a commoner, Xiao He more than once used his office to shield him from trouble.
entries.literal: When Gaozu was still a commoner, [He] repeatedly used official business as a pretext to shield Gaozu.

entries.zh: 高祖為亭長，常佑之。
entries.en: After Liu Bang became a village head, Xiao He habitually looked out for him.
entries.literal: When Gaozu became a village head, [He] constantly assisted him.

entries.zh: 高祖以吏繇咸陽，吏皆送奉錢三，何獨以五。
entries.en: When Liu Bang, as a conscripted clerk, went to Xianyang for corvée duty, his colleagues each gave him three hundred cash for the road; Xiao He alone gave five hundred.
entries.literal: When Gaozu as an official performed corvée labor at Xianyang, the clerks all presented three hundred cash in parting gifts; He alone presented five hundred.

entries.zh: 秦御史監郡者，與從事辨之。
entries.en: The Qin censor who oversaw the commandery, and the clerk who served under him, took up administrative questions with him.
entries.literal: The Qin imperial clerk who supervised the commandery, together with his attendant, debated matters with him.

entries.zh: 何乃給泗水卒史事，第一。
entries.en: He was posted as a clerk in the Sishui commandery office and placed first in the assessment.
entries.literal: He was then assigned to the office of a clerk of the Si River commandery, and ranked first.

entries.zh: 秦御史欲入言徵何，何固請，得毋行。
entries.en: The censor meant to recommend him to the court for appointment, but Xiao He held firm and was spared from having to go.
entries.literal: The Qin censor wished to memorialize the throne and summon He for appointment; He firmly declined the request, and so was not required to go.

entries.zh: 及高祖起為沛公，何嘗為丞督事。
entries.en: When Liu Bang was proclaimed Duke of Pei, Xiao He served as his assistant magistrate in charge of administration.
entries.literal: When Gaozu rose as Duke of Pei, He ever served as assistant magistrate overseeing affairs.

entries.zh: 沛公至咸陽，諸將皆爭走金帛財物之府分之，何獨先入收秦丞相御史律令圖書臧之。
entries.en: When the Duke of Pei entered Xianyang, his generals rushed to loot the treasuries; Xiao He alone went straight to the archives and secured the Qin government’s statutes, ordinances, maps, and registers.
entries.literal: When the Duke of Pei reached Xianyang, the generals all raced to seize gold, silk, wealth, and goods from the treasuries and divide them; He alone went in first and collected the laws, orders, maps, and documents of the Qin chancellor and censor and stored them away.

entries.zh: 沛公具知天下阨塞，戶口多少，彊弱處，民所疾苦者，以何得秦圖書也。
entries.en: Liu Bang knew the lie of the land—its defiles, population, relative strength, and the people’s grievances—only because Xiao He had preserved the Qin maps and records.
entries.literal: That the Duke of Pei fully knew where the strategic passes of the empire lay, how many households there were, where strength and weakness lay, and what the people’s hardships were, was because He obtained the Qin maps and documents.

entries.zh: 初，諸侯相與約，先入關破秦者王其地。
entries.en: The rebel lords had agreed among themselves that whoever first broke through the passes and overthrew Qin would rule that territory.
entries.literal: At first the feudal lords mutually agreed that whoever first entered the Pass and destroyed Qin would be king of that territory.

entries.zh: 沛公既先定秦，項羽後至，欲攻沛公，沛公謝之得解。
entries.en: Liu Bang was first to subdue the Qin heartland; when Xiang Yu arrived later and meant to strike him, Liu Bang apologized and defused the threat.
entries.literal: The Duke of Pei having first pacified Qin, Xiang Yu arrived afterward and wished to attack the Duke of Pei; the Duke of Pei apologized to him and the crisis was resolved.

entries.zh: 羽遂屠燒咸陽，與范增謀曰：「巴蜀道險，秦之遷民皆居蜀。」
entries.en: Xiang Yu then sacked and torched Xianyang. With Fan Zeng he reasoned, “The routes into Ba and Shu are treacherous, and Qin’s exiles have been settled in Shu.”
entries.literal: Yu then slaughtered and burned Xianyang, and consulted with Fan Zeng, saying, “The roads into Ba and Shu are perilous, and Qin’s banished people all dwell in Shu.”

entries.zh: 乃曰：「蜀漢亦關中地也。」
entries.en: So they declared, “Shu and Hanzhong still count as territory inside the passes.”
entries.literal: They therefore said, “Shu and Hanzhong are also lands within the Pass.”

entries.zh: 故立沛公為漢王，而三分關中地，王秦降將以距漢王。
entries.en: They named Liu Bang King of Han, carved the Guanzhong region into three kingdoms for Qin’s surrendered generals, and set those kings there to hem him in.
entries.literal: Therefore they established the Duke of Pei as King of Han, while they divided the territory within the Pass into three parts and enfeoffed Qin’s surrendered generals as kings to block the King of Han.

entries.zh: 漢王怒，欲謀攻項羽。
entries.en: Enraged, the King of Han prepared to march against Xiang Yu.
entries.literal: The King of Han was angry and planned to attack Xiang Yu.

entries.zh: 周勃、灌嬰、樊噲皆勸之，何諫之曰：「雖王漢中之惡，不猶愈於死乎？」
entries.en: Zhou Bo, Guan Ying, and Fan Kuai urged him to fight, but Xiao He objected: “Even Hanzhong is preferable to annihilation.”
entries.literal: Zhou Bo, Guan Ying, and Fan Kuai all urged him on; He remonstrated, saying, “Though ruling Hanzhong is hateful, is it not still better than death?”

entries.zh: 漢王曰：「何為乃死也？」
entries.en: The King of Han asked, “What makes you say that would mean our death?”
entries.literal: The King of Han said, “How could that mean death?”

entries.zh: 何曰：「今眾弗如，百戰百敗，不死何為？
entries.en: Xiao He replied, “Our forces cannot match his. Fight a hundred times and you lose a hundred times—what then but death?
entries.literal: He said, “Now our multitude does not match his; a hundred battles would mean a hundred defeats—if not death, then what?

entries.zh: 周書曰『天予不取，反受其咎』。
entries.en: The Documents of Zhou say, ‘What Heaven bestows, if you refuse it, you bring blame on yourself.
entries.literal: The Zhou Documents say, ‘What Heaven grants, if you do not take, you will instead receive its blame.

entries.zh: 語曰『天漢』，其稱甚美。
entries.en: The very phrase ‘Han of Heaven’ is a splendid omen.
entries.literal: The saying calls it ‘the Han of Heaven’—the name is most auspicious.

entries.zh: 夫能詘於一人之下，而信於萬乘之上者，湯武是也。
entries.en: Tang and King Wu could submit to one ruler for a time and ultimately rise above the sovereign of ten thousand chariots.
entries.literal: Those able to bend beneath one man and then rise above the ruler of ten thousand chariots were Tang and King Wu.

entries.zh: 臣願大王王漢中，養其民以致賢人，收用巴蜀，還定三秦，天下可圖也。」
entries.en: I urge Your Majesty to accept Hanzhong, cherish the people and draw men of talent to you, draw on the resources of Ba and Shu, then strike east to secure the Three Qin—the whole realm can still be yours.”
entries.literal: Your servant wishes the Great King to take his throne in Hanzhong, nurture the people to attract worthy men, gather Ba and Shu to his use, then return to settle the three Qin regions—the empire may yet be won.”

entries.zh: 漢王曰：「善。」
entries.en: The King of Han said, “Well spoken.”
entries.literal: The King of Han said, “Good.”

entries.zh: 乃遂就國，以何為丞相。
entries.en: He went to his new domain and appointed Xiao He chancellor.
entries.literal: He then proceeded to his kingdom, with He as chancellor.

entries.zh: 何進韓信，漢王以為大將軍，說漢王令引兵東定三秦。
entries.en: Xiao He recommended Han Xin, whom the King of Han named grand general. Han Xin then persuaded the king to let him lead the army east and conquer the Three Qin.
entries.literal: Xiao He recommended Han Xin, and the King of Han made him grand general. Han Xin persuaded the king, who ordered him to lead the army east to pacify the Three Qin.

entries.zh: 語在信傳。
entries.en: The full story is told in the biography of Han Xin.
entries.literal: The account is given in Han Xin’s biography.

entries.zh: 漢五年，已殺項羽，即皇帝位，論功行封，群臣爭功，歲餘不決。
entries.en: In the fifth Han year, with Xiang Yu dead, Liu Bang took the throne. Merit titles were debated, the ministers squabbled over precedence, and for more than a year nothing was settled.
entries.literal: In the fifth year of Han, after Yu had been killed, he immediately assumed the imperial position; when discussing merit and conferring enfeoffments, the ministers wrangled over credit, and for more than a year no decision was reached.

entries.zh: 上以何功最盛，先封為酇侯，食邑八千戶。
entries.en: The Sovereign judged Xiao He’s service supreme and first enfeoffed him as Marquis of Zan with eight thousand households.
entries.literal: The Sovereign held He’s achievement the greatest, and first enfeoffed him as Marquis of Zan with an estate of eight thousand households.

entries.zh: 功臣皆曰：「臣等身被堅執兵，多者百餘戰，少者數十合，攻城略地，大小各有差。
entries.en: The generals protested: “We wore armor and bore arms—some through a hundred fights, others dozens—we took cities and ground, each according to his deserts.
entries.literal: The meritorious ministers all said, “We personally wore armor and grasped weapons; the more had over a hundred battles, the fewer several tens of engagements; we stormed cities and seized territory, each with his measure of achievement.

entries.zh: 今蕭何未有汗馬之勞，徒持文墨議論，不戰，顧居臣等上，何也？」
entries.en: Xiao He never rode a charge or drew a bow; he only shuffled documents. How can he rank above us?”
entries.literal: Now Xiao He has had no sweat-of-the-horse toil; he merely holds brush and ink and discourses; he does not fight, yet still ranks above us—why?”

entries.zh: 上曰：「諸君知獵乎？」
entries.en: The Sovereign asked, “Do you know hunting?”
entries.literal: The Sovereign said, “Do you gentlemen know hunting?”

entries.zh: 曰：「知之。」
entries.en: They said, “We know.”
entries.literal: They said, “We know.”

entries.zh: 「知獵狗乎？」
entries.en: “And hunting dogs?”
entries.literal: “Do you know the hunting dogs?”

entries.zh: 曰：「知之。」
entries.en: They said, “We know.”
entries.literal: They said, “We know.”

entries.zh: 上曰：「夫獵，追殺獸者狗也，而發縱指示獸處者人也。
entries.en: The Sovereign said, “In a hunt, the hounds run down the game; the hunter slips the leash and shows them where to strike.
entries.literal: The Sovereign said, “In hunting, those who pursue and kill the beasts are the dogs; those who release the leash and point out where the beasts are are the men.

entries.zh: 今諸君徒能走得獸耳，功狗也；
entries.en: You only run the quarry down—you are the hounds’ share of the credit;
entries.literal: Now you gentlemen can only pursue and catch beasts—achievement of dogs;

entries.zh: 至如蕭何，發縱指示，功人也。
entries.en: Xiao He tracked the game and gave the signal—that is the hunter’s share.
entries.literal: As for Xiao He, releasing the leash and pointing—achievement of men.

entries.zh: 且諸君獨以身從我，多者三兩人；
entries.en: Besides, you followed me with only your own persons, two or three at most;
entries.literal: Moreover you gentlemen followed me with your persons alone, at most two or three men;

entries.zh: 蕭何舉宗數十人皆隨我，功不可忘也！」
entries.en: Xiao He brought his entire clan, dozens of kinsmen, into my service. Never forget that debt!”
entries.literal: Xiao He raised his whole lineage, several tens of men, all following me—his achievement must not be forgotten!”

entries.zh: 群臣後皆莫敢言。
entries.en: The assembly fell silent and dared not answer.
entries.literal: Afterward the ministers none dared speak.

entries.zh: 高祖崩，何事惠帝。
entries.en: After Gaozu’s death Xiao He served Emperor Hui.
entries.literal: When Gaozu died, He served Emperor Hui.

entries.zh: 何病，上親自臨視何疾，因問曰：「君即百歲後，誰可代君？」
entries.en: When Xiao He fell ill, the Sovereign came to his bedside and asked, “When you are gone, who can take your place?”
entries.literal: He fell ill; the Sovereign personally visited to observe his illness and then asked, “When you reach a hundred years, who may replace you?”

entries.zh: 對曰：「知臣莫如主。」
entries.en: He answered, “No one knows his servant better than his master.”
entries.literal: He replied, “None knows a minister like his lord.”

entries.zh: 帝曰：「曹參何如？」
entries.en: “What of Cao Shen?” asked the Emperor.
entries.literal: The Emperor said, “How about Cao Shen?”

entries.zh: 何頓首曰：「帝得之矣。
entries.en: Xiao He kowtowed. “Your Majesty has chosen well.
entries.literal: He knocked his head and said, “The Emperor has found the right man.

entries.zh: 何死不恨矣！」
entries.en: I may die content.”
entries.literal: I can die without regret!”

entries.zh: 孝惠二年，何薨，諡曰文終侯。
entries.en: In the second year of Emperor Hui’s reign Xiao He died; his posthumous title was Marquis Wenzhong.
entries.literal: In the second year of Emperor Hui’s reign, He died and was posthumously titled Marquis Wenzhong.

entries.zh: 子祿嗣，薨，無子。
entries.en: His son Lu inherited the title, then died without issue.
entries.literal: His son Lu succeeded, died, and had no son.

entries.zh: 高后乃封何夫人同為酇侯，小子延為筑陽侯。
entries.en: Empress Lü thereupon made Xiao He’s widow Tong Marquis of Zan and his younger son Yan Marquis of Zhuyang.
entries.literal: Empress Gao therefore enfeoffed He’s wife Tong as Marquis of Zan, and the younger son Yan as Marquis of Zhuyang.

entries.zh: 孝文元年，罷同，更封延為酇侯。
entries.en: In Emperor Wen’s first year Tong was stripped of her fief and Yan was reassigned as Marquis of Zan.
entries.literal: In the first year of Emperor Wen’s reign, Tong was removed and Yan was transferred to be Marquis of Zan.

entries.zh: 薨，子遺嗣。
entries.en: When Yan died, his son Yi succeeded.
entries.literal: Yan died; his son Yi succeeded.

entries.zh: 薨，無子。
entries.en: Yi died childless.
entries.literal: He died; there was no son.

entries.zh: 文帝復以遺弟則嗣，有罪免。
entries.en: Emperor Wen then named Yi's younger brother Ze heir; Ze was later dismissed for an offense.
entries.literal: Emperor Wen again had Yi's younger brother Ze succeed; for a crime he was removed.

entries.zh: 景帝二年，制詔御史：「故相國蕭何，高皇帝大功臣，所與為天下也。
entries.en: In Emperor Jing’s second year the throne ordered the censor: “Xiao He, late minister of state, was a pillar of the August Emperor’s rise; with him the founder won the realm.
entries.literal: In the second year of Emperor Jing’s reign, an edict was issued to the imperial clerk: “The former minister of state Xiao He was a great meritorious minister of the August Emperor, with whom he took possession of the empire.

entries.zh: 今其祀絕，朕甚憐之。
entries.en: His line now lacks heirs to tend his shrine, and We grieve for it.
entries.literal: Now his sacrifices are cut off; We are deeply moved.

entries.zh: 其以武陽縣戶二千封何孫嘉為列侯。」
entries.en: We therefore create his grandson Jia a ranked marquis with two thousand households at Wuyang.”
entries.literal: We therefore enfeoff his grandson Jia as a ranked marquis with two thousand households in Wuyang county.”

entries.zh: 嘉，則弟也。
entries.en: Jia was Ze’s younger brother.
entries.literal: Jia was Ze’s younger brother.

entries.zh: 薨，子勝嗣，後有罪免。
entries.en: Jia died; his son Sheng inherited, then lost the title for a crime.
entries.literal: He died; his son Sheng succeeded, and later for a crime was removed.

entries.zh: 武帝元狩中，復下詔御史：「以酇戶二千四百封何曾孫慶為酇侯，布告天下，令明知朕報蕭相國德也。」
entries.en: Under Emperor Wu, in the Yuanshou period, another edict ran: “With twenty-four hundred households at Zan We enfeoff Xiao He’s great-grandson Qing as Marquis of Zan and publish this so the world knows We honor the house of Minister Xiao.”
entries.literal: In the Yuanshou era of Emperor Wu, an edict was again issued to the clerk: “With twenty-four hundred households at Zan, We enfeoff Xiao He’s great-grandson Qing as Marquis of Zan, and proclaim it to the empire so all plainly know We repay the virtue of Minister Xiao.”

entries.zh: 慶，則子也。
entries.en: Qing was Ze’s son.
entries.literal: Qing was Ze’s son.

entries.zh: 薨，子壽成嗣，坐為太常儀牲瘦免。
entries.en: Qing died; Shoucheng succeeded but was dismissed because, as Grand Master of ceremonies, his sacrificial animals were judged too lean.
entries.literal: He died; his son Shoucheng succeeded, and was removed for the offense that, as Grand Master of ceremonies, his ritual victims were emaciated.

entries.zh: 宣帝時，詔丞相御史求問蕭相國後在者，得玄孫建世等十二人，復下詔以酇戶二千封建世為酇侯。
entries.en: Emperor Xuan ordered the chancellor and censor to locate any surviving descendants of Minister Xiao; twelve men were found, among them Jianshi, whom the court again enfeoffed at Zan with two thousand households.
entries.literal: In Emperor Xuan’s time an edict ordered the chancellor and imperial clerk to seek survivors among Minister Xiao’s posterity; they found twelve men including great-great-grandson Jianshi, and an edict was issued again enfeoffing Jianshi as Marquis of Zan with two thousand households at Zan.

entries.zh: 傳子至孫獲，坐使奴殺人減死論。
entries.en: The title passed to a son and then to the grandson Huo, who was convicted of ordering a slave to kill a man but received a sentence one degree below death.
entries.literal: It passed to a son and then to the grandson Huo, who was convicted of ordering a slave to kill a man and sentenced one degree below death.

entries.zh: 成帝時，復封何玄孫之子南讀長喜為酇侯。
entries.en: Under Emperor Cheng, Xi, a sixth-generation descendant of Xiao He and chief of Nanluan, was again named Marquis of Zan.
entries.literal: In Emperor Cheng's time, Xi, the son of Xiao He's great-great-grandson and chief of Nanluan, was again enfeoffed as Marquis of Zan.

entries.zh: 傳子至曾孫，王莽敗乃絕。
entries.en: The title passed to his son and eventually to his great-grandson; the line ended only when Wang Mang fell.
entries.literal: It passed to his son and eventually to his great-grandson, and only with Wang Mang's fall did the line end.

entries.zh: 何以丞相留收巴蜀，填撫諭告，使給軍食。
entries.en: As chancellor, Xiao He stayed behind to consolidate Ba and Shu, keep order, issue instructions, and provision the army.
entries.literal: He, as chancellor, remained behind to gather Ba and Shu, pacify and instruct the people, and supply the army with provisions.

entries.zh: 漢二年，漢王與諸侯擊楚，何守關中，侍太子，治櫟陽。
entries.en: In the second Han year, while the King of Han campaigned against Chu with the allied lords, Xiao He held Guanzhong, attended the heir apparent, and ran the government from Liyang.
entries.literal: In the second year of Han, the King of Han with the feudal lords struck Chu; He guarded Guanzhong, attended the heir apparent, and administered from Liyang.

entries.zh: 為令約束，立宗廟、社稷、宮室、縣邑，輒奏，上可許以從事；
entries.en: He promulgated laws and rules, founded the imperial temple, the altars of state, palaces, and county seats, and routinely memorialized the throne; whatever the Sovereign approved, he carried out;
entries.literal: He issued ordinances and regulations, established the ancestral temple, altars of soil and grain, palaces, and county seats, and for each matter submitted memorials; when the Sovereign approved, he might act accordingly;

entries.zh: 即不及奏，輒以便宜施行，上來以聞。
entries.en: when there was no time to wait for approval, he acted at his own discretion for the emergency and informed the Sovereign afterward.
entries.literal: If there was no time to memorialize, he would act on his own authority as expedient and report when the Sovereign came.

entries.zh: 計戶轉漕給軍，漢王數失軍遯去，何常興關中卒，輒補缺。
entries.en: He levied taxes by household, ran the grain barges, and kept the armies fed; each time the King of Han’s host was shattered and he fled, Xiao He raised fresh levies in Guanzhong to replace the losses.
entries.literal: He counted households, rotated transport by water, and supplied the army; the King of Han repeatedly lost his army and fled, but He constantly raised troops in Guanzhong and filled the gaps.

entries.zh: 上以此剸屬任何關中事。
entries.en: The Sovereign therefore left the entire administration of Guanzhong in Xiao He’s hands.
entries.literal: For this reason the Sovereign wholly entrusted all Guanzhong affairs to He.

entries.zh: 陳豨反，上自將，至邯鄲。
entries.en: When Chen Xi rose in revolt, the Sovereign took the field in person and marched to Handan.
entries.literal: When Chen Xi rebelled, the Sovereign personally led the army and reached Handan.

entries.zh: 而韓信謀反關中。
entries.en: Meanwhile Han Xin plotted revolt inside Guanzhong.
entries.literal: Meanwhile Han Xin plotted rebellion in Guanzhong.

entries.zh: 呂后用何計誅信。
entries.en: Empress Lü used Xiao He’s stratagem to put Han Xin to death.
entries.literal: Empress Lü used He’s plan to execute Xin.

entries.zh: 語在信傳。
entries.en: The details are recorded in Han Xin’s biography.
entries.literal: The account is given in Han Xin’s biography.

entries.zh: 上已聞誅信，使使拜丞相為相國，益封五千戶，令卒五百人一都尉為相國衛。
entries.en: Learning of Han Xin's death, he promoted Xiao He to minister of state, added five thousand households to his fief, and assigned him a guard of five hundred soldiers under a commandant.
entries.literal: When the Sovereign heard that Xin had been executed, he sent envoys to appoint the chancellor as minister of state and added five thousand households to his fief, assigning five hundred soldiers under a commandant as the minister of state's guard.

entries.zh: 諸君皆賀，召平獨弔。
entries.en: His colleagues offered congratulations; only Zhao Ping came to condole.
entries.literal: The gentlemen all congratulated him; Zhao Ping alone mourned.

entries.zh: 召平者，故秦東陵侯。
entries.en: Zhao Ping was the former Marquis of Dongling under Qin.
entries.literal: Zhao Ping had been the Marquis of Dongling of Qin.

entries.zh: 秦破，為布衣，貧，種瓜長安城東，瓜美，故世謂「東陵瓜」，從召平始也。
entries.en: After Qin’s fall he lived as a commoner in poverty, growing melons east of Chang’an so fine that people still speak of “Dongling melons,” after him.
entries.literal: When Qin fell he became a commoner; poor, he planted melons east of Chang’an; the melons were fine, so the world calls them “Dongling melons,” beginning from Zhao Ping.

entries.zh: 平謂何曰：「禍自此始矣。
entries.en: Zhao Ping told Xiao He, “Your troubles start here.
entries.literal: Ping said to He, “From here your calamity begins.

entries.zh: 上暴露於外，而君守於內，非被矢石之難，而益君封置衛者，以今者淮陰新反於中，有疑君心。
entries.en: The Sovereign braves the frontier while you sit in the capital, never dodging arrows or stones, yet he enlarges your fief and stations guards about you—because the Marquis of Huaiyin has just risen inside the passes, he no longer trusts you.
entries.literal: The Sovereign is exposed in the field while you guard within; you have not endured the hardship of arrows and stones, yet he increases your fief and posts guards—because the Marquis of Huaiyin has lately rebelled within, he harbors doubts about you.

entries.zh: 夫置衛衛君，非以寵君也。
entries.en: Those guards are not posted for your glory.
entries.literal: Posting guards to guard the lord is not to honor the lord.

entries.zh: 願君讓封勿受，悉以家私財佐軍。」
entries.en: Refuse the extra enfeoffment and pour your private fortune into the war effort instead.”
entries.literal: I wish you to decline the added fief and not accept it, and devote all your private wealth to aid the army.”

entries.zh: 何從其計，上說。
entries.en: Xiao He obeyed, and the Sovereign was pleased.
entries.literal: He followed his plan, and the Sovereign was pleased.

entries.zh: 上罷布軍歸，民道遮行，上書言相國彊賤買民田宅數千人。
entries.en: On the way home from the Qing Bu campaign, commoners mobbed the road with petitions accusing Minister of State Xiao He of bullying thousands of families into selling land and houses for a pittance.
entries.literal: When the Sovereign dismissed the army after Qing Bu and returned, the people along the road blocked his progress and submitted memorials saying the minister of state He forcibly bought the fields and houses of the common people at low price, several thousand persons.

entries.zh: 上至，何謁。
entries.en: When the Sovereign reached the capital, Xiao He came to audience.
entries.literal: When the Sovereign arrived, He paid his respects.

entries.zh: 上笑曰：「今相國乃利民！」
entries.en: The Sovereign laughed and said, “So my minister of state has been fleecing the people for their own good!”
entries.literal: The Sovereign laughed and said, “Now the minister of state profits the people!”

entries.zh: 民所上書皆以與何，曰：「君自謝民。」
entries.en: He handed Xiao He the sheaf of petitions and told him, “You may apologize to them yourself.”
entries.literal: The memorials the people had submitted he all gave to He, saying, “You yourself apologize to the people.”

entries.zh: 後何為民請曰：「長安地狹，上林中多空地，棄，願令民得入田，毋收稿為獸食。」
entries.en: Later Xiao He pleaded for the people: “Chang’an is crowded, while the Shanglin hunting park lies largely empty; let commoners till those fields, and do not collect the straw as fodder for the beasts.”
entries.literal: Later He made a request on behalf of the people, saying, “The land in Chang’an is cramped, while much ground in Shanglin Park lies empty and abandoned. I ask that the people be allowed to enter and farm it, without the straw being collected as fodder for the beasts.”

entries.zh: 上大怒曰：「相國多受賈人財物，為請吾苑！」
entries.en: The Sovereign exploded: “The minister of state has been bribed by merchants to beg for my hunting preserve!”
entries.literal: The Sovereign was greatly angry and said, “The minister of state has received much wealth from merchants and on their behalf requests my park!”

entries.zh: 乃下何廷尉，械繫之。
entries.en: He had Xiao He clapped in fetters and handed to the commandant of justice.
entries.literal: Thereupon he handed He to the commandant of the court, shackling and binding him.

entries.zh: 數日，王衛尉侍，前問曰：「相國胡大罪，陛下繫之暴也？」
entries.en: A few days later Commandant Wang of the palace guard, on duty at court, stepped forward: “What grave offense could warrant clapping the minister of state in irons like a common criminal?”
entries.literal: After several days, Commandant of the Guards Wang, while in attendance, stepped forward and asked, “What great crime has the minister of state committed, that Your Majesty has bound him so harshly?”

entries.zh: 上曰：「吾聞李斯相秦皇帝，有善歸主，有惡自予。
entries.en: The Sovereign said, “They say Li Si, as Qin’s chancellor, credited the throne with every success and himself with every failure;
entries.literal: The Sovereign said, “I have heard that when Li Si served as chancellor to the First Emperor of Qin, whatever was good he attributed to his lord; whatever was bad he took on himself.

entries.zh: 今相國多受賈豎金，為請吾苑，以自媚於民。
entries.en: Now my minister of state is said to have taken merchants’ gold to beg my hunting park—plainly to buy popularity.
entries.literal: Now the minister of state has accepted much gold from huckster merchants, and on their behalf has requested my park, thereby to curry favor with the people for himself.

entries.zh: 故繫治之。」
entries.en: So I had him arrested.”
entries.literal: Therefore I bound and tried him.”

entries.zh: 王衛尉曰：「夫職事苟有便於民而請之，真宰相事也。
entries.en: Wang answered, “When an officer petitions for anything that helps the people, that is precisely what a chief minister should do.
entries.literal: Wang said, “In official duty, if something benefits the people and one requests it—that is truly a chancellor’s business.

entries.zh: 陛下柰何乃疑相國受賈人錢乎！
entries.en: How can you imagine he lined his pockets from shopkeepers?
entries.literal: How can Your Majesty suspect the minister of state of taking merchants’ money!

entries.zh: 且陛下距楚數歲，陳豨、黥布反時，陛下自將往，當是時相國守關中，關中搖足則關西非陛下有也。
entries.en: For years you faced Chu in the field; when Chen Xi and Qing Bu rose, you marched yourself—while the minister of state held Guanzhong. Had that heartland wavered, nothing west of the passes would still be yours.
entries.literal: Moreover, for several years Your Majesty resisted Chu; when Chen Xi and Qing Bu rebelled, Your Majesty personally led the army thither; at that time the minister of state guarded Guanzhong—had Guanzhong so much as shifted a foot, the land west of the Pass would no longer have been Yours.

entries.zh: 相國不以此時為利，乃利賈人之金乎？
entries.en: If he meant to profit from crisis, he had his chance then—would he wait to scrape cash from peddlers?
entries.literal: Would the minister of state not have profited then, and instead profit from merchants’ gold?

entries.zh: 且秦以不聞其過亡天下，夫李斯之分過，又何足法哉！
entries.en: Qin lost the empire because its ruler never heard of his faults. Why imitate Li Si’s practice of assuming blame for his sovereign?
entries.literal: Moreover, Qin lost the empire because its ruler did not hear of his faults. Why is Li Si’s practice of taking his sovereign’s faults upon himself worth following?

entries.zh: 陛下何疑宰相之淺也！」
entries.en: You misjudge your chancellor badly.”
entries.literal: How shallowly Your Majesty doubts your chancellor!”

entries.zh: 上不懌。
entries.en: The Sovereign’s face darkened.
entries.literal: The Sovereign was displeased.

entries.zh: 是日，使使持節赦出何。
entries.en: That same day he sent an envoy with imperial credentials to free Xiao He.
entries.literal: That day he sent an envoy bearing credentials to pardon and release He.

entries.zh: 何年老，素恭謹，徒跣入謝。
entries.en: Old and habitually deferential, Xiao He came barefoot to beg forgiveness.
entries.literal: He being old, always respectful and careful, went in barefoot to apologize.

entries.zh: 上曰：「相國休矣！
entries.en: “Enough, minister of state,” said the Sovereign.
entries.literal: The Sovereign said, “Minister of state, enough!

entries.zh: 相國為民請吾苑不許，我不過為桀紂主，而相國為賢相。
entries.en: Had I refused your plea for the people, I would have ranked with Jie and Zhou, while you stood as the good minister.
entries.literal: The minister of state requested my park for the people and I would not grant it; I would have been no more than a Jie or Zhou of a lord, while the minister of state would have been the worthy chancellor.

entries.zh: 吾故繫相國，欲令百姓聞吾過。」
entries.en: I jailed you so the realm would hear of my mistake.”
entries.literal: I deliberately bound the minister of state because I wished the common people to hear of my fault.”

entries.zh: 列侯畢已受封，奏位次，皆曰：「平陽侯曹參身被七十創，攻城略地，功最多，宜第一。」
entries.en: After the ranked marquises had received their enfeoffments, the court submitted a proposed order of precedence. Everyone said, “Cao Shen, Marquis of Pingyang, personally suffered seventy wounds while storming cities and seizing territory. His merit was the greatest, and he should rank first.”
entries.literal: When the ranked marquises had all received their enfeoffments and submitted the order of precedence, all said, “Marquis of Pingyang Cao Shen personally received seventy wounds in storming cities and seizing territory; his achievement was the greatest and he should be first.”

entries.zh: 上已橈功臣多封何，至位次未有以復難之，然心欲何第一。
entries.en: The emperor had already overruled the meritorious ministers to give Xiao He the larger fief. He had no further argument when it came to precedence, though he still wanted Xiao He ranked first.
entries.literal: The Sovereign had already overruled the meritorious ministers to grant He the larger fief; when it came to precedence he had no further grounds on which to oppose them, yet in his heart he wished He to be first.

entries.zh: 關內侯鄂千秋時為謁者，進曰：「群臣議皆誤。
entries.en: E Qianqiu, Marquis Guannei, then a court usher, stepped forward: “They are wrong.
entries.literal: Marquis Guannei E Qianqiu, then serving as usher, advanced and said, “The assembled ministers are mistaken.

entries.zh: 夫曹參雖有野戰略地之功，此特一時之事。
entries.en: Cao Shen’s battlefield conquests matter only for a single campaign.
entries.literal: Though Cao Shen has achievement in field campaigns and seizing territory, that is merely a moment’s work.

entries.zh: 夫上與楚相距五歲，失軍亡眾，跳身遯者數矣，然蕭何常從關中遣軍補其處。
entries.en: For five years the Sovereign grappled with Chu, again and again shattered and fleeing alone, while Xiao He repeatedly refilled his ranks from Guanzhong.
entries.literal: When the Sovereign for five years faced Chu, losing armies and multitudes, several times leaping his person to escape, yet Xiao He constantly from Guanzhong sent troops to fill those places.

entries.zh: 非上所詔令召，而數萬眾會上乏絕者數矣。
entries.en: Without waiting for an edict, Xiao He repeatedly assembled tens of thousands of men just when the emperor's forces were depleted.
entries.literal: Without an edict summoning them, tens of thousands of men assembled just when the Sovereign's forces were exhausted; this happened several times.

entries.zh: 夫漢與楚相守滎陽數年，軍無見糧，蕭何轉漕關中，給食不乏。
entries.en: Years at Xingyang without grain in camp—yet Xiao He’s barges from Guanzhong never let the men go hungry.
entries.literal: When Han and Chu held each other at Xingyang for years, the army had no grain in sight, yet Xiao He transported grain by water from Guanzhong and provisions did not fail.

entries.zh: 陛下雖數亡山東，蕭何常全關中待陛下，此萬世功也。
entries.en: You lost Shandong again and again, but Xiao He kept Guanzhong whole for your return—that is merit for the ages.
