entries.literal: Because he was close at hand and they feared him, they transferred Fen to be chancellor to the feudal lords.

entries.zh: 奮長子建，次甲，次乙，次慶，皆以馴行孝謹，官至二千石。
entries.en: His sons Jian, Jia, Yi, and Qing—every one dutiful, filial, and careful—each rose to two-thousand-picul office.
entries.literal: Fen’s eldest son was Jian, next Jia, next Yi, next Qing; all by docile conduct, filial piety, and caution reached salaries of two thousand piculs.

entries.zh: 於是景帝曰：「石君及四子皆二千石，人臣尊寵乃舉集其門。」
entries.en: Emperor Jing remarked, “The Shi household now holds five posts at two thousand piculs; favor has massed at one door.”
entries.literal: Thereupon Emperor Jing said, “Lord Shi and his four sons all hold two-thousand-picul posts; a subject’s honor and favor have gathered in a single gate.”

entries.zh: 凡號奮為萬石君。
entries.en: Hence people called him the Lord of Wan—the “ten thousand piculs” lord.
entries.literal: In all they called Fen the Lord of Wan.

entries.zh: 孝景季年，萬石君以上大夫祿歸老于家，以歲時為朝臣。
entries.en: In Emperor Jing’s closing years he retired on a senior grandee’s stipend, appearing at court only on seasonal occasions.
entries.literal: In the last years of Emperor Jing, the Lord of Wan retired to his home on the salary of a senior grandee and, by the seasons, attended court as a minister.

entries.zh: 過宮門闕必下車趨，見路馬必軾焉。
entries.en: He would dismount and quicken his step at every palace gate; if he saw the emperor’s horses on the road he touched the chariot rail in respect.
entries.literal: Passing palace gates and towers he always dismounted and hurried on foot; seeing the ruler’s horses on the road he always laid his hand on the chariot rail in salute.

entries.zh: 子孫爲小吏，來歸謁，萬石君必朝服見之，不名。
entries.en: When a grandson who held even a minor post came to visit, he received him in full court dress and never used a familiar name.
entries.literal: When grandsons who served as petty clerks came home to pay their respects, the Lord of Wan always received them in court dress and never called them by personal name.

entries.zh: 子孫有過失，不誚讓，爲便坐，對案不食。
entries.en: When they erred he offered no sharp rebuke—only withdrew to a side seat and refused to eat at the table.
entries.literal: If grandsons had faults he did not scold aloud; he sat to one side at a side seat and would not eat facing the table.

entries.zh: 然後諸子相責，因長老肉袒固謝罪，改之，迺許。
entries.en: The sons then rebuked one another; the elders stripped to the waist to plead until the fault was amended and he relented.
entries.literal: Then the sons blamed one another; through the elders they bared their shoulders and firmly apologized; once corrected, only then would he grant pardon.

entries.zh: 子孫勝冠者在側，雖燕必冠，申申如也。
entries.en: Grandsons who had come of age kept their caps on even in private leisure, their bearing solemn and composed.
entries.literal: Grandsons who had passed cap-pledging age and were present at his side always wore their caps even at leisure, grave and composed in bearing.

entries.zh: 僮僕訢訢如也，唯謹。
entries.en: The servants were easy and orderly; discipline ran through every detail.
entries.literal: The household servants were respectful and mild; all was done with utmost care.

entries.zh: 上時賜食於家，必稽首俯伏而食，如在上前。
entries.en: Imperial gifts of food he accepted on his knees, touching his forehead to the floor, as though dining in the ruler’s presence.
entries.literal: When the emperor sent food to his house, he always knocked his head on the ground and ate prostrate, as if the ruler stood before him.

entries.zh: 其執喪，哀戚甚。
entries.en: In mourning he showed profound grief.
entries.literal: In conducting mourning he was deeply grief-stricken.

entries.zh: 子孫遵教，亦如之。
entries.en: The younger generations imitated him in this as in everything else.
entries.literal: The grandsons followed his teaching and did likewise.

entries.zh: 萬石君家以孝謹聞乎郡國，雖齊魯諸儒質行，皆自以為不及也。
entries.en: Word of their filial care spread through every province; the sober Confucians of Qi and Lu conceded they could not equal the household.
entries.literal: The Lord of Wan’s house was known through the commanderies and kingdoms for filial piety and caution; even the Confucian gentlemen of Qi and Lu, for all their plain virtue, thought themselves inferior.

entries.zh: 衛綰，代大陵人也，以戲車為郎，事文帝，功次遷中郎將，醇謹無它。
entries.en: Wei Wan of Daling in Dai entered the guard corps as a stunt charioteer, rose under Emperor Wen to General of the Household, and was stolidly reliable.
entries.literal: Wei Wan was a man of Daling in Dai; by acrobatic chariotry he became a gentleman-at-court and served Emperor Wen, advancing by merit to General of the Household and was pure and careful beyond ordinary.

entries.zh: 孝景為太子時，召上左右飲，而綰稱病不行。
entries.en: When still heir apparent Jing had invited the emperor’s attendants to a banquet; Wan declined on grounds of illness.
entries.literal: When Emperor Jing was Heir Apparent he summoned those about the emperor to drink, but Wan pleaded illness and did not go.

entries.zh: 文帝且崩時，屬孝景曰：「綰長者，善遇之。」
entries.en: Wen’s deathbed words to Jing were, “Wan is a steady man—keep him close.”
entries.literal: When Emperor Wen was about to die he charged Emperor Jing, saying, “Wan is a man of mature years; treat him well.”

entries.zh: 及景帝立，歲餘，不孰何綰，綰日以謹力。
entries.en: Jing never investigated him; year by year Wan only grew more careful.
entries.literal: When Emperor Jing had been on the throne a little more than a year he had not scrutinized Wan, and Wan daily grew more careful and diligent.

entries.zh: 景帝幸上林，詔中郎將參乘，還而問曰：「君知所以得驂乘乎？」
entries.en: When Emperor Jing visited Shanglin Park, he ordered the General of the Household to ride beside him in the chariot. On returning, he asked, “Do you know why you were allowed to ride beside me?”
entries.literal: When Emperor Jing favored Shanglin Park he ordered the General of the Household to ride as guard in the chariot; on returning he asked, “Do you know why you were allowed to ride as guard?”

entries.zh: 綰曰：「臣代戲車士，幸得功次遷，待罪中郎將，不知也。」
entries.en: Wan said, “I was a Dai chariot acrobat who rose by seniority; I am honored to hold this post—I cannot guess.”
entries.literal: Wan said, “I am a stunt charioteer from Dai who by fortune of merit rose in rank; I await punishment as General of the Household—I do not know.”

entries.zh: 上問曰：「吾為太子時召君，君不肯來，何也？」
entries.en: The emperor pressed: “As heir I called you to a feast and you stayed away—why?”
entries.literal: The emperor asked, “When I was Heir Apparent I summoned you and you would not come—why?”

entries.zh: 對曰：「死罪，病。」
entries.en: “I deserve death for it—I was ill,” he answered.
entries.literal: He replied, “Death-worthy crime—I was ill.”

entries.zh: 上賜之劍，綰曰：「先帝賜臣劍凡六，不敢奉詔。」
entries.en: Offered a new sword, he said, “The late emperor gave me six; I cannot take another.”
entries.literal: The emperor bestowed a sword; Wan said, “The late emperor gave me swords, six in all; I dare not accept the decree.”

entries.zh: 上曰：「劍，人之所施易，獨至今乎？」
entries.en: “Swords are traded every day—have you hoarded yours alone?”
entries.literal: The emperor said, “Swords are what people exchange; do you alone keep them to this day?”

entries.zh: 綰曰：「具在。」
entries.en: “They are all here,” said Wan.
entries.literal: Wan said, “They are all there.”

entries.zh: 上使取六劍，劍常盛，未嘗服也。
entries.en: Messengers brought the six blades—still bright in their sheaths, never worn.
entries.literal: The emperor sent for the six swords; they were always full and bright; he had never worn them.

entries.zh: 明年，上廢太子，誅栗卿之屬。
entries.en: The following year the crown prince was cast aside and Li Qing’s faction was put to the sword.
entries.literal: The next year the emperor deposed the Heir Apparent and executed Li Qing and his kind.

entries.zh: 上以綰為長者，不忍，乃賜綰告歸，而使郅都治捕栗氏。
entries.en: Jing still treated Wan as an elder he would not soil with that purge, sent him on leave, and handed the Li roundup to Zhi Du.
entries.literal: The emperor, holding Wan a man of mature years, could not bear to use him in it, therefore gave Wan leave to go home while he sent Zhi Du to arrest the Li clan.

entries.zh: 既已，上立膠東王為太子，召綰拜為太子太傅，遷為御史大夫。
entries.en: Once the heir from Jiaodong was chosen, Wan was recalled as his tutor and soon advanced to Imperial Clerk.
entries.literal: When that was done, the emperor established the Prince of Jiaodong as Heir Apparent, summoned Wan, appointed him Grand Tutor to the Heir Apparent, and promoted him to Imperial Clerk.

entries.zh: 五歲，代桃侯舍為丞相，朝奏事如職所奏。
entries.en: Five years on he succeeded Marquis Liu She of Tao as chancellor, filing routine memorials without flourish.
entries.literal: After five years he replaced Marquis of Tao She as chancellor, and at court he reported affairs as his office required.

entries.zh: 然自初宦以至相，終無可言。
entries.en: From first appointment to the highest seat he left almost no policy record.
entries.literal: Yet from his first office to the chancellorship there was in the end nothing memorable to say.

entries.zh: 上以為敦厚可相少主，尊寵之，賞賜甚多。
entries.en: The emperor deemed him steady enough for a boy emperor, showered him with favor, and piled on rewards.
entries.literal: The emperor thought him staunch enough to assist a young ruler, honored and favored him, and bestowed many gifts.

entries.zh: 為丞相三歲，景帝崩，武帝立。
entries.en: He held the seal three years; Jing died and Wu took the throne.
entries.literal: He was chancellor three years when Emperor Jing died and Emperor Wu ascended.

entries.zh: 建元中，丞相以景帝病時諸官囚多坐不辜者，而君不任職，免之。
entries.en: Early in Emperor Wu’s Jianyuan reign the court stripped him of the chancellorship, citing the jailings of the innocent during Emperor Jing’s final illness and his own failure to act while in that post.
entries.literal: In the Jianyuan era the chancellor was removed from office on the charge that, while Emperor Jing was ill, many officials and prisoners had been held under unjust conviction, yet you, sir, had not discharged your duties.

entries.zh: 後薨，諡曰哀侯。
entries.en: He died not long after, posthumously styled Marquis Ai.
entries.literal: Later he died; his posthumous title was Marquis Ai (“Lamentable”).

entries.zh: 子信嗣，坐酎金，國除。
entries.en: His heir Xin lost the fief over the vassals’ gold offering.
entries.literal: His son Xin inherited; for the fault of the sacrificial gold the marquisate was abolished.

entries.zh: 吳楚反時，不疑以二千石將擊之。
entries.en: During the revolt of Wu and Chu he commanded troops as a two-thousand-bushel minister.
entries.literal: When the Wu and Chu revolted, Buyi led troops as a two-thousand-bushel official to strike them.

entries.zh: 景帝後元年，拜爲御史大夫。
entries.en: In the first year of Emperor Jing's later reign, he was made Grand Secretary.
entries.literal: In the first year of the latter reign of Emperor Jing, he was appointed Grand Secretary.

entries.zh: 天子脩吳楚時功，封不疑爲塞侯。
entries.en: For his Wu-Chu service the emperor enfeoffed him as Marquis of Sai.
entries.literal: The Son of Heaven rewarded his service in the Wu-Chu campaign and enfeoffed Buyi as Marquis of Sai.

entries.zh: 武帝即位，與丞相綰俱以過免。
entries.en: At Wu's accession both he and Chancellor Wan were removed for misconduct.
entries.literal: When Emperor Wu took the throne, he and Chancellor Wan were both dismissed for faults.

entries.zh: 周仁，其先任城人也。
entries.en: Zhou Ren’s family hailed from Rencheng.
entries.literal: Zhou Ren’s ancestors were men of Rencheng.

entries.zh: 以毉見。
entries.en: He entered court on the strength of his medical skill.
entries.literal: He gained audience through medicine.

entries.zh: 景帝為太子時，為舍人，積功遷至太中大夫。
entries.en: While Jing was still heir apparent Ren served as household attendant and climbed to Grand Counselor of the Palace.
entries.literal: When Emperor Jing was Heir Apparent, Ren was a household attendant and accumulated merit until Grand Counselor of the Palace.

entries.zh: 景帝初立，拜仁為郎中令。
entries.en: At the beginning of Jing’s reign Ren became Palace Commandant.
entries.literal: When Emperor Jing first ascended the throne, he appointed Ren Palace Commandant.

entries.zh: 仁為人陰重不泄。
entries.en: Ren was close-mouthed, imperturbable, and impossible to read.
entries.literal: Ren’s person was secretive, weighty, and reticent.

entries.zh: 常衣弊補衣溺袴，期爲不絜清，以是得幸，入卧內。
entries.en: He affected torn, patched garments and urine-stained trousers so he would look too foul for intrigue—exactly the disguise that won him access to the inner rooms.
entries.literal: He constantly wore ragged patched clothes and urine-soiled trousers, intending to seem unclean; by this he won favor and was admitted to the bedchamber.

entries.zh: 於後宮祕戲，仁常在旁，終無所言。
entries.en: When the consorts staged their private entertainments he stood by in silence year after year.
entries.literal: During the harem’s private amusements Ren was always at hand yet never spoke.

entries.zh: 上時問人，仁曰：「上自察之。」
entries.en: If the emperor asked his opinion of a man, he answered only, “Your Majesty must judge that yourself.”
entries.literal: When the emperor sometimes asked him about people, Ren said, “Let Your Majesty examine them yourself.”

entries.zh: 然亦無所毀，如此。
entries.en: He maligned no one either; his neutrality was absolute.
entries.literal: Yet he also slandered no one; it was always thus.

entries.zh: 景帝再自幸其家。
entries.en: Jing called at his home twice in person.
entries.literal: Emperor Jing twice in person visited his house.

entries.zh: 家徙陽陵。
entries.en: The family later relocated to Yangling.
entries.literal: The household moved to Yangling.

entries.zh: 上所賜甚多，然終常讓，不敢受也。
entries.en: Imperial largesse flowed freely, yet he habitually refused it.
entries.literal: What the emperor bestowed was very much, yet he always declined and did not dare accept.

entries.zh: 諸侯群臣賂遺，終無所受。
entries.en: He took nothing—from princes, ministers, or anyone who offered gifts or bribes.
entries.literal: From feudal lords and ministers, gifts and bribes, he never accepted.

entries.zh: 武帝立，為先帝臣重之。
entries.en: Wu honored him as a survivor of his father’s court.
entries.literal: When Emperor Wu ascended, as a minister of the late emperor he was held in high regard.

entries.zh: 仁乃病免，以二千石祿歸老，子孫咸至大官。
entries.en: He resigned on grounds of illness, retired on a minister’s stipend, and left descendants who rose to the highest ranks.
entries.literal: Ren then pleaded illness and retired, returning home on a two-thousand-picul salary; grandsons and descendants all reached high office.

entries.zh: 贊曰：仲尼有言「君子欲訥於言而敏於行」，其萬石君、建陵侯、塞侯、張叔之謂與？
entries.en: The appraisal says: Confucius said, “The gentleman wishes to be slow in speech yet quick in action.” Was he not speaking of the Lord of Wan, the Marquis of Jianling, the Marquis of Sai, and Zhang Shu?
entries.literal: The appraisal says: Confucius said, “The gentleman wishes to be slow in speech yet quick in action”—does this not speak of the Lord of Wan, the Marquis of Jianling, the Marquis of Sai, and Zhang Shu?

entries.zh: 是以其教不肅而成，不嚴而治。
entries.en: Their example brought order without thunder, discipline without the rod.
entries.literal: Therefore their instruction was accomplished without severity, and order was achieved without harshness.

entries.zh: 至石建之澣衣，周仁為垢汙，君子譏之。
entries.en: Still, later moralists have smiled at Shi Jian scrubbing bedpans and Zhou Ren’s studied squalor.
entries.literal: Yet when it comes to Shi Jian rinsing clothes and Zhou Ren’s filthy disguise, gentlemen have mocked them.

entries.zh: 建元二年，郎中令王臧以文學獲罪皇太后。
entries.en: In the second year of Jianyuan, Palace Commandant Wang Zang incurred the Grand Empress Dowager's displeasure because of his Confucian learning.
entries.literal: In the second year of the Jianyuan era, Palace Commandant Wang Zang incurred punishment over literary factional politics involving the Grand Empress Dowager.

entries.zh: 太后以為儒者文多質少，今萬石君家不言而躬行，乃以長子建為郎中令，少子慶為內史。
entries.en: She distrusted bookish rhetoric and prized the Shis’ silent example, so she named Jian Palace Commandant and Qing Secretary of the Capital.
entries.literal: The Grand Empress Dowager held that Confucians had much ornament and little substance; now the Lord of Wan’s house did not speak but acted; she therefore made the eldest son Jian Palace Commandant and the youngest son Qing Secretary of the Capital.

entries.zh: 萬石君元朔五年卒，建哭泣哀思，杖乃能行。
entries.en: He died in the fifth year of Yuanshuo; Jian mourned until he could barely walk without a staff.
entries.literal: In the fifth year of Yuanshuo the Lord of Wan died; Jian wept in grief so that he needed a staff to walk.

entries.zh: 歲餘，建亦死。
entries.en: A year later Jian followed him.
entries.literal: After a little more than a year Jian also died.

entries.zh: 諸子孫咸孝，然建最甚，甚於萬石君。
entries.en: Every descendant was dutiful, yet none surpassed Jian—not even the old lord himself.
entries.literal: All the grandsons were filial, but Jian was the most so—more than even the Lord of Wan.

entries.zh: 萬石君徙居陵里。
entries.en: The household later moved to Mausoleum ward.
entries.literal: The Lord of Wan moved his residence to Mausoleum ward.

entries.zh: 內史慶醉歸，入外門不下車。
entries.en: Qing, drunk one night, rode through the outer gate without dismounting.
entries.literal: Secretary of the Capital Qing, drunk, came home and did not get out of his chariot at the outer gate.

entries.zh: 萬石君聞之，不食。
entries.en: The old man heard and went on a hunger strike.
entries.literal: When the Lord of Wan heard of it, he refused to eat.

entries.zh: 慶恐，肉袒謝請罪，不許。
entries.en: Qing stripped to the waist to apologize; the father would not relent.
entries.literal: Qing was afraid; he bared his shoulder and begged forgiveness; it was not granted.

entries.zh: 舉宗及兄建肉袒，萬石君讓曰：「內史貴人，入閭里，里中長老皆走匿，而內史坐車中自如，固當！」
entries.en: The whole family, with Jian, bared their shoulders until the patriarch cried, “A capital secretary is a grandee: the elders scatter when you enter the lane, yet you ride through at ease—how fitting!”
entries.literal: The whole clan and his elder brother Jian bared their shoulders; the Lord of Wan rebuked him, saying, “The Secretary of the Capital is a nobleman; when he enters the lane the village elders all flee and hide, yet he sits in his chariot at ease—as indeed he should!”

entries.zh: 乃謝罷慶。
entries.en: Only then did he forgive Qing and send him off.
entries.literal: Thereupon he excused Qing and dismissed him.

entries.zh: 慶及諸子入里門，趨至家。
entries.en: After that Qing and his sons dismounted at the ward gate and ran the rest of the way.
entries.literal: Qing and his sons thereafter entered the lane gate at a run and hurried home.

entries.zh: 建老白首，萬石君尚無恙。
entries.en: Jian’s hair had turned white while his father remained vigorous.
entries.literal: Jian was old and white-haired, yet the Lord of Wan was still hale.

entries.zh: 每五日洗沐歸謁親，入子舍，竊問侍者，取親中帬厠牏，身自澣洒，復與侍者，不敢令萬石君知之，以為常。
entries.en: On each five-day rest he went home, slipped into his parents’ rooms, took the old man’s undergarment and bedpan screen from the servants, scrubbed them himself, and handed them back—all without Father’s knowledge, week after week.
entries.literal: Every five days, on bath-leave, he would return to visit his parents, enter their quarters, secretly ask the attendants, take his father’s undergarment and privy-screen liner, wash and rinse it himself, return it to the attendants, and never let the Lord of Wan know—making this his constant practice.

entries.zh: 建奏事於上前，即有可言，屏人乃言極切；
entries.en: Before the throne he spoke his mind bluntly once the room was cleared;
entries.literal: When Jian reported affairs before the emperor, if there was something to be said he sent others away and spoke with utmost frankness;

entries.zh: 至廷見，如不能言者。
entries.en: in open session he looked tongue-tied.
entries.literal: at court audience he seemed unable to speak.

entries.zh: 上以是親而禮之。
entries.en: The emperor therefore trusted and honored him.
entries.literal: For this the emperor drew close to him and treated him with ceremony.

entries.zh: 建為郎中令，奏事下，建讀之，驚恐曰：「書『馬』者與尾而五，今乃四，不足一，獲譴死矣！」
entries.en: As Palace Commandant he once read an edict and panicked: “The character ma ‘horse’ should have five strokes; this copy has four—I am a dead man for the blunder!”
entries.literal: When Jian was Palace Commandant, a document came down from above; Jian read it and said in alarm, “In writing ‘horse’ one joins the tail and has five strokes; now there are only four—one short; I shall die for the fault!”

entries.zh: 其為謹慎，雖他皆如是。
entries.en: That was his level of care in everything he did.
entries.literal: Such was his caution; in other matters it was always thus.

entries.zh: 元狩元年，上立太子，選群臣可傅者，慶自沛守為太子太傅，七歲遷御史大夫。
entries.en: In the first year of Yuanshou, when the heir apparent was installed, ministers fit to tutor him were chosen; Qing rose from governor of Pei to Grand Tutor, then after seven years to Grand Clerk.
entries.literal: In the first year of Yuanshou the emperor established the Heir Apparent and chose from the ministers who could tutor him; Qing went from governor of Pei to Grand Tutor to the Heir Apparent, and after seven years was promoted Grand Clerk.

entries.zh: 元鼎五年，丞相趙周坐酎金免，制詔御史：「萬石君先帝尊之，子孫至孝，其以御史大夫慶為丞相，封牧丘侯。」
entries.en: In the fifth year of Yuanding, Chancellor Zhao Zhou was dismissed over the sacrificial gold. An edict to the Imperial Clerk said, “The late emperor honored the Lord of Wan, and his descendants are deeply filial. Let Grand Clerk Qing be made chancellor and enfeoffed as Marquis of Muqiu.”
entries.literal: In the fifth year of Yuanding Chancellor Zhao Zhou was dismissed for the fault of the sacrificial gold; an edict to the Imperial Clerk said, “The Lord of Wan was honored by the late emperor; his descendants are supremely filial; let Grand Clerk Qing be made chancellor and enfeoffed as Marquis of Muqiu.”

entries.zh: 是時漢方南誅兩越，東擊朝鮮，北逐匈奴，西伐大宛，中國多事。
entries.en: The empire was at war on every frontier—Yue, Joseon, the Xiongnu, and Dayuan—while the heartland churned with business.
entries.literal: At that time Han was in the south destroying the two Yue, in the east attacking Joseon, in the north driving off the Xiongnu, and in the west campaigning against Dayuan; the central lands had many affairs.

entries.zh: 天子巡狩海內，修古神祠，封禪，興禮樂。
entries.en: The emperor toured the empire, refurbished ancient cults, carried out Feng and Shan, and revived rites and music.
entries.literal: The Son of Heaven toured the realm within the seas, restored ancient shrines, performed the Feng and Shan sacrifices, and promoted ritual and music.

entries.zh: 公家用少，桑弘羊等致利，王溫舒之屬峻法，兒寬等推文學，九卿更進用事，事不關決於慶，慶醇謹而已。
entries.en: Treasury was lean: Sang Hongyang squeezed revenue, Wang Wenshu’s faction wielded harsh codes, Ni Kuan’s circle pushed scholarship; ministers jostled for influence while Qing, ever cautious, scarcely decided a thing.
entries.literal: Public expense was tight; Sang Hongyang and others brought profit; men like Wang Wenshu enforced harsh law; Ni Kuan and others pushed literary learning; the Nine Ministers rotated in power; affairs did not await Qing’s decision—Qing was only pure and careful.

entries.zh: 在位九歲，無能有所匡言。
entries.en: Nine years in the chancellorship passed without a memorable policy from him.
entries.literal: In office nine years he was able to offer no corrective counsel.

entries.zh: 嘗欲請治上近臣所忠、九卿咸宣，不能服，反受其過，贖罪。
entries.en: He tried to indict the favorites Suozhong and Xian Xuan, failed, and was fined for his trouble.
entries.literal: He once wished to impeach the emperor’s close attendant Suozhong and Minister Xian Xuan but could not prevail and instead suffered blame, paying a fine in lieu.

entries.zh: 上報曰：「間者，河水滔陸，泛濫十餘郡，隄防勤勞，弗能陻塞，朕甚憂之。
entries.en: The reply ran: “Lately the river has overrun its banks and swamped a dozen commanderies; dikes have failed despite every effort, and I am gravely worried.
entries.literal: The emperor replied, saying, “Recently the Yellow River overflowed the dry land, flooded more than ten commanderies, and though dikes and levees toiled, they could not be secured; I am deeply troubled.

entries.zh: 是故巡方州，禮嵩嶽，通八神，以合宣房。
entries.en: Therefore I toured the regions, performed rites at Mount Song, and communed with the Eight Spirits, following the precedent of Xuanfang.
entries.literal: Therefore I toured the provinces, sacrificed at Mount Song, and communicated with the Eight Gods, thereby bringing these acts into accord with Xuanfang.

entries.zh: 濟淮江，歷山濱海，問百年民所疾苦。
entries.en: I crossed the Ji, Huai, and Chang Jiang, traced coast and hill, and asked the aged what ailed the common folk.
entries.literal: I crossed the Ji, Huai, and Yangzi, passed mountains and skirted the sea, and asked centenarians what pained the people.

entries.zh: 惟吏多私，徵求無已，去者便，居者擾，故為流民法，以禁重賦。
entries.en: Local officials still line their pockets and tax without end, driving people from their homes; I issued statutes for refugees to curb extortion.
entries.literal: Only the clerks are much given to private ends; exactions never cease; those who leave find it easy, those who stay are harassed; therefore I made a law for displaced persons to forbid heavy levies.

entries.zh: 乃者封泰山，皇天嘉況，神物並見。
entries.en: At the recent Feng on Mount Tai Heaven signaled approval and omens multiplied.
entries.literal: Recently I performed the Feng sacrifice on Mount Tai; High Heaven showed favor; divine tokens appeared together.

entries.zh: 朕方答氣應，未能承意，是以切比閭里，知吏姦邪。
entries.en: I was occupied with answering Heaven’s signs and had not yet taken your meaning to heart; therefore I have gone close to the villages to learn clerical corruption.
entries.literal: I was then responding to the cosmic manifestations and had not yet been able to heed your counsel; therefore I have gone close to the villages to learn clerical corruption.

entries.zh: 委任有司，然則官曠民愁，盜賊公行。
entries.en: I left affairs to the bureaus—only to see posts neglected, popular resentment rise, and robbery flourish in the open.
entries.literal: I entrusted matters to the responsible offices; yet offices stood idle and the people grew bitter, and bandits walked openly.

entries.zh: 往年覲明堂，赦殊死，無禁錮，咸自新，與更始。
entries.en: Last time I visited the Bright Hall I spared capital offenders and lifted legal disabilities so men could begin anew.
entries.literal: In former years I visited the Bright Hall, pardoned capital crimes, lifted prohibitions and bonds, so all might renew themselves with a fresh start.

entries.zh: 今流民愈多，計文不改，君不繩責長吏，而請以興徙四十萬口，搖蕩百姓，孤兒幼年未滿十歲，無罪而坐率，朕失望焉。
entries.en: Refugees increase while your tallies lie; instead of punishing magistrates you would uproot four hundred thousand innocents, even children under ten, by mass banishment—I expected better.
entries.literal: Now the displaced grow more numerous; the accounts are unchanged; you do not bind and punish the chief officials, yet you ask to move four hundred thousand mouths, shaking the people; orphans not yet ten, without crime, would sit under collective guilt—I am disappointed.

entries.zh: 今君上書言倉庫城郭不充實，民多貧，盜賊眾，請入粟為庶人。
entries.en: Now you write that granaries gape, the poor swarm, thieves multiply, and you offer to pay grain and resign.
entries.literal: Now you submit a memorial saying granaries and walls are not full, the people are many and poor, bandits are numerous, and you ask to yield grain and become a commoner.

entries.zh: 夫懷知民貧而請益賦，動危之而辭位，欲安歸難乎？
entries.en: You know their want yet talk of new taxes; you stir crisis then quit—how is that to bring peace?
entries.literal: You harbor the knowledge that the people are poor yet ask to increase levies; you stir danger yet leave your post—where do you think difficulty will go?

entries.zh: 君其反室！」
entries.en: Go back to your office!”
entries.literal: You shall return to your quarters!”

entries.zh: 老篤，請免，天子亦寵以上大夫祿，歸老于家。
entries.en: Age and frailty brought a request for release; the court kept him on a senior grandee’s pay at home.
entries.literal: Old and infirm, he begged to be dismissed; the emperor also favored him with a senior grandee’s salary and let him retire home.

entries.zh: 家陽陵。
entries.en: He ended his days at Yangling.
entries.literal: His home was at Yangling.

entries.zh: 子孫咸至大官。
entries.en: His posterity likewise rose to great posts.
entries.literal: Grandsons and descendants all reached high office.

entries.zh: 卷四十六 萬石衛直周張傳第十六
entries.en: Volume 46: Biography 16 — The Lords of Wan, Wei, Zhi, Zhou, and Zhang.
entries.literal: Volume 46: Biography 16 — The Lords of Wan, Wei, Zhi, Zhou, and Zhang.

entries.zh: 孝文皇帝四男：竇皇后生孝景帝、梁孝王武，諸姬生代孝王參、梁懷王揖。
entries.en: Emperor Wen had four sons. Empress Dou gave birth to Emperor Jing and King Xiao Wu of Liang; other consorts bore King Xiao Can of Dai and King Huai Yi of Liang.
entries.literal: Emperor Xiaowen had four sons: Empress Dou bore Emperor Xiaojing and King Xiao Wu of Liang; various concubines bore King Xiao Can of Dai and King Huai Yi of Liang.

entries.zh: 二十九年十月，孝王入朝。
entries.en: In the tenth month of his twenty-ninth year as king he came to court.
entries.literal: In the twenty-ninth year, tenth month, the Filial King entered court.

entries.zh: 景帝使使持乘輿駟，迎梁王於關下。
entries.en: Emperor Jing dispatched officials with the imperial team of four bays to meet the king of Liang outside the frontier passes.
entries.literal: Emperor Jing sent envoys bearing the imperial four-horse carriage to welcome the King of Liang below the passes.

entries.zh: 既朝，上疏，因留。
entries.en: After his audience he petitioned to remain, and was allowed to stay.
entries.literal: Having had audience, he submitted a memorial and therefore stayed.

entries.zh: 以太后故，入則侍帝同輦，出則同車遊獵上林中。
entries.en: For his mother’s sake he rode with the emperor in the same palanquin when they went in, and hunted together in the imperial park in the same chariot when they went out.
entries.literal: Because of the empress dowager, when entering he attended the emperor sharing the same palanquin; when going out he rode the same chariot hunting in Shanglin Park.

entries.zh: 梁之侍中、郎、謁者著引籍出入天子殿門，與漢宦官亡異。
entries.en: Liang’s household chamberlains, gentlemen-in-attendance, and ushers entered the palace gates on registry tallies exactly like the emperor’s own staff.
entries.literal: Liang’s palace attendants, gentlemen, and petitioners, wearing their tallies, passed in and out of the Son of Heaven’s hall gates; there was no difference from Han eunuchs.

entries.zh: 孝王十四年，入朝。
entries.en: In his fourteenth year as king, he came to the capital for an audience.
entries.literal: In the Filial King’s fourteenth year, he entered court for an audience.

entries.zh: 十七年、十八年，比年入朝，留。
entries.en: In the seventeenth and eighteenth years he came to court two years running and remained at the capital.
entries.literal: In the seventeenth and eighteenth years, in successive years he entered court and stayed.

entries.zh: 其明年，乃之國。
entries.en: The following year he returned to his kingdom.
entries.literal: The next year, then he went to his state.

entries.zh: 二十一年，入朝。
entries.en: In his twenty-first year he came to court again.
entries.literal: In the twenty-first year, he entered court.

entries.zh: 二十二年，文帝崩。
entries.en: In the twenty-second year Emperor Wen died.
entries.literal: In the twenty-second year, Emperor Wen died.

entries.zh: 二十四年，入朝。
entries.en: In the twenty-fourth year he came to court.
entries.literal: In the twenty-fourth year, he entered court.

entries.zh: 二十五年，復入朝。
entries.en: In the twenty-fifth year he came once more.
entries.literal: In the twenty-fifth year, again he entered court.

entries.zh: 是時，上未置太子，與孝王宴飲，從容言曰：「千秋萬歲後傳於王。」
entries.en: The emperor had not yet named an heir. At a banquet with the king of Liang he said at ease, “When a thousand autumns and ten thousand years have passed, I will transmit the throne to you, my king.”
entries.literal: At this time the sovereign had not yet installed a crown prince; feasting and drinking with the Filial King, he spoke at ease, saying: “After a thousand autumns and ten thousand years I will transmit to the king.”

entries.zh: 王辭謝。
entries.en: The king demurred and thanked him.
entries.literal: The king declined and thanked him.

entries.zh: 雖知非至言，然心內喜。
entries.en: He knew these were not words meant in earnest, yet he could not help rejoicing inwardly.
entries.literal: Although he knew it was not sincere speech, yet inwardly he was pleased.

entries.zh: 太后亦然。
entries.en: The empress dowager felt the same way.
entries.literal: The empress dowager was likewise so.

entries.zh: 其夏，上立膠東王為太子。
entries.en: That summer the emperor named the prince of Jiaodong crown prince.
entries.literal: That summer, the sovereign established the King of Jiaodong as crown prince.

entries.zh: 梁王怨爰盎及議臣，乃與羊勝、公孫詭之屬謀，陰使人刺殺爰盎及他議臣十餘人。
entries.en: The king of Liang blamed Yuan Ang and the ministers who had opposed him. With Yang Sheng, Gongsun Gui, and their confederates he arranged the secret murder of Yuan Ang and more than a dozen others who had spoken against him.
entries.literal: The King of Liang resented Yuan Ang and the deliberating ministers; then with Yang Sheng, Gongsun Gui, and their sort he plotted; secretly he sent men to assassinate Yuan Ang and more than ten other deliberating ministers.

entries.zh: 賊未得也。
entries.en: The assassins were not caught.
entries.literal: The bandits were not yet obtained.

entries.zh: 於是天子意梁，逐賊，果梁使之。
entries.en: The emperor’s suspicions fell on Liang; when the trail was followed, the killers proved to have been sent from Liang.
entries.literal: Thereupon the Son of Heaven’s mind was on Liang; pursuing the bandits, it turned out Liang had sent them.

entries.zh: 遣使冠蓋相望於道，復案梁事。
entries.en: Imperial messengers shuttled along the roads while the court reopened the case against Liang.
entries.literal: He dispatched envoys; canopies and covers filled the road one after another; again he investigated Liang’s affair.

entries.zh: 捕公孫詭、羊勝，皆匿王后宮。
entries.en: Gongsun Gui and Yang Sheng were ordered seized, but both had taken refuge in the queen of Liang’s apartments.
entries.literal: They arrested Gongsun Gui and Yang Sheng; both hid in the queen of Liang’s palace.

entries.zh: 使者責二千石急，梁相軒丘豹及內史安國皆泣諫王，王乃令勝、詭皆自殺，出之。
entries.en: Under relentless pressure from the envoys, Chancellor Xuanqiu Bao and Inner Scribe Anguo wept as they urged the king to yield; at last he had Yang Sheng and Gongsun Gui kill themselves and handed over their bodies.
entries.literal: The envoys pressed the two-thousand-bushel officials urgently; Liang’s chancellor Xuanqiu Bao and inner scribe Anguo all wept and remonstrated with the king; the king then ordered Sheng and Gui both to kill themselves and produced them.

entries.zh: 上由此怨望於梁王。
entries.en: From that day the emperor nursed a grudge against the king of Liang.
entries.literal: The sovereign from this harbored resentment toward the King of Liang.

entries.zh: 梁王恐，乃使韓安國因長公主謝罪太后，然後得釋。
entries.en: Terrified, he sent Han Anguo to plead through the Eldest Princess before the empress dowager, and only then escaped worse punishment.
entries.literal: The King of Liang was afraid; then he sent Han Anguo through the Eldest Princess to beg forgiveness of the empress dowager; afterward he obtained release.

entries.zh: 上怒稍解，因上書請朝。
entries.en: As the emperor’s wrath cooled, the king petitioned for permission to come to court.
entries.literal: The sovereign’s anger gradually eased; the king therefore submitted a memorial requesting audience.

entries.zh: 既至關，茅蘭說王，使乘布車，從兩騎入，匿於長公主園。
entries.en: When he reached the frontier, Mao Lan advised him to enter in a plain covered cart with only two outriders and conceal himself in the Eldest Princess’s villa.
entries.literal: Having reached the passes, Mao Lan persuaded the king to ride a cloth-covered cart with two riders following, and hide in the Eldest Princess’s garden.

entries.zh: 漢使迎王，王已入關，車騎盡居外，外不知王處。
entries.en: The imperial escort came to meet him, but he had already slipped through the gates; his train waited outside while no one knew his whereabouts.
entries.literal: Han’s envoys welcomed the king; the king had already entered the passes; chariots and riders all remained outside; those outside did not know where the king was.

entries.zh: 太后泣曰：「帝殺吾子！」
entries.en: The empress dowager wept, “The emperor has murdered my son!”
entries.literal: The empress dowager wept, saying: “The emperor has killed my son!”

entries.zh: 弟憂恐。
entries.en: The younger brother was stricken with fear.
entries.literal: The younger brother was anxious and afraid.

entries.zh: 於是梁王伏斧質，之闕下謝罪。
entries.en: Then the king of Liang appeared at the palace gate with the executioner’s axe and chopping-block across his neck to offer his submission.
entries.literal: Thereupon the King of Liang lay on the axe and block and went below the palace gate to beg forgiveness.

entries.zh: 然後太后、帝皆大喜，相與泣，復如故。
entries.en: Then the empress dowager and the emperor were both greatly pleased; they wept together and were reconciled as before.
entries.literal: Afterward the empress dowager and the emperor were both greatly pleased; they wept together with each other and returned as before.

entries.zh: 悉召王從官入關。
entries.en: The emperor summoned every member of the king’s entourage to enter the passes.
entries.literal: They summoned all the king’s followers to enter the passes.

entries.zh: 然帝益疏王，不與同車輦矣。
entries.en: Even so, the emperor grew cooler toward him and never again shared a palanquin.
entries.literal: Yet the emperor increasingly kept the king at a distance and did not share the same palanquin with him.

entries.zh: 孝王慈孝，每聞太后病，口不能食，常欲留長安侍太后。
entries.en: The king was devoted to his mother: whenever he heard she was unwell he lost his appetite and longed to stay in Chang’an to nurse her.
entries.literal: The Filial King was kind and filial; every time he heard the empress dowager was ill, his mouth could not eat; he always wished to stay in Chang’an to attend the empress dowager.

entries.zh: 太后亦愛之。
entries.en: She loved him in return.
entries.literal: The empress dowager also loved him.

entries.zh: 及聞孝王死，竇太后泣極哀，不食，曰：「帝果殺吾子！」
entries.en: When news came that King Xiao had died, Empress Dou wept with extreme grief and would not eat, saying, “The emperor has truly killed my son!”
entries.literal: When she heard the Filial King had died, Empress Dou wept with extreme grief, did not eat, saying: “The emperor truly killed my son!”

entries.zh: 帝哀懼，不知所為。
entries.en: The emperor was grief-stricken and at a loss.
entries.literal: The emperor was sorrowful and afraid and did not know what to do.

entries.zh: 與長公主計之，乃分梁為五國，盡立孝王男五人為王，女五人皆令食湯沐邑。
entries.en: He and the Eldest Princess agreed to split Liang into five kingdoms, enfeoffing each of the king’s five sons as a ruler and assigning each of his five daughters an income from a bathing-fief town.
entries.literal: He consulted with the Eldest Princess; then they divided Liang into five states, all establishing the Filial King’s five sons as kings; the five daughters all were ordered to receive bathing-fief towns.

entries.zh: 奏之太后，太后乃說，為帝壹餐。
entries.en: When this was laid before the empress dowager she relented and took a single meal for her son’s sake.
entries.literal: They presented it to the empress dowager; the empress dowager then was pleased and for the emperor ate one meal.

entries.zh: 梁孝王子五人為王。
entries.en: King Xiao’s five sons were each made kings.
entries.literal: The Filial King’s five sons became kings.

entries.zh: 太子買為梁共王，次子明為濟川王，彭離為濟東王，定為山陽王，不識為濟陰王，皆以孝景中六年同日立。
entries.en: The heir Mai became King Gong of Liang; his brothers Ming, Pengli, Ding, and Bushi received Jichuan, Jidong, Shanyang, and Jiyin respectively—all invested on the same day in the sixth year of Emperor Jing’s mid-reign.
entries.literal: The crown prince Mai was King Gong of Liang; the second son Ming was King of Jichuan; Pengli was King of Jidong; Ding was King of Shanyang; Bushi was King of Jiyin; all were established the same day in the sixth year of Xiaojing’s middle period.

entries.zh: 梁孝王武以孝文二年與太原王參、梁王揖同日立。
entries.en: In the second year of Emperor Wen’s reign, King Xiao Wu of Liang was enfeoffed on the same day as the King of Taiyuan, Can, and the King of Liang, Yi.
entries.literal: King Xiao Wu of Liang, in the second year of Xiaowen, was enfeoffed the same day as King Can of Taiyuan and King Yi of Liang.

entries.zh: 武為代王，四年徙為淮陽王，十二年徙梁，自初王通歷已十一年矣。
entries.en: He was first King of Dai, then in his fourth year as king was moved to Huaiyang, and in his twelfth year to Liang—eleven years in all from his initial appointment as king.
entries.literal: Wu was King of Dai; in the fourth year he was transferred to be King of Huaiyang; in the twelfth year he was transferred to Liang; from his first enfeoffment as king through the whole span it was already eleven years.

entries.zh: 明年，漢立太子。
entries.en: The next year the court formally invested a crown prince.
entries.literal: The next year, Han established a crown prince.

entries.zh: 梁最親，有功，又為大國，居天下膏腴地，北界泰山，西至高陽，四十餘城，多大縣。
entries.en: Liang was the emperor’s closest kin, had earned distinction in the war, and remained a vast domain—the richest soil in the realm, stretching from Mount Tai in the north to Gaoyang in the west, with over forty counties, many of them populous.
entries.literal: Liang was most closely related, had merit, and was again a great state; it occupied the fat and fertile land under heaven; its north border was Mount Tai, its west reached to Gaoyang; more than forty cities, many of them large counties.

entries.zh: 孝王，太后少子，愛之，賞賜不可勝道。
entries.en: As the empress dowager’s youngest son, King Xiao was her favorite; the gifts showered on him were beyond counting.
entries.literal: The Filial King was the empress dowager’s youngest son; she loved him; rewards and gifts could not be reckoned.

entries.zh: 於是孝王築東苑，方三百餘里，廣睢陽城七十里，大治宮室，為復道，自宮連屬於平台三十餘里。
entries.en: He built the Eastern Park, over three hundred li on a side, expanded Suiyang’s walls to seventy li, raised palaces on a grand scale, and ran covered walkways more than thirty li from his residence to the terrace park.
entries.literal: Thereupon the Filial King built the Eastern Park, more than three hundred li square; he widened the city of Suiyang seventy li; he greatly built palaces and halls, and made covered passages; from the palace continuous connection to the terrace platform was more than thirty li.

entries.zh: 得賜天子旌旗，從千乘萬騎，出稱警，入言蹕，擬於天子。
entries.en: He was allowed the imperial pennants and escort of a thousand chariots and ten thousand horsemen; when he left his precincts heralds cleared the way, and when he entered they enforced the halt—privileges that mirrored the emperor’s own.
entries.literal: He obtained the gift of the Son of Heaven’s banners and flags; with a thousand chariots and ten thousand riders he went out declaring “jing” and entered saying “bi”; he was comparable to the Son of Heaven.

entries.zh: 招延四方豪桀，自山東游士莫不至：齊人羊勝、公孫詭、鄒陽之屬。
entries.en: He drew in adventurers from every quarter; no notable wandering scholar east of the mountains failed to answer his call—among them Yang Sheng, Gongsun Gui, and Zou Yang of Qi.
entries.literal: He summoned and retained bold men from the four quarters; from east of the mountains wandering scholars none failed to come: men of Qi such as Yang Sheng, Gongsun Gui, Zou Yang, and their sort.

entries.zh: 公孫詭多奇邪計，初見日，王賜千金，官至中尉，號曰公孫將軍。
entries.en: Gongsun Gui trafficked in devious stratagems. The king gave him a thousand pieces of gold the day they met, raised him to commandant of the capital, and called him “General Gongsun.”
entries.literal: Gongsun Gui had many strange and wicked schemes; on the day he was first seen, the king gifted him a thousand in gold; his office reached to commandant of the capital guard; he was styled General Gongsun.

entries.zh: 多作兵弩弓數十萬，而府庫金錢且百巨萬，珠玉寶器多於京師。
entries.en: He stockpiled tens of thousands of crossbows and bows; his treasuries held nearly a hundred million in cash, and his hoard of jewels and curios outshone the imperial storehouses.
entries.literal: He made many tens of thousands of crossbows and bows, and the treasury’s cash and money approached a hundred “great myriads”; pearls, jade, and precious vessels exceeded those in the capital.

entries.zh: 梁懷王揖，文帝少子也。
entries.en: King Huai Yi of Liang was the last son born to Emperor Wen.
entries.literal: King Huai Yi of Liang, he was Emperor Wen’s youngest son.

entries.zh: 好《詩》、《書》，帝愛之，異於他子。
entries.en: He loved the Classics of Poetry and History, and the emperor favored him above his other sons.
entries.literal: He loved the Odes and Documents; the emperor loved him, different from other sons.

entries.zh: 五年一朝，凡再入朝。
entries.en: He was required to attend court once every five years and did so twice in all.
entries.literal: Once every five years an audience; in all twice he entered court.

entries.zh: 因墮馬死，立十年薨。
entries.en: He died from a fall from his horse in the tenth year of his reign.
entries.literal: Because of falling from a horse he died; established ten years he died.

entries.zh: 無子，國除。
entries.en: He left no heir, so the kingdom was abolished.
entries.literal: He had no son; the state was abolished.

entries.zh: 明年，梁孝王武徙王梁。
entries.en: The following year King Xiao Wu of Liang was moved to the vacant Liang domain.
entries.literal: The next year, Filial King Wu of Liang was transferred to be king of Liang.

entries.zh: 其春，吳、楚、齊、趙七國反，先擊梁棘壁，殺數萬人。
entries.en: That spring the seven kingdoms of Wu, Chu, Qi, Zhao, and the rest rose in revolt. Their first blow fell on Liang at Ji Rampart, where they slaughtered tens of thousands.
entries.literal: That spring, Wu, Chu, Qi, Zhao—the seven states rebelled; they first attacked Liang at Ji Rampart and killed several tens of thousands.

entries.zh: 梁王城守睢陽，而使韓安國、張羽等為將軍以距吳、楚。
entries.en: The king of Liang held Suiyang while Han Anguo, Zhang Yu, and others led his troops against Wu and Chu.
entries.literal: The King of Liang defended the city at Suiyang, and sent Han Anguo, Zhang Yu, and others as generals to resist Wu and Chu.

entries.zh: 吳、楚以梁為限，不敢過而西，與太尉亞夫等相距三月。
entries.en: Wu and Chu could not get past Liang to march west; for three months they were locked in stalemate with Grand Commandant Zhou Yafu and the imperial army.
entries.literal: Wu and Chu took Liang as their limit; they did not dare pass west of it, and with Grand Commandant Zhou Yafu and others they faced each other for three months.

entries.zh: 吳、楚破，而梁所殺虜略與漢中分。
entries.en: When Wu and Chu were crushed, the casualties Liang inflicted were roughly on a par with those of the central army.
entries.literal: Wu and Chu were broken, and as for those whom Liang killed and captured, it was roughly half with Han.

entries.zh: 三十五年冬，復入朝。
entries.en: In the winter of his thirty-fifth year as king he returned to the capital.
entries.literal: In the thirty-fifth year, winter, again he entered court.

entries.zh: 上疏欲留，上弗許。
entries.en: He asked leave to remain; the emperor refused.
entries.literal: He submitted a memorial wishing to stay; the sovereign did not permit.

entries.zh: 歸國，意忽忽不樂。
entries.en: Back in his kingdom he sank into restless gloom.
entries.literal: Returning to his state, his mind was absent and unhappy.

entries.zh: 北獵梁山，有獻牛，足上出背上，孝王惡之。
entries.en: While hunting north of Mount Liang he was given an ox whose hooves grew from its back—a monstrous omen he found deeply ominous.
entries.literal: Hunting north at Mount Liang, someone presented an ox whose feet emerged on its back; the Filial King detested it.

entries.zh: 六月中，病熱，六日薨。
entries.en: He took fever in the sixth month and died on the sixth day.
entries.literal: In the sixth month, he was ill with fever; on the sixth day he died.

entries.zh: 贊曰：梁孝王雖以愛親故王膏腴之地，然會漢家隆盛，百姓殷富，故能殖其貨財，廣其宮室車服。
entries.en: The historian’s verdict: King Xiao Wu of Liang owed his rich domain to imperial favor, but he also lived when the Han was at its zenith and the people were prosperous—conditions that let him pile up treasure and expand palaces, chariots, and wardrobe beyond any prince’s needs.
entries.literal: The appraisal says: Although Filial King Wu of Liang because of a dear relation was king over fat land, yet he met the Han house at its height and the hundred surnames abundant and wealthy; therefore he was able to increase his goods and wealth, widen his palaces, chariots, and robes.

entries.zh: 然亦僭矣。
entries.en: Even so, he exceeded what a vassal may claim.
entries.literal: Yet also he overstepped.

entries.zh: 怙親亡厭，牛禍告罰，卒用憂死，悲夫！
entries.en: He trusted blood ties too greedily; heaven sent the monstrous ox as warning, and worry consumed him in the end—a bitter lesson.
entries.literal: Relying on kinship without satiety, an ox’s portent announced punishment; in the end he used worry and died—how sad!

entries.zh: 初，孝王有膑尊，直千金，戒後世善寶之，毋得以與人。
entries.en: At first the Filial King possessed a precious bin-vessel worth a thousand in gold and charged posterity to treasure it and never give it away.
entries.literal: Initially, the Filial King had a bin-vessel worth a thousand gold; he admonished posterity to treasure it well and never give it to anyone.

entries.zh: 任后聞而欲得之。
entries.en: Consort Ren heard of it and wanted it for herself.
entries.literal: Consort Ren heard of it and wished to obtain it.

entries.zh: 李太后曰：「先王有命，毋得以尊與人。
entries.en: Empress Dowager Li said, "The former king commanded that the vessel must not be given to anyone.
entries.literal: Empress Dowager Li said: "The former king left a command: the vessel may not be given to anyone.

entries.zh: 他物雖百鉅萬，猶自恣。」
entries.en: Other goods, though they run to millions, you may use as you please."
entries.literal: Though other goods amount to millions, you may dispose of them as you please."

entries.zh: 任后絕欲得之。
entries.en: Consort Ren was desperate to obtain it.
entries.literal: Consort Ren desperately wanted to obtain it.

entries.zh: 王襄直使人開府取尊賜任后，又王及母陳太后事李太后多不順。
entries.en: King Xiang at once sent men to open the treasury, take the vessel, and give it to Consort Ren; and both the king and his mother Empress Dowager Chen treated Empress Dowager Li with much disrespect.
entries.literal: King Xiang directly sent men to open the treasury, take the vessel, and grant it to Consort Ren; and both the king and his mother Empress Dowager Chen showed much disrespect toward Empress Dowager Li.

entries.zh: 有漢使者來，李太后欲自言，王使謁者中郎胡等遮止，閉門。
entries.en: When imperial envoys arrived, Empress Dowager Li wished to speak for herself, but the king sent Usher Attendant-of-the-Interior Hu and others to stop her and shut the gate.
entries.literal: When Han envoys came, Empress Dowager Li wished to speak for herself; the king sent Usher Attendant-of-the-Interior Hu and others to block and bar the gate.

entries.zh: 李太后與爭門，措指，太后啼謼，不得見漢使者。
entries.en: Empress Dowager Li struggled at the gate and injured her fingers; she wept and cried out but could not see the imperial envoys.
entries.literal: Empress Dowager Li struggled at the gate, injured her fingers; the dowager wept and cried out, and could not see the Han envoys.

entries.zh: 李太后亦私與食官長及郎尹霸等姦亂，王與任后以此使人風止李太后。
entries.en: Empress Dowager Li also carried on secretly with the chief of the food office and Gentleman Yin Ba and others; the king and Consort Ren used this to send men to warn Empress Dowager Li into silence.
entries.literal: Empress Dowager Li also secretly had illicit relations with the chief of the food office and Gentleman Yin Ba and others; the king and Consort Ren used this to send men to warn Empress Dowager Li to stop.

entries.zh: 李太后亦已，後病薨。
entries.en: Empress Dowager Li yielded; later she fell ill and died.
entries.literal: Empress Dowager Li gave in; afterward she fell ill and died.

entries.zh: 病時，任后未嘗請疾；
entries.en: While she was ill, Consort Ren never once asked after her;
entries.literal: While she was ill, Consort Ren never once inquired after her illness;

entries.zh: 薨，又不侍喪。
entries.en: when she died, Consort Ren did not attend the mourning.
entries.literal: when she died, she did not attend the mourning.

entries.zh: 十一月，上廢栗太子，太后心欲以梁王為嗣。
entries.en: That November the emperor deposed Crown Prince Li; the empress dowager privately hoped that the king of Liang might succeed him.
entries.literal: In the eleventh month, the sovereign deposed Crown Prince Li; the empress dowager in her heart wished to make the King of Liang heir.

entries.zh: 大臣及爰盎等有所關說於帝，太后議格，孝王不敢復言太后以嗣事。
entries.en: Ministers led by Yuan Ang remonstrated with the emperor until the dowager’s plan stalled; the king of Liang never again raised the succession with his mother.
entries.literal: Great ministers and Yuan Ang and others had explanations they presented to the emperor; the empress dowager’s deliberations were blocked; the Filial King did not dare again speak to the empress dowager about the heir matter.

entries.zh: 事秘，世莫知，乃辭歸國。
entries.en: The matter was kept so close that the world knew nothing of it until the king asked leave and went home.
entries.literal: The affair was secret; the age did not know; then he took leave and returned to his state.

entries.zh: 孝王未死時，財以巨萬計，不可勝數。
entries.en: Before his death his fortune already ran to uncountable millions.
entries.literal: Before the Filial King died, his wealth was reckoned in “great myriads” and could not be counted.

entries.zh: 及死，藏府余黃金尚四十餘萬斤，他財物稱是。
entries.en: At his death the treasuries still held over forty ten-thousand jin of gold, with goods to match.
entries.literal: When he died, the storehouses still had more than forty myriads of jin of yellow gold; other wealth matched this.

entries.zh: 代孝王參初立為太原王。
entries.en: King Xiao Can of Dai was first enfeoffed as King of Taiyuan.
entries.literal: King Xiao Can of Dai was first enfeoffed as King of Taiyuan.

entries.zh: 四年，代王武徙為淮陽王，而參徙為代王，並得復太原，都晉陽如故。
entries.en: In the fourth year, King Wu of Dai was moved to Huaiyang while Can was moved to Dai; both recovered Taiyuan, and the capital remained at Jinyang as before.
entries.literal: In the fourth year, King Wu of Dai was transferred to be King of Huaiyang, while Can was transferred to be King of Dai; both recovered Taiyuan, and the capital remained at Jinyang as before.

entries.zh: 五年一朝，凡三朝。
entries.en: He came to court once every five years and attended court three times in all.
entries.literal: Once every five years he came to court for an audience; in all he attended court three times.

entries.zh: 十七年薨，子共王登嗣。
entries.en: In his seventeenth year he died; his son King Gong Deng succeeded him.
entries.literal: In his seventeenth year he died; his son King Gong Deng succeeded.

entries.zh: 二十九年薨，子義嗣。
entries.en: In his twenty-ninth year he died; his son Yi succeeded him.
entries.literal: In his twenty-ninth year he died; his son Yi succeeded.

entries.zh: 元鼎中，漢廣關，以常山為阻，徙代王於清河，是為剛王。
entries.en: During the Yuanding reign, Han broadened the frontier passes; because Mount Chang stood in the way, the king of Dai was moved to Qinghe and became known as King Gang.
entries.literal: In the Yuanding era, Han expanded the passes; because Mount Chang barred the way, the King of Dai was moved to Qinghe—this was the Gang King.

entries.zh: 並前在代凡立四十年薨，子頃王湯嗣。
entries.en: Counting his earlier tenure in Dai, he had ruled forty years in all when he died; his son Qing King Tang succeeded him.
entries.literal: Counting his time in Dai, in all he had ruled forty years and died; his son Qing King Tang succeeded.

entries.zh: 二十四年薨，子年嗣。
entries.en: In his twenty-fourth year he died; his son Nian succeeded him.
entries.literal: In his twenty-fourth year he died; his son Nian succeeded.

entries.zh: 元始二年，新都侯王莽興滅繼絕，白太皇太后，立年弟子如意為廣宗王，奉代孝王后。
entries.en: In Yuanshi 2, Wang Mang, Marquis of Xindu, petitioned the Grand Empress Dowager to restore the extinct line. Nian's nephew Ruyi was enfeoffed as King of Guangzong to continue King Xiao of Dai's line.
entries.literal: In the second year of Yuanshi, Marquis of Xindu Wang Mang raised the fallen and continued the cut off; he informed the Grand Empress Dowager and established Nian’s younger brother’s son Ruyi as King of Guangzong, to continue the ancestral sacrifices of King Xiao of Dai.

entries.zh: 莽篡位，國絕。
entries.en: When Wang Mang seized the throne the line ended again.
entries.literal: When Mang usurped the throne, the state was cut off.

entries.zh: 孝王支子四王，皆絕於身。
entries.en: The four collateral kings descended from King Xiao all died without issue.
entries.literal: The Filial King’s four sons by secondary wives, four kings, all ended in their own persons.

entries.zh: 元始中，立坐與平帝外家中山衛氏交通，新都侯王莽奏廢立為庶人，徙漢中。
entries.en: Under Yuanshi, Li was convicted of dealing with the Wei family of Zhongshan, in-laws of Emperor Ping; Wang Mang of Xindu had him reduced to commoner rank and banished to Hanzhong.
entries.literal: In the Yuanshi period, Li sat guilty of communicating with the Zhongshan Wei clan, the empress of Emperor Ping’s maternal kin; Marquis of Xindu Wang Mang memorialized to abolish Li as commoner and move him to Hanzhong.

entries.zh: 立自殺。
entries.en: Li took his own life.
entries.literal: Li killed himself.

entries.zh: 二十七年，國除。
entries.en: Twenty-seven years after his accession the kingdom was abolished.
entries.literal: Twenty-seven years, the state was abolished.

entries.zh: 後二歲，莽白太皇太后立孝王玄孫之曾孫沛郡卒史音為梁王，奉孝王后。
entries.en: Two years later Wang Mang persuaded the Grand Empress Dowager to install Yin, a registrar from Pei Commandery and a remote descendant of King Xiao, as king of Liang so that King Xiao's line would continue.
entries.literal: Two years later Wang Mang reported to the Grand Empress Dowager and established Yin, a registrar of Pei Commandery and a descendant several generations removed from King Xiao, as king of Liang to continue the line of King Xiao.

entries.zh: 莽篡，國絕。
entries.en: When Wang Mang seized the throne the line was extinguished again.
entries.literal: When Mang usurped, the state was cut off.

entries.zh: 濟川王明以垣邑侯立。
entries.en: The king of Jichuan, Ming, had previously held the marquisate of Yuanyi.
entries.literal: King Ming of Jichuan was established from Marquis of Yuanyi.

entries.zh: 七年，坐射殺其中尉，有司請誅，武帝弗忍，廢為庶人，徙房陵，國除。
entries.en: In his seventh year he was convicted of murdering his capital commandant with a crossbow; though officials demanded his death, Emperor Wu spared his life, stripped him of rank, banished him to Fangling, and abolished his kingdom.
entries.literal: In the seventh year, sitting guilty of shooting and killing his lieutenant in the capital, the responsible officials requested execution; Emperor Wu could not bear it; he was demoted to commoner, moved to Fangling, the state abolished.

entries.zh: 濟東王彭離立二十九年。
entries.en: King Pengli of Jidong reigned twenty-nine years.
entries.literal: King Pengli of Jidong was established twenty-nine years.

entries.zh: 彭離驕悍，昏暮私與其奴亡命少年數十人行剽，殺人取財物以為好。
entries.en: Pengli was violent and headstrong. At nightfall he would slip out with slaves and a band of young outlaws to rob and kill for sport.
entries.literal: Pengli was arrogant and fierce; at dusk in private with his slaves and dozens of young men who had fled their obligations he went plundering; killing people and taking their goods and wealth he took as his pleasure.

entries.zh: 所殺發覺者百餘人，國皆知之，莫敢夜行。
entries.en: More than a hundred victims were traced to him; everyone in the kingdom knew, and no one dared walk abroad after dark.
entries.literal: Those killed and discovered were more than a hundred; the whole state knew it; none dared travel by night.

entries.zh: 所殺者子上書告言，有司請誅，武帝弗忍，廢為庶人，徙上庸，國除，為大河郡。
entries.en: When a victim’s son petitioned the throne, officials again demanded his life; the emperor commuted the sentence to commoner status, exile to Shangyong, and annexation of the territory as Great River commandery.
entries.literal: The son of one of those killed submitted a memorial accusing him; the responsible officials requested execution; Emperor Wu could not bear it; he was demoted to commoner, moved to Shangyong, the state abolished, becoming Great River commandery.

entries.zh: 元朔中，睢陽人犴反，人辱其父，而與睢陽太守客俱出同車。
entries.en: Under Emperor Wu’s Yuanshuo reign, a Suiyang commoner named Han Fan, whose father had been publicly shamed, happened to share a carriage leaving town with one of the grand administrator’s retainers.
entries.literal: In the Yuanshuo period, a man of Suiyang named Han Fan—someone had insulted his father—and he rode out in the same carriage with a client of the Suiyang grand administrator.

entries.zh: 犴反殺其仇車上，亡去。
entries.en: Fan stabbed his enemy to death in the cart and fled.
entries.literal: Han Fan killed his enemy on the carriage and fled.

entries.zh: 睢陽太守怒，以讓梁二千石。
entries.en: The grand administrator was furious and called Liang’s senior officials to account.
entries.literal: The Suiyang grand administrator was angry and reproached Liang’s two-thousand-bushel officials.

entries.zh: 二千石以下求反急，執反親戚。
entries.en: Officials down the line hunted Fan relentlessly and rounded up his relatives.
entries.literal: Below the rank of two thousand bushels they urgently sought Fan and seized Fan’s kin.

entries.zh: 反知國陰事，乃上變告梁王與大母爭尊狀。
entries.en: Fan knew the kingdom's private affairs, so he submitted a denunciation to the throne, accusing the king of Liang of contending with his grandmother, Empress Dowager Li, over ritual precedence.
entries.literal: Fan, knowing the court’s dirty secrets, filed a capital denunciation accusing the king of Liang of lording it over his grandmother, Empress Dowager Li, in matters of precedence.

entries.zh: 時相以下具知之，欲以傷梁長吏，書聞。
entries.en: From the chancellor on down everyone already knew the story; they let the memorial go up the chain, hoping to wound Liang’s high commissioners.
entries.literal: At the time from the chancellor downward all knew of it; they wished thereby to injure Liang’s chief officials; the memorial was forwarded.

entries.zh: 天子下吏驗問，有之。
entries.en: The emperor ordered an inquiry, and the charges proved true.
entries.literal: The Son of Heaven sent down officials to verify and question; there was substance to it.

entries.zh: 公卿治，奏以為不孝，請誅王及太后。
entries.en: The council of state tried the affair, ruled it grossly unfilial, and asked that both the king and the dowager empress be put to death.
entries.literal: The high ministers tried the case; they memorialized deeming it unfilial conduct and requested execution of the king and the empress dowager.

entries.zh: 天子曰：「首惡失道，任後也。
entries.en: The emperor said, “The principal evildoer who lost the Way was Consort Ren.
entries.literal: The Son of Heaven said: “The principal evildoer who lost the way was Consort Ren.

entries.zh: 朕置相吏不逮，無以輔王，故陷不誼，不忍致法。」
entries.en: I appointed a chancellor and officials who fell short and could not assist the king, so he sank into unrighteous conduct—but I cannot bear to apply the full penalty of the law.”
entries.literal: I appointed a chancellor and officials who fell short; there was none to assist the king; therefore he sank into unrighteousness; I cannot bear to apply full punishment.”

entries.zh: 削梁王五縣，奪王太后湯沐成陽邑，梟任後首於市，中郎胡等皆伏誅。
entries.en: Five counties were cut from Liang, the dowager’s bathing-town income at Chengyang was seized, Consort Ren’s head was spiked in the marketplace, and Palace Gentleman Hu and his accomplices went to the block.
entries.literal: They stripped five counties from the King of Liang, confiscated the king’s empress dowager’s bathing fief at Chengyang, displayed Consort Ren’s head in the market; Palace Gentleman Hu and others were all executed.

entries.zh: 梁余尚有八城。
entries.en: Eight cities were left to the kingdom of Liang.
entries.literal: Liang still had eight cities remaining.

entries.zh: 積數歲，永始中，相禹奏立對外家怨望，有惡言。
entries.en: Years later, in the Yongshi era, Chancellor Yu impeached Li for muttering slander against his in-laws.
entries.literal: Accumulating several years, in the Yongshi period, Chancellor Yu memorialized that Li, toward his wife’s kin, bore resentment and had evil words.

entries.zh: 有司案驗，因發淫亂事，奏立禽獸行，請誅。
entries.en: A full investigation exposed the incest; the prosecutors denounced Li for bestial conduct and demanded his life.
entries.literal: The responsible officials investigated and verified; thereby they uncovered the debauched affair; they memorialized that Li had the conduct of birds and beasts; they requested execution.

entries.zh: 太中大夫谷永上疏曰：「臣聞『禮，天子外屏，不欲見外』也。
entries.en: Gu Yong of the Palace submitted a long memorial: “The Rites prescribe an outer screen for the Son of Heaven so that he need not gaze upon what lies beyond.
entries.literal: Grand Counsellor of the Palace Gu Yong submitted a memorial, saying: “Your servant has heard, ‘In ritual, the Son of Heaven has an outer screen; he does not wish to look upon the outer.’

entries.zh: 是故帝王之意，不窺人閨門之私，聽聞中□之言。
entries.en: For that reason true kings do not pry into bedroom secrets or traffic in gossip from the inner quarters [one character illegible in the received text].
entries.literal: Therefore the intention of emperors and kings is not to peep into the private affairs of others’ inner chambers, nor to listen to words from within the inner [text damaged].

entries.zh: 《春秋》為親者諱。
entries.en: The Spring and Autumn Annals teach us to cover the shame of those near the throne.
entries.literal: The Spring and Autumn conceals for kin.

entries.zh: 《詩》云『戚戚兄弟，莫遠具爾』。
entries.en: As the Odes put it, ‘Brothers should cling to one another, not stand aloof.’
entries.literal: The Odes says, ‘Anxious anxious are brothers; do not distance yourselves from one another.’

entries.zh: 今梁王年少，頗有狂病，始以惡言按驗，既亡事實，而發閨門之私，非本章所指。
entries.en: The king of Liang is young and somewhat unstable; you began with vague charges of slander, found no solid proof, and are now airing bedroom scandal—far from the point of the original accusation.
entries.literal: Now the King of Liang is young and somewhat deranged; at first because of evil words he was investigated; already there are no facts, yet the private affairs of the inner gate are exposed; this is not what the original chapter intended.

entries.zh: 王辭又不服，猥強劾立，傅致難明之事，獨以偏辭成罪斷獄，亡益於治道。
entries.en: He denies the indictment, yet you would convict him on strained charges and one-sided testimony, which does nothing for good government.
entries.literal: The king’s plea also does not submit; basely and forcibly impeaching Li, attaching hard-to-clarify matters, alone by partial words completing guilt and deciding the prison case—there is no benefit to the way of rule.

entries.zh: 污蔑宗室，以內亂之惡披布宣揚於天下，非所以為公族隱諱，增朝廷之榮華，昭聖德之風化也。
entries.en: To drag the Liu house through the mire and broadcast a tale of incest across the realm neither shields the imperial clan nor adds luster to the throne or to sagely example.
entries.literal: Slandering the imperial house, spreading the evil of internal disorder over the whole world under heaven—this is not the means to conceal shame for the ducal lineage, increase the court’s glory, or display sagely virtue’s transforming influence.

entries.zh: 臣愚以為王少，而父同產長，年齒不倫；
entries.en: The king is still a youth, while his father’s cousins by the same mother are grown men—there is no parity between them;
entries.literal: Your servant foolishly thinks the king is young, while his father’s uterine kin are elders; their years and standing do not match;

entries.zh: 梁國之富，足以厚聘美女，招致妖麗；
entries.en: Liang is rich enough to buy any beauty he wants;
entries.literal: Liang’s wealth is sufficient to richly engage beautiful women and summon bewitching loveliness;

entries.zh: 父同產亦有恥辱之心。
entries.en: and his father’s cousins still retain some sense of shame.
entries.literal: the father’s uterine kin also have a mind of shame.

entries.zh: 案事者乃驗問惡言，何故猥自發舒？
entries.en: If investigators press only on loose talk, why should they themselves broadcast every lurid detail?
entries.literal: Those who handle the case then verify and question evil words—why basely themselves disclose and expand?

entries.zh: 以三者揆之，殆非人情，疑有所迫切，過誤失言，文吏躡尋，不得轉移。
entries.en: Weigh those three points and the story strains credulity: I suspect someone spoke rashly under pressure, and petty clerks simply ran with it.
entries.literal: Measuring by these three, it is probably not human feeling; I suspect there was something pressing, a mistake in speech, and clerks followed the trail unable to shift course.

entries.zh: 萌牙之時，加恩勿治，上也。
entries.en: The best policy is to show mercy while the offense is still a bud and let the matter drop.
entries.literal: At the time of sprouting buds, add grace and do not prosecute—this is the highest course.

entries.zh: 既已案驗舉憲，宜及王辭不服，詔廷尉選上德通理之吏，更審考清問，著不然之效，定失誤之法，而反命於下吏，以廣公族附疏之德，為宗室刷污亂之恥，甚得治親之誼。」
entries.en: If you must pursue it, then while the king still protests his innocence, name an upright judge to rehear the case, expose any fabrication, correct procedural abuse, and discipline the minor officials who stirred the pot—thus showing generosity to distant kin of the throne and wiping the stain from the house of Liu. That would be true justice among kinsmen.”
entries.literal: Already having investigated and raised the statute, it is fitting, since the king’s plea does not submit, to order the commandant of justice to select a superior and principled official to examine anew with clear questioning, set forth the appearance of untruth, fix the law of error, and in turn charge the lower clerks—thereby extending grace to the collateral branches of the ducal lineage, for the imperial house brushing away the shame of defilement and disorder; this greatly obtains the righteousness of ruling kin.”

entries.zh: 天子由是寢而不治。
entries.en: On that plea the emperor shelved the case and took no further action.
entries.literal: The Son of Heaven from this shelved it and did not prosecute.

entries.zh: 哀帝建平中，立復殺人。
entries.en: Under Emperor Ai’s Jianping reign he killed yet another man.
entries.literal: In Emperor Ai’s Jianping period, Li again killed a person.

entries.zh: 天子遣廷尉賞、大鴻鼐由持節即訊。
entries.en: The emperor sent Commandant of Justice Shang and Grand Herald You, rod of authority in hand, to take his deposition on site in Liang.
entries.literal: The Son of Heaven sent Commandant of Justice Shang and Grand Herald You, bearing credentials, to go and interrogate on the spot.

entries.zh: 至，移書傅、相、中尉曰：「王背策戒，悖暴妄行，連犯大辟，毒流吏民。
entries.en: On arrival they wrote to his tutor, chancellor, and capital commandant, saying, “The king has turned his back on the admonitions in his investiture patent; he acts perversely and violently, repeatedly violating capital crimes, and poison flows to clerks and commoners.
entries.literal: When they arrived, they sent documents to tutor, chancellor, and commandant of the capital guard, saying: “The king has turned his back on the admonitions in his investiture patent; he acts perversely and violently, repeatedly violating capital crimes; poison flows to clerks and commoners.

entries.zh: 比比蒙恩，不伏重誅，不思改過，復賊殺人。
entries.en: Time after time he has received grace and not submitted to heavy execution, yet he does not think to reform his faults and has again murdered people treacherously.
entries.literal: Time after time he has received grace, not submitting to heavy execution, not thinking to reform his faults; again he has murdered people treacherously.

entries.zh: 幸得蒙恩，丞相長史、大鴻臚丞即問。
entries.en: Fortunately having received grace, the chief clerk of the chancellor and the assistant to the grand herald shall go and question him at once.
entries.literal: Fortunately having received grace, the chief clerk of the chancellor and the assistant to the grand herald shall go and question.

entries.zh: 王陽病抵讕，置辭驕嫚，不首主令，與背畔亡異。
entries.en: The king is pretending illness and answering with evasions. His statements are arrogant and insulting, and he refuses to confess in response to his superiors' commands; this is no different from rebellion and flight.
entries.literal: The king feigns illness and stalls with evasions; his submitted statements are arrogant and rude; he will not confess to the orders of his superiors—no different from rebellion and flight.

entries.zh: 丞相、御史請收王璽綬，送陳留獄。
entries.en: The chancellor and censorate request that his seal and sash be seized and that he be sent to the jail at Chenliu.
entries.literal: The chancellor and imperial clerk request to seize the king’s seal and ribbon and send him to prison in Chenliu.

entries.zh: 明詔加恩，復遣廷尉、大鴻臚雜問。
entries.en: An enlightened edict added grace and again sent the commandant of justice and grand herald jointly to question him.
entries.literal: The enlightened edict added grace; again they sent the commandant of justice and grand herald jointly to question.

entries.zh: 今王當受詔置辭，恐復不首實對。
entries.en: Now the king ought to receive the edict and set forth his plea; I fear he will again not confess truthfully in reply.
entries.literal: Now the king ought to receive the edict and set forth his plea; I fear again he will not confess truth in reply.

entries.zh: 《書》曰：『至於再三，有不用，我降爾命。』
entries.en: The Documents say, ‘If it comes to the third and fourth time and still there is no compliance, I will lower my command upon you.’
entries.literal: The Documents says: ‘If it comes to the third and fourth time and still there is no compliance, I will lower my command upon you.’

entries.zh: 傅、相、中尉皆以輔正為職，『虎兕出於匣，龜玉毀於匱中，是誰之過也？』
entries.en: The tutor, chancellor, and capital commandant all take assisting rectification as their duty: ‘When the tiger and rhinoceros escape from their cage, when the tortoise and jade are destroyed in their casket—whose fault is it?’
entries.literal: Tutor, chancellor, and commandant of the capital guard all take assisting rectification as their duty—‘When the tiger and rhinoceros escape from their cage, when the tortoise and jade are destroyed in their casket—whose fault is it?’

entries.zh: 書到，明以誼曉王。
entries.en: When the document arrives, clearly enlighten the king with righteousness.
entries.literal: When the document arrives, clearly with righteousness enlighten the king.

entries.zh: 敢復懷詐，罪過益深。
entries.en: If he dares again to harbor deceit, his guilt and fault will deepen.
entries.literal: If he dares again harbor deceit, his guilt and fault will deepen.

entries.zh: 傅、相以下，不能輔導，有正法。」
entries.en: From tutor and chancellor downward, any who cannot assist and guide him will face regular punishment.”
entries.literal: From tutor and chancellor downward, those who cannot assist and guide have regular punishment.”

entries.zh: 卷四十七 文三王傳第十七
entries.en: Book 47: “The Three Princes of Emperor Wen,” Treatise 17.
entries.literal: Scroll 47: Biography of the Three Kings of Wen, Number 17.

entries.zh: 盎常引大體慷慨。
entries.en: Yuan Ang was known for invoking the larger interests of the state in passionate terms.
entries.literal: Ang often cited the great principles and spoke with fervor.

entries.zh: 宦者趙談以數幸，常害盎，盎患之。
entries.en: The palace eunuch Zhao Tan, often in the emperor's confidence, worked steadily against him, and Yuan Ang lived in dread of it.
entries.literal: The eunuch Zhao Tan, because he was repeatedly favored, constantly harmed Ang, and Ang worried about it.

entries.zh: 盎兄子種為常侍騎，諫盎曰：「君眾辱之，後雖惡君，上不覆信。」
entries.en: His nephew Zhong, a household cavalry attendant, warned him: "Humiliate him before the court and, however much he hates you afterward, the Son of Heaven will not give him the same credence."
entries.literal: Ang's nephew Zhong, who was a mounted attendant of the household, remonstrated with Ang, saying, "If you publicly humiliate him, afterward though he hates you, the emperor will no longer wholly trust him."

entries.zh: 於是上朝東宮，趙談驂乘，盎伏車前曰：「臣聞天子所與共六尺輿者，皆天下豪英。
entries.en: At the next audience in the Eastern Palace Zhao Tan took the attendant's seat in the imperial car; Yuan Ang threw himself across the shafts and said, "They say whoever rides beside the ruler must be a champion of the empire.
entries.literal: Thereupon at court in the Eastern Palace Zhao Tan rode as attendant in the chariot; Ang prostrated himself before the chariot and said, "I have heard that those who share the six-foot carriage with the Son of Heaven are all the heroes and worthies of the realm.

entries.zh: 今漢雖乏人，陛下獨奈何與刀鋸之余共載！」
entries.en: Han may be short of talent, but must you share your coach with a man mutilated by the executioner's blade?"
entries.literal: Now Han may lack men, but how can Your Majesty alone share a carriage with the leavings of knife and saw!"

entries.zh: 於是上笑，下趙談。
entries.en: The emperor laughed and ordered Zhao Tan down from the chariot.
entries.literal: Thereupon the emperor laughed and dismissed Zhao Tan from the chariot.

entries.zh: 談泣下車。
entries.en: Zhao Tan climbed down in tears.
entries.literal: Tan wept as he left the chariot.

entries.zh: 然盎亦以數直諫，不得久居中。
entries.en: Because he spoke his mind too often, he could not long stay at court.
entries.literal: Yet Ang also because he repeatedly remonstrated bluntly could not long remain at the center.

entries.zh: 調為隴西都尉，仁愛士卒，士卒皆爭為死。
entries.en: Posted as commandant of Longxi, he treated his men with kindness and they would have died for him willingly.
entries.literal: He was transferred to be commandant of Longxi; he loved the soldiers benevolently, and the soldiers all vied to die for him.

entries.zh: 遷齊相，徙為吳相。
entries.en: He was promoted to chancellor of Qi, then transferred to be chancellor of Wu.
entries.literal: He was promoted to chancellor of Qi, then transferred to be chancellor of Wu.

entries.zh: 辭行，種謂盎曰：「吳王驕日久，國多奸，今絲欲刻治，彼不上書告君，則利劍刺君矣。
entries.en: As he set out, Zhong warned him: "The king of Wu has been proud a long time; his domain crawls with villains. If you try to rule him with a tight rein, he will denounce you to the throne or put a blade in your ribs.
entries.literal: On his departure Zhong said to Ang, "The King of Wu has long been arrogant; the state swarms with scoundrels; now if you, Ang, wish to govern strictly, he will either submit a memorial accusing you or run you through with a sharp sword.

entries.zh: 南方卑濕，絲能日飲，亡何，說王毋反而已。
entries.en: The south is steamy and low; drink your wine every day, mind your own business, and do no more than talk him out of rebellion.
entries.literal: The south is low and damp; Ang can drink daily, do nothing else, and merely persuade the king not to rebel.

entries.zh: 如此幸得脫。」
entries.en: That is how you may come through alive."
entries.literal: In this way you may perhaps escape."

entries.zh: 盎用種之計，吳王厚遇盎。
entries.en: Yuan Ang followed the advice, and the king of Wu showered him with hospitality.
entries.literal: Ang employed Zhong's plan, and the King of Wu treated Ang generously.

entries.zh: 上從霸陵上，欲西馳下峻阪，盎攬轡。
entries.en: On a visit to Baling the emperor wished to race his team down the western escarpment; Yuan Ang caught the horses' bits.
entries.literal: When the emperor went up on the Baling tumulus and wished to gallop west down a steep slope, Ang seized the reins.

entries.zh: 上曰：「將軍怯邪？」
entries.en: "Are you afraid?" asked the emperor.
entries.literal: The emperor said, "Is the general a coward?"

entries.zh: 盎言曰：「臣聞千金之子不垂堂，百金之子不騎衡，聖主不乘危，不僥倖。
entries.en: Yuan Ang replied: "They say the heir to a great fortune does not court danger under a high roof, the heir to a middling fortune does not ride the balance-beam, and a wise ruler neither hazards his person nor trusts to chance.
entries.literal: Ang said, "I have heard that the son of a thousand in gold does not sit beneath a high hall, the son of a hundred in gold does not straddle the crossbar of a scale, and the enlightened ruler does not take risks or trust to luck.

entries.zh: 今陛下聘六飛，馳不測山，有如馬驚車敗，陛下縱自輕，奈高廟、太后何？」
entries.en: Now Your Majesty drives a team of six swift horses over perilous mountains. If the horses were startled and the chariot overturned, even if Your Majesty held your own life lightly, what would become of Gaozu's temple and the Empress Dowager?"
entries.literal: Now Your Majesty drives six flying horses, galloping over unfathomable hills; if the horses should bolt and the chariot overturn, though Your Majesty might think lightly of yourself, what of Gaozu's temple and the empress dowager?"
