entries.zh: 上乃止。
entries.en: The emperor reined in.
entries.literal: The emperor then stopped.

entries.zh: 盎告歸，道逢丞相申屠嘉，下車拜謁，丞相從車上謝。
entries.en: On leave bound for home he met Chancellor Shentu Jia, dismounted to pay his respects, and received only a nod from the passing carriage.
entries.literal: When Ang took leave to return home, on the road he met Chancellor Shen Tu Jia, dismounted, and bowed in obeisance; the chancellor from his chariot returned thanks.

entries.zh: 盎還，愧其吏，乃之丞相捨上謁，求見丞相。
entries.en: Mortified before his own staff, he went to the chancellor's gate and asked for a formal interview.
entries.literal: Ang returned, felt ashamed before his clerks, and therefore went to the chancellor's lodging to pay a formal visit and request an audience.

entries.zh: 丞相良久乃見。
entries.en: He was kept waiting a long time before being admitted.
entries.literal: The chancellor only after a long while received him.

entries.zh: 因跪曰：「願請間。」
entries.en: He therefore knelt and said, "I beg to speak in private."
entries.literal: He therefore knelt and said, "I beg to speak in private."

entries.zh: 丞相曰：「使君所言公事，之曹與長史掾議之，吾且奏之；
entries.en: The chancellor said: "If this is state business, take it to my office and let the senior clerks hear it; I will memorialize whatever they endorse;
entries.literal: The chancellor said, "If what the lord says is public business, take it to the bureau and discuss it with the chief clerk and his assistants, and I will memorialize it;

entries.zh: 則私，吾不受私語。」
entries.en: if it is personal, I do not hear private pleas."
entries.literal: if it is private, I do not accept private words."

entries.zh: 盎即起說曰：「君為相，自度孰與陳平、絳侯？」
entries.en: Yuan Ang rose and said: "You sit as chancellor—how do you rank yourself beside Chen Ping and the Marquis of Jiang?"
entries.literal: Ang immediately rose and said, "You are chancellor—do you measure yourself against Chen Ping and the Marquis of Jiang?"

entries.zh: 丞相曰：「不如。」
entries.en: "I am not in their class," said the chancellor.
entries.literal: The chancellor said, "I am not their match."

entries.zh: 盎曰：「善，君自謂弗如。
entries.en: Yuan Ang said, "You admit you fall short—that is honest.
entries.literal: Ang said, "Good—you yourself say you are not their match.

entries.zh: 夫陳平、絳侯輔翼高帝，定天下，為將相，而誅諸呂，存劉氏；
entries.en: Chen Ping and the Marquis of Jiang raised Gaozu, won the empire, served as general and chancellor, extirpated the Lü, and saved the Liu line;
entries.literal: Chen Ping and the Marquis of Jiang aided and supported Gaodi, settled the realm, became general and chancellor, executed the Lü clan, and preserved the house of Liu;

entries.zh: 君乃為材官蹶張，遷為隊帥，積功至淮陽守，非有奇計攻城野戰之功。
entries.en: you began as a crossbow-puller in the engineers, made company captain, and climbed to governor of Huaiyang on routine service—you never took a city by stratagem or won a field battle.
entries.literal: you were a crossbowman of the materials corps, rose to be a company commander, and accumulated merit until you became governor of Huaiyang—you had no marvelous stratagems or merit from storming cities or fighting in the open field.

entries.zh: 且陛下從代來，每朝，郎官者上書疏，未嘗不止輦受。
entries.en: Since the emperor returned from Dai, not once has he let a coach roll past a memorial from the gentlemen attendants without stopping to take it in hand.
entries.literal: Moreover, since the emperor came from Dai, at each court when gentlemen of the palace submitted memorials, the emperor never failed to halt the carriage and receive them.

entries.zh: 其言不可用，置之；
entries.en: What could not be used he set aside;
entries.literal: If their words could not be used, he set them aside;

entries.zh: 言可采，未嘗不稱善。
entries.en: what was sound he praised without stint.
entries.literal: if the words could be adopted, he never failed to praise them well.

entries.zh: 何也？
entries.en: Why?
entries.literal: Why was this?

entries.zh: 欲以致天下賢英士大夫，日聞所不聞，以益聖。
entries.en: To draw the best men of the empire to his ear, to learn something new every day, and to grow in wisdom.
entries.literal: He wished thereby to draw to him the worthy knights and great officers of the realm, daily to hear what he had not heard, and thereby to increase his sageliness.

entries.zh: 而君自閉箝天下之口，而日益愚。
entries.en: You have bolted every mouth in the land and grown more ignorant by the day.
entries.literal: Yet you yourself shut and bolt the mouths of the realm and daily grow more foolish.

entries.zh: 夫以聖主責愚相，君受禍不久矣。」
entries.en: When a wise sovereign finds his chief minister a fool, retribution follows soon enough."
entries.literal: When a sagely ruler calls a foolish chancellor to account, you will not long escape disaster."

entries.zh: 丞相乃再拜曰：「嘉鄙人，乃不知，將軍幸教。」
entries.en: Shentu Jia bowed twice and said, "I am a boor; I did not understand—thank you for the lesson, general."
entries.literal: The chancellor then bowed twice and said, "Jia is a rustic; I did not know; the general has favored me with instruction."

entries.zh: 引與入坐，為上客。
entries.en: He led Yuan Ang inside, seated him as an honored guest, and heard him out.
entries.literal: He led him in to sit and treated him as a guest of honor.

entries.zh: 盎雖居家，景帝時時使人問籌策。
entries.en: Even in retirement Emperor Jing's messengers came often for his advice on policy.
entries.literal: Although Ang dwelt at home, under Emperor Jing men were constantly sent to ask his counsel.

entries.zh: 梁王欲求為嗣，盎進說，其後語塞。
entries.en: The prince of Liang pressed to be named crown prince; Yuan Ang spoke against it, and the proposal died.
entries.literal: The Prince of Liang wished to be named heir; Ang advanced remonstrance, and afterward the matter was blocked.

entries.zh: 梁王以此怨盎，使人刺盎。
entries.en: The prince of Liang nursed a grudge and hired killers.
entries.literal: The Prince of Liang therefore resented Ang and sent men to assassinate him.

entries.zh: 刺者至關中，問盎，稱之皆不容口。
entries.en: The killer reached Guanzhong and asked after Yuan Ang; everywhere he went men praised him to the skies.
entries.literal: When the assassin reached the Guanzhong region and asked about Ang, everyone praised him without stint.

entries.zh: 乃見盎曰：「臣受梁王金刺君，君長者，不忍刺君。
entries.en: He presented himself and said, "The prince of Liang paid me to cut you down, but you are a gentleman—I will not strike.
entries.literal: He therefore went to see Ang and said, "I received the Prince of Liang's gold to stab you, my lord; you are a man of honor, and I cannot bear to stab you.

entries.zh: 然後刺者十餘曹，備之！」
entries.en: Ten more bands are behind me—you must guard yourself."
entries.literal: Yet afterward there are more than ten parties of assassins—prepare yourself!"

entries.zh: 盎心不樂，家多怪，乃之□生所問占。
entries.en: Uneasy in mind and troubled by omens at home, he went to a fortune-teller for a reading.
entries.literal: Ang was unhappy at heart; many strange things happened in his house, and he therefore went to a certain diviner's place to inquire by divination.

entries.zh: 還，梁刺客後曹果遮刺殺盎安陵郭門外。
entries.en: On his way back the second team of Liang hit men caught him outside the Anling gate and cut him down.
entries.literal: Returning, a later party of Liang assassins indeed waylaid and stabbed Ang to death outside the gate tower of Anling.

entries.zh: 盎素不好晁錯，錯所居坐，盎輒避；
entries.en: Yuan Ang had long disliked Chao Cuo; whenever Cuo took a seat, Ang would avoid it;
entries.literal: Ang had long disliked Chao Cuo; whenever Cuo was seated, Ang would avoid the place;

entries.zh: 盎所居坐，錯亦避：兩人未嘗同堂語。
entries.en: when Ang was seated, Cuo avoided him as well—the two had never spoken in the same hall.
entries.literal: when Ang was seated, Cuo also avoided it: the two had never spoken in the same hall.

entries.zh: 及孝景即位，晁錯為御史大夫，使吏案盎受吳王財物，抵罪，詔赦以為庶人。
entries.en: When Emperor Jing took the throne, Chao Cuo became imperial counselor and had officials prosecute Yuan Ang for taking gifts from the King of Wu; though convicted, an edict pardoned him and reduced him to commoner status.
entries.literal: When Emperor Jing took the throne, Chao Cuo became imperial counselor and had officials investigate Ang for accepting goods from the King of Wu; convicted, an edict pardoned him and made him a commoner.

entries.zh: 吳楚反聞，錯謂丞史曰：「爰盎多受吳王金錢，專為蔽匿，言不反。
entries.en: When news came that Wu and Chu had rebelled, Chao Cuo told his clerks, "Yuan Ang took large bribes from the King of Wu and hid the truth, insisting they would not rebel.
entries.literal: When word came that Wu and Chu had rebelled, Cuo said to the clerks, "Yuan Ang accepted much gold from the King of Wu and deliberately concealed it, saying they would not rebel.

entries.zh: 今果反，欲請治盎，宜知其計謀。」
entries.en: Now they have rebelled; I want to prosecute Ang—he must know their plans."
entries.literal: Now they have indeed rebelled; I wish to request that Ang be prosecuted—he should know their schemes."

entries.zh: 丞史曰：「事未發，治之有絕。
entries.en: The clerks replied, "Before the rebellion broke out, prosecuting him would have cut off our line to him.
entries.literal: The clerks said, "Before the matter had broken, prosecuting him would have severed the tie.

entries.zh: 今兵西向，治之何益！
entries.en: Now the armies face west—what good would prosecuting him do!
entries.literal: Now the armies face west—what profit in prosecuting him!

entries.zh: 且盎不宜有謀。」
entries.en: Besides, Ang is unlikely to have plotted."
entries.literal: Moreover, Ang is unlikely to have plotted."

entries.zh: 錯猶與未決。
entries.en: Chao Cuo still wavered and could not decide.
entries.literal: Cuo still hesitated and could not decide.

entries.zh: 人有告盎，盎恐，夜見竇嬰，為言吳所以反，願致前，口對狀。
entries.en: Someone informed on Yuan Ang; terrified, he visited Dou Ying by night, explained why Wu had rebelled, and asked to be brought before the throne to testify in person.
entries.literal: Someone reported Ang; in fear he visited Dou Ying by night, explained why Wu had rebelled, and asked to be brought before the throne to testify face to face.

entries.zh: 嬰入言，上乃召盎。
entries.en: Dou Ying reported to the throne, and the emperor summoned Yuan Ang.
entries.literal: Dou Ying entered and reported; the emperor then summoned Ang.

entries.zh: 盎入見，竟言吳所以反，獨急斬錯以謝吳，吳可罷。
entries.en: Yuan Ang entered audience, explained at length why Wu had rebelled, and urged that only by swiftly executing Chao Cuo to appease Wu could the rebellion be ended.
entries.literal: Ang entered audience and fully explained why Wu had rebelled, saying that only by urgently executing Cuo to appease Wu could the rebellion be ended.

entries.zh: 上拜盎為泰常，竇嬰為大將軍。
entries.en: The emperor named Yuan Ang Grand Master of Ceremonies and Dou Ying Grand General.
entries.literal: The emperor appointed Ang Grand Master of Ceremonies and Dou Ying Grand General.

entries.zh: 兩人素相善。
entries.en: The two had long been close allies.
entries.literal: The two had long been on good terms.

entries.zh: 是時，諸陵長安中賢大夫爭附兩人，車騎者日數百乘。
entries.en: At that time the worthy grandees of the imperial tombs around Chang'an vied to attach themselves to the two men; horsemen and carriages numbered in the hundreds each day.
entries.literal: At that time the worthy grandees among the imperial tombs in Chang'an competed to attach themselves to the two men; horsemen and carriages numbered several hundred each day.

entries.zh: 錯為人峭直刻深。
entries.en: Chao Cuo was rigid, uncompromising, and unforgiving.
entries.literal: In person Cuo was harsh, upright, and cutting deep.

entries.zh: 孝文時，天下亡治《尚書》者，獨聞齊有伏生，故秦博士，治《尚書》，年九十餘，老不可征。
entries.en: Under Emperor Wen no one in the empire still taught the Book of Documents except old Master Fu in Qi—a former Qin academician, past ninety and too frail to travel to court.
entries.literal: In the time of Emperor Wen, in the realm there was none who could expound the Documents; it was heard only that in Qi there was Master Fu, a former erudite of Qin who studied the Documents, more than ninety years old, too aged to be summoned.

entries.zh: 乃詔太常，使人受之。
entries.en: The throne ordered the Grand Master of Ceremonies to dispatch a student to learn the text at his side.
entries.literal: Thereupon an edict was issued to the Grand Master of Ceremonies to send someone to receive instruction from him.

entries.zh: 太常遣錯受《尚書》伏生所，還，因上書稱說。
entries.en: The office sent Chao Cuo to study with Master Fu; when he came back he memorialized in glowing terms on what he had learned.
entries.literal: The Grand Master of Ceremonies sent Cuo to receive the Documents at Master Fu's place; on returning, he therefore submitted a memorial praising and expounding it.

entries.zh: 詔以為太子舍人，門大夫，遷博士。
entries.en: He was named gentleman attendant on the heir apparent, then gatehouse grandee, and soon rose to erudite.
entries.literal: By edict he was made gentleman attendant on the heir apparent, gatehouse grandee, and promoted to erudite.

entries.zh: 又上書言：「人主所以尊顯功名揚於萬世之後者，以知術數也。
entries.en: He wrote again: "A sovereign's fame endures because he masters the arts of rule.
entries.literal: He again submitted a memorial saying, "The reason a ruler achieves honored display and a name that shines for myriad ages afterward is that he understands methods and calculations.

entries.zh: 故人主知所以臨制臣下而治其眾，則群臣畏服矣；
entries.en: Know how to command ministers and manage the people, and every official will obey;
entries.literal: Therefore if the ruler knows how to oversee and control his ministers and govern the multitude, then the host of officials will fear and submit;

entries.zh: 知所以聽言受事，則不欺蔽矣；
entries.en: know how to hear petitions and dispatch business, and flattery cannot hide the truth;
entries.literal: if he knows how to listen to words and receive affairs, then he will not be deceived or blinded;

entries.zh: 知所以安利萬民，則海內必從矣；
entries.en: know how to enrich and protect the common folk, and the realm will rally;
entries.literal: if he knows how to secure benefit and comfort the myriad people, then within the seas they will surely follow;

entries.zh: 知所以忠孝事上，則臣子之行備矣：此四者，臣竊為皇太子急之。
entries.en: know how loyalty and filial piety bind subject to sovereign, and the way of the minister and the son is whole. These four lessons, I submit, the heir apparent needs above all.
entries.literal: if he knows how with loyalty and filial piety to serve those above, then the conduct of ministers and sons will be complete: these four, your servant privately thinks, should be urgently taught the crown prince.

entries.zh: 人臣之議或曰皇太子亡以知事為也，臣之愚，誠以為不然。
entries.en: Some say the heir need not trouble with government yet; I respectfully disagree.
entries.literal: Some among the ministers say the crown prince need not yet understand affairs of state; your servant's foolish opinion sincerely holds that this is not so.

entries.zh: 竊觀上世之君，不能奉其宗廟而劫殺於其臣者，皆不知術數者也。
entries.en: Every ancient lord who lost his temples to a minister's dagger had failed to learn those arts.
entries.literal: Your servant has observed that rulers of high antiquity who could not preserve their ancestral shrines and were seized and slain by their ministers were all men who did not understand methods and calculations.

entries.zh: 皇太子所讀書多矣，而未深知術數者也。
entries.en: The Crown Prince has read many books, but he does not yet deeply understand methods and calculations.
entries.literal: The books that the Crown Prince has read are many, but he has not yet deeply understood methods and calculations.

entries.zh: 皇太子所讀書多矣，而未深知術數者，不問書說也。
entries.en: The heir has read widely but not pressed the glosses—so the techniques of rule still elude him.
entries.literal: The crown prince has read many books, yet he has not deeply grasped methods and calculations because he has not questioned the explanations of the texts.

entries.zh: 夫多誦而不知其說，所謂勞苦而不為功。
entries.en: Recitation without understanding is labor wasted.
entries.literal: To recite much without knowing the doctrine is what is called toiling without achievement.

entries.zh: 臣竊觀皇太子材智高奇，馭射技藝過人絕遠，然於術數未有所守者，以陛下為心也。
entries.en: His wit and his riding and shooting are superb, yet he has no anchor in statecraft because he trusts wholly in you.
entries.literal: Your servant has observed that the crown prince's talents and wisdom are lofty and rare, his horsemanship and archery surpass others by far, yet in methods and calculations he has nothing to hold to because he takes Your Majesty as his heart.

entries.zh: 竊願陛下幸擇聖人之術可用今世者，以賜皇太子，因時使太子陳明於前。
entries.en: Choose from the sages' teaching what fits this age, give it to the heir, and bid him rehearse it in your presence from time to time.
entries.literal: Your servant humbly wishes Your Majesty would deign to select among the techniques of the sages those usable in the present age and grant them to the crown prince, and from time to time cause the heir apparent to set them forth before you.

entries.zh: 唯陛下裁察。」
entries.en: I beg you to weigh this memorial."
entries.literal: May Your Majesty judge and examine."

entries.zh: 上善之，於是拜錯為太子家令。
entries.en: The emperor approved the plea and named Chao Cuo household commandant to the crown prince.
entries.literal: The emperor approved it, and thereupon appointed Cuo household commandant to the heir apparent.

entries.zh: 以其辯得幸太子，太子家號曰「智囊」。
entries.en: His sharp tongue won the heir's confidence, and the inner household nicknamed him the "wisdom bag."
entries.literal: Because of his eloquence he won the heir apparent's favor, and in the heir's household he was called the "wisdom satchel."

entries.zh: 景帝即位，以錯為內史。
entries.en: Jing named him inner secretary to the capital.
entries.literal: When Emperor Jing took the throne, he appointed Cuo metropolitan superintendent.

entries.zh: 錯數請間言事，輒聽，幸傾九卿，法令多所更定。
entries.en: He won private audiences, overshadowed the nine ministers, and rewrote half the regulations.
entries.literal: Cuo repeatedly requested private audience to speak on affairs and was always heard; favored, he tilted the nine ministers and statutes were much altered and fixed.

entries.zh: 丞相申屠嘉心弗便，力未有以傷。
entries.en: Chancellor Shentu Jia bridled but could not strike.
entries.literal: Chancellor Shen Tu Jia was displeased at heart but had not yet strength to wound him.

entries.zh: 內史府居太上廟□中，門東出，不便，錯乃穿門南出，鑿廟□垣。
entries.en: His office sat inside the high temple precinct; the official gate faced east and was awkward, so he opened a southern gate through the temple's outer wall—the lacuna marks an illegible graph in the text.
entries.literal: The metropolitan superintendent's yamen stood within the Grand Supreme Emperor's temple compound (text damaged); the gate opened east—inconvenient—therefore Cuo bored a gate opening south and cut through the temple's rammed-earth wall (text damaged).

entries.zh: 丞相大怒，欲因此過為奏請誅錯。
entries.en: The chancellor meant to hang the sacrilege charge on him and demand his head.
entries.literal: The chancellor was greatly angry and wished by this fault to memorialize and request Cuo's execution.

entries.zh: 錯聞之，即請間為上言之。
entries.en: Chao Cuo raced to the palace for a private word with the emperor.
entries.literal: When Cuo heard of it, he immediately requested private audience and spoke to the emperor.

entries.zh: 丞相奏事，因言錯擅鑿廟垣為門，請下廷尉誅。
entries.en: At the next audience Shentu Jia accused him of breaching the temple wall and asked the Minister of Justice to behead him.
entries.literal: When the chancellor memorialize on affairs, he therefore said Cuo had on his own authority cut the temple wall to make a gate and requested that he be handed to the Minister of Justice for execution.

entries.zh: 上曰：「此非廟垣，乃□中垣，不致於法。」
entries.en: The emperor replied, "That was the outer screen wall, not the sacred enclosure itself—no crime worth the courts." (The manuscript has a lacuna.)
entries.literal: The emperor said, "This is not the temple wall; it is the rammed-earth wall of the compound (text damaged); it does not reach the level of law."

entries.zh: 丞相謝。
entries.en: The chancellor withdrew his charge.
entries.literal: The chancellor apologized.

entries.zh: 罷朝，因怒謂長史曰：「吾當先斬以聞，乃先請，固誤。」
entries.en: After court he snarled to his chief clerk, "I should have cut him down first and reported afterward—asking leave was my blunder."
entries.literal: When court ended, in anger he said to his chief clerk, "I ought first to have beheaded him and reported; to have requested permission first was surely a mistake."

entries.zh: 丞相遂發病死。
entries.en: He sickened with rage and died.
entries.literal: Thereupon the chancellor fell ill with anger and died.

entries.zh: 錯以此愈貴。
entries.en: Chao Cuo climbed higher still.
entries.literal: Cuo from this grew more honored.

entries.zh: 文帝嘉之，乃賜錯璽書寵答焉，曰：「皇帝問太子家令：上書言兵體三章，聞之。
entries.en: Wen praised the memorial and answered with an edict under the imperial seal: "The throne acknowledges your three-part essay on the nature of war.
entries.literal: Emperor Wen commended him and bestowed on Cuo a sealed imperial edict with a gracious reply, saying, "The emperor inquires of the household commandant of the heir apparent: your memorial setting forth the three divisions of military principle has been received.

entries.zh: 書言『狂夫之言，而明主擇焉』。
entries.en: You yourself quoted the saying that a clear-sighted lord picks sense even from a madman's mouth.
entries.literal: The document says, 'The madman's words, yet the enlightened ruler selects from them.

entries.zh: 今則不然。
entries.en: Yet the case before us is the opposite.
entries.literal: Now it is not so.

entries.zh: 言者不狂，而擇者不明，國之大患，故在於此。
entries.en: The adviser is no lunatic, but the listener fails to see—that is how a realm courts ruin.
entries.literal: The speaker is not mad, yet the chooser is not enlightened; the great peril of the state lies right here.

entries.zh: 使夫不明擇於不狂，是以萬聽而萬不當也。」
entries.en: When a dim ruler sorts sane counsel, every audience miscarries."
entries.literal: To make the unenlightened choose among the not-mad is why ten thousand hearings yield ten thousand wrong decisions."

entries.zh: 吳、楚已破，上更以元王子平陸侯禮為楚王，以盎為楚相。
entries.en: After Wu and Chu were defeated, the emperor made Prince Yuan’s son, Marquis Pinglu Li, King of Chu and appointed Yuan Ang chancellor of Chu.
entries.literal: When Wu and Chu had been defeated, the emperor further appointed Marquis Pinglu Li, a son of Prince Yuan of Chu, as King of Chu, and made Ang chancellor of Chu.

entries.zh: 嘗上書，不用。
entries.en: He once sent up a memorial; the court took no action on it.
entries.literal: He once submitted a memorial; it was not adopted.

entries.zh: 盎病免家居，與閭里浮湛，相隨行鬥雞走狗。
entries.en: Illness forced him home, where he kept loose company—cockfights, dog races, the life of the lanes.
entries.literal: Ang fell ill, resigned, and lived at home, drifting with his neighbors in cockfighting and dog racing.

entries.zh: 雒陽劇孟嘗過盎，盎善待之。
entries.en: Ju Meng of Luoyang called on him once, and Yuan Ang received him as an honored guest.
entries.literal: Ju Meng of Luoyang once visited Ang, and Ang treated him well.

entries.zh: 安陵富人有謂盎曰：「吾聞劇孟博徒，將軍何自通之？」
entries.en: A wealthy Anling burgher asked him, "Ju Meng is nothing but a gamester—why should a man of your rank seek him out?"
entries.literal: A rich man of Anling said to Ang, "I have heard Ju Meng is a gambler—why do you, a general, associate with him of your own accord?"

entries.zh: 盎曰：「劇孟雖博徒，然母死，客送喪車千餘乘，此亦有過人者。
entries.en: Yuan Ang replied, "Ju Meng may haunt the gaming houses, but when his mother died over a thousand carriages followed her bier—there was greatness in him.
entries.literal: Ang said, "Although Ju Meng is a gambler, when his mother died guests sent more than a thousand funeral carts—there too he surpassed others.

entries.zh: 且緩急人所有。
entries.en: Besides, every man meets moments of peril or reprieve.
entries.literal: Moreover urgency and ease are what all men may meet.

entries.zh: 夫一旦叩門，不以親為解，不以在亡為辭，天下所望者，獨季心、劇孟。
entries.en: When disaster strikes your gate, you will want men who ask no questions about kinship or whether you are at home—the names the empire trusts are Ji Xin and Ju Meng alone.
entries.literal: If one day someone knocks at the gate, not pleading kinship as an excuse, not pleading absence as a pretext, those whom the realm looks to are Ji Xin and Ju Meng alone.

entries.zh: 今公陽從數騎，一旦有緩急，寧足恃乎！」
entries.en: You ride abroad with a handful of escorts—when trouble comes, what good will they do you?"
entries.literal: Now you openly follow only a few horsemen—if crisis comes, will they suffice!"

entries.zh: 遂罵富人，弗與通。
entries.en: He cursed the man roundly and cut him off.
entries.literal: He therefore reviled the rich man and would not associate with him.

entries.zh: 諸公聞之，皆多盎。
entries.en: The gentlemen of the capital heard the story and esteemed him the more.
entries.literal: When the great men heard it, they all thought the more of Ang.

entries.zh: 惟十有五年九月壬子，皇帝曰：「昔者大禹勤求賢士，施及方外，四極之內，舟車所至，人跡所及，靡不聞命，以輔其不逮；
entries.en: On renzi, in the ninth month of the fifteenth year, the emperor said, "In former times, Great Yu diligently sought out worthy men, extending his search even beyond the settled lands. Within the four extremities, wherever boats and carts could reach and wherever human footprints went, all heard his command, so that they might aid him where he fell short;
entries.literal: On the renzi day of the ninth month of the fifteenth year, the emperor said, "In former times Great Yu diligently sought worthy men, extending to the outer regions; within the four extremities, wherever boats and carts reached and human tracks extended, none failed to hear his command, to assist what he could not reach;

entries.zh: 近者獻其明，遠者通厥聰，比善戮力，以翼天子。
entries.en: the near brought vision, the far brought news, all striving together to shoulder the Son of Heaven;
entries.literal: the near offered their clarity, the distant communicated their keen hearing, comparing goodness and joining strength to wing the Son of Heaven.

entries.zh: 是以大禹能亡失德，夏以長□。
entries.en: and so Yu never slipped from the Way, and the house of Xia endured—though the tablet here is damaged.
entries.literal: thereby Great Yu could lose no virtue, and Xia thereby endured long (the text has a lacuna).

entries.zh: 高皇帝親除大害，去亂從，並建豪英，以為官師，為諫爭，輔天子之闕，而翼戴漢宗也。
entries.en: Gaozu swept away the tyrant, raised lieutenants as teachers and critics to fill his gaps, and propped the Han altars;
entries.literal: The Supreme Emperor in person removed great harm, cast off chaos and followed order, and together established heroes and champions to be masters and instructors, to remonstrate and contend, to supply the Son of Heaven's deficiencies, and to support and uphold the Han house.

entries.zh: 賴天之靈，宗廟之福，方內以安，澤及四夷。
entries.en: Heaven and the shrines smiled within the passes and the favor spread beyond the four barrens.
entries.literal: relying on the numen of Heaven and the blessing of the ancestral temples, within the square was peace and grace reached the four barbarians.

entries.zh: 今朕獲執天子之正，以承宗廟之祀，朕既不德，又不敏，明弗能燭，而智不能治，此大夫之所著聞也。
entries.en: We hold the regalia yet lack both virtue and wit—our sight does not reach, our judgment does not rule—as you ministers know too well.
entries.literal: Now We have grasped the correctness of the Son of Heaven to continue the sacrifices of the ancestral temples; We are neither virtuous nor keen, Our clarity cannot illumine, Our wisdom cannot govern—this is what the great officers have plainly heard.

entries.zh: 故詔有司、諸侯王、三公、九卿及主郡吏，各帥其志，以選賢良明於國家之大體，通於人事之終始，及能直言極諫者，各有人數，將以匡朕之不逮。
entries.en: We therefore order the offices, the feudal kings, the three dukes, the nine ministers, and the officials in charge of commanderies each to follow his own judgment and select worthy men who understand the great principles of the state, grasp the course of human affairs from beginning to end, and can speak frankly and remonstrate to the utmost. Each has an assigned quota, so that they may correct what We lack.
entries.literal: Therefore We have ordered the relevant offices, feudal kings, the three dukes, the nine ministers, and chief clerks of commanderies, each to lead forth his intent, to select the worthy and good who are clear on the great principles of the state, comprehend the beginning and end of human affairs, and are able to speak bluntly and remonstrate to the utmost—each in fixed numbers—to correct Our deficiencies.

entries.zh: 二三大夫之行當此三道，朕甚嘉之，故登大夫於朝，親諭朕志。
entries.en: You few who walk those three paths have Our praise; We have called you to the hall to hear Our mind plain.
entries.literal: That the two or three great officers conduct themselves in accord with these three paths We greatly commend; therefore We have advanced the great officers to court and personally declared Our intent.

entries.zh: 大夫其上三道之要，及永惟朕之不德，吏之不平，政之不宣，民之不寧，四者之闕，悉陳其志，毋有所隱。
entries.en: Speak the three themes plainly, then weigh Our want of virtue, corrupt clerks, blocked policy, restless commons—four gaps—and hide nothing.
entries.literal: Let the great officers set forth the essentials of the three paths, and forever consider Our lack of virtue, the unfairness of clerks, the failure of government to reach everywhere, the unquiet of the people—these four lacks—and exhaust their intent in stating them, hiding nothing.

entries.zh: 上以薦先帝之宗廟，下以興愚民之休利，著之於篇，朕親覽焉，觀大夫所以佐朕，至與不至。
entries.en: Write answers that may honor the dead emperors and profit the living; We will read each page and see how far you truly steady Our hand.
entries.literal: Above to recommend to the ancestral temples of the former emperors, below to raise the rest and profit of the foolish people, fix it in writing; We will personally peruse it and observe whether the great officers' aid to Us reaches the mark or not.

entries.zh: 書之，周之密之，重之閉之。
entries.en: Record your replies, bind them close, seal them thrice.
entries.literal: Write it, surround it with care, weight it, seal it closed.

entries.zh: 興自朕躬，大夫其正論，毋枉執事。
entries.en: The fault is Ours; speak straight and do not trim for your portfolios.
entries.literal: It arises from Our person; let the great officers correct their discourse and not twist the duties they hold.

entries.zh: 烏乎，戒之！
entries.en: Take heed.
entries.literal: Alas—be warned!

entries.zh: 二三大夫其帥志毋怠！」
entries.en: You who were chosen—do not fail Us."
entries.literal: Let the two or three great officers lead forth their intent and not slacken!"

entries.zh: 平陽侯臣窋、汝陰侯臣灶、潁陰侯臣何、廷尉臣宜昌、隴西太守臣昆邪所選賢良太子家令臣錯昧死再拜言：臣竊聞古之賢主莫不求賢以為輔翼，故黃帝得力牧而為五帝先，大禹得咎繇而為三王祖，齊桓得管子而為五伯長。
entries.en: The men who recommended me as Worthy and Good were your servants the Marquis of Pingyang, Cao Zhu; the Marquis of Ruyin, Xiahou Zao; the Marquis of Yingyin, Guan He; the Commandant of Justice, Yichang; and the Administrator of Longxi, Kunxie. Your servant Chao Cuo bows twice and, risking death, states: I have heard that every worthy ruler of antiquity sought worthy men as his wings and helpers. Thus the Yellow Emperor obtained Limu and became foremost of the Five Thearchs; Great Yu obtained Gao Yao and became progenitor of the Three Kings; and Duke Huan of Qi obtained Guan Zhong and became leader of the Five Hegemons.
entries.literal: Your servants Cao Zhu, Marquis of Pingyang; Xiahou Zao, Marquis of Ruyin; Guan He, Marquis of Yingyin; Yichang, Commandant of Justice; and Kunxie, Administrator of Longxi, recommended your servant Chao Cuo, Household Steward of the Heir Apparent, as Worthy and Good. Bowing twice and risking death, I state: I have heard that no worthy ruler of antiquity failed to seek worthy men as wings and helpers. Thus the Yellow Emperor obtained Limu and became foremost of the Five Thearchs; Great Yu obtained Gao Yao and became progenitor of the Three Kings; and Duke Huan of Qi obtained Guan Zhong and became leader of the Five Hegemons.

entries.zh: 今陛下講於大禹及高皇帝之建豪英也，退托於不明，以求賢良，讓之至也。
entries.en: You rehearse the deeds of Yu and Gaozu, then call yourself dim while summoning talent—that is humility carried almost too far.
entries.literal: Now Your Majesty discourses on Great Yu and the Supreme Emperor's establishment of heroes and champions, yet modestly withdraws into "lack of clarity" to seek the worthy and good—this is yielding to the utmost.

entries.zh: 臣竊觀上世之傳，若高皇帝之建功業，陛下之德厚而得賢佐，皆有司之所覽，刻於玉版，藏於金匱，歷之春秋，紀之後世，為帝者祖宗，與天地相終。
entries.en: Your servant has privately examined the traditions of high antiquity: matters such as the High Emperor's founding of merit and enterprise, and Your Majesty's deep virtue in obtaining worthy assistants, are all surveyed by the responsible offices, engraved on jade tablets, stored in golden coffers, passed through the years, and recorded for later generations, so that they become ancestral models for emperors and endure together with Heaven and Earth.
entries.literal: Your servant has privately examined the transmissions of high antiquity: as the Supreme Emperor's establishment of merit and enterprise, and Your Majesty's thick virtue in obtaining worthy assistants, are matters within the ken of the offices, carved on jade tablets, stored in metal coffer, passed through springs and autumns, recorded for later ages, as imperial ancestors ending only with Heaven and earth.

entries.zh: 今臣□等乃以臣錯充賦，甚不稱明詔求賢之意。
entries.en: Yet the board has stuffed the quota with me—hardly what your call for sages intended.
entries.literal: Now your servants (text damaged) have filled the quota with your servant Cuo, which very ill matches the enlightened edict's intent to seek worthies.

entries.zh: 臣錯草茅臣，亡識知，昧死上愚對，曰：
entries.en: I am a nobody from the thatch; risking execution I offer this dull response:
entries.literal: Your servant Cuo is a man of straw huts, without knowledge; risking death he submits a foolish reply, saying:

entries.zh: 後十餘日，吳、楚七國俱反，以誅錯為名。
entries.en: Within a fortnight Wu, Chu, and five other kingdoms rose in arms demanding Chao Cuo's head as their public pretext.
entries.literal: After more than ten days, Wu and Chu with seven states together rebelled, taking the execution of Cuo as their proclaimed cause.

entries.zh: 上與錯議出軍事，錯欲令上自將兵，而身居守。
entries.en: In council Chao Cuo urged the emperor to take the field in person while he held the capital.
entries.literal: The emperor debated with Cuo on dispatching troops; Cuo wished to have the emperor personally lead the army while he himself remained to guard.

entries.zh: 會竇嬰言爰盎，詔召入見，上方與錯調兵食。
entries.en: Dou Ying mentioned Yuan Ang; a summons brought him to court while Jing was still haggling over grain and battalions with Chao Cuo.
entries.literal: It happened that Dou Ying spoke of Yuan Ang; an edict summoned him for audience while the emperor was just adjusting troop dispositions and rations with Cuo.

entries.zh: 上問盎曰：「君嘗為吳相，知吳臣田祿伯為人乎？
entries.en: The emperor asked, "You governed Wu—what sort of man is Tian Lubo?
entries.literal: The emperor asked Ang, "You once were chancellor of Wu—do you know the Wu minister Tian Lubo's character?

entries.zh: 今吳、楚反，於公意何如？」
entries.en: With Wu and Chu in revolt, what is your reading?"
entries.literal: Now Wu and Chu have rebelled—what is your opinion?"

entries.zh: 對曰：「不足憂也，今破矣。」
entries.en: Yuan Ang said, "Do not fret—they are already beaten in spirit."
entries.literal: He replied, "It is not worth worry; they are already broken."

entries.zh: 上曰：「吳王即山鑄錢，煮海為鹽，誘天下豪桀，白頭舉事，此其計不百全，豈發乎？
entries.en: "The king of Wu mints his own cash and boils the sea for salt; he has bought every adventurer in the empire and now moves with white hair—would he strike without a sure plan?
entries.literal: The emperor said, "The King of Wu casts coin from his mountains and boils the sea for salt, luring the bold spirits of the realm; raising the affair with white hair—if his plan were not a hundredfold sure, would he have launched it?

entries.zh: 何以言其無能為也？」
entries.en: Why call him a hollow threat?"
entries.literal: Why do you say they cannot accomplish anything?"

entries.zh: 盎對曰：「吳銅、鹽之利則有之，安得豪桀而誘之！
entries.en: Yuan Ang answered, "Copper and salt do not buy heroes;
entries.literal: Ang replied, "Wu may have the profit of copper and salt—how could it obtain bold spirits and lure them!

entries.zh: 誠令吳得豪桀，亦且輔而為誼，不反矣。
entries.en: had he real champions they would steady his hand, not fire a rebellion;
entries.literal: if Wu truly obtained bold spirits, they would moreover assist it in good faith and it would not rebel.

entries.zh: 吳所誘，皆亡賴子弟，亡命鑄錢奸人，故相誘以亂。」
entries.en: his camp is drifters, counterfeiters, and wastrels egging each other on."
entries.literal: what Wu lures are all worthless sons of families, men fleeing the law who coin money illicitly—therefore they egg one another on to chaos."

entries.zh: 錯曰：「盎策之善。」
entries.en: Cuo said, "Ang's calculation is good."
entries.literal: Cuo said, "Ang's calculation is good."

entries.zh: 上問曰：「計安出？」
entries.en: "Then what is your counsel?" asked the emperor.
entries.literal: The emperor asked, "What plan should come forth?"

entries.zh: 盎對曰：「願屏左右。」
entries.en: Ang replied, "I beg to dismiss those at left and right."
entries.literal: Ang replied, "I beg to dismiss those at left and right."

entries.zh: 上屏人，獨錯在。
entries.en: The room emptied except for Chao Cuo.
entries.literal: The emperor dismissed the others; only Cuo remained.

entries.zh: 盎曰：「臣所言，人臣不得知。」
entries.en: Yuan Ang said, "What follows is for the throne alone."
entries.literal: Ang said, "What your servant will speak of, ministers may not hear."

entries.zh: 乃屏錯。
entries.en: He motioned Chao Cuo out.
entries.literal: Thereupon Cuo was dismissed.

entries.zh: 錯趨避東箱，甚恨。
entries.en: Chao Cuo withdrew to the eastern gallery, furious at the slight.
entries.literal: Cuo hurried aside to the eastern chamber, very resentful.

entries.zh: 上卒問盎，對曰：「吳、楚相遺書，言高皇帝王子弟各有分地，今賊臣晁錯擅適諸侯，削奪之地，以故反名為西共誅錯，復故地而罷。
entries.en: The emperor finally asked Yuan Ang, who replied, "Wu and Chu have exchanged letters saying that Gaozu's sons and younger brothers were each granted allotted territories, but now the wicked minister Chao Cuo has arbitrarily punished the feudal lords and cut away their lands. For this reason, they have raised the banner of marching west to join in executing Chao Cuo, restoring their former lands, and then standing down.
entries.literal: The emperor finally asked Ang; he replied, "Wu and Chu exchanged letters saying that Gaodi's sons and younger brothers each had allotted territory, but now the wicked minister Chao Cuo has on his own authority punished the feudal lords and carved away their lands; therefore they took as their slogan marching west to execute Chao Cuo jointly, restore their old lands, and then stand down.

entries.zh: 方今計，獨有斬錯，發使赦吳、楚七國，復其故地，則兵可毋血刃而俱罷。」
entries.en: Execute Chao Cuo, send heralds offering pardon, return their lands—then the armies melt away without a battle."
entries.literal: For the plan now, only beheading Cuo, dispatching envoys to pardon Wu and the seven states, and restoring their old lands—then the armies can all stand down without blood on the blades."

entries.zh: 於是上默然良久，曰：「顧誠何如，吾不愛一人謝天下。」
entries.en: Jing sat silent, then said, "If that ends it, one life is a cheap price."
entries.literal: Thereupon the emperor was silent a long while and said, "If it truly comes to that, I do not grudge one man to answer the realm."

entries.zh: 盎曰：「愚計出此，唯上孰計之。」
entries.en: Yuan Ang added, "It is a bitter remedy—weigh it yourself."
entries.literal: Ang said, "This is a foolish plan; only may Your Majesty weigh it carefully."

entries.zh: 乃拜盎為泰常，密裝治行。
entries.en: He was named Grand Master of Ceremonies and packed for a secret mission.
entries.literal: Thereupon Ang was appointed Grand Master of Ceremonies and secretly fitted out for travel.

entries.zh: 錯已死，謁者僕射鄧公為校尉，擊吳、楚為將。
entries.en: When Chao Cuo was dead, Deng Gong—grand usher—was serving as a colonel against Wu and Chu.
entries.literal: After Cuo was dead, Deng Gong, chamberlain for attendants, was a colonel and served as general attacking Wu and Chu.

entries.zh: 還，上書言軍事，見上。
entries.en: He came back from the front, wrote up the campaign, and was received in audience.
entries.literal: Returning, he submitted a memorial on military affairs and was granted audience.

entries.zh: 上問曰：「道軍所來，聞晁錯死，吳、楚罷不？」
entries.en: "On the march," asked Jing, "did you hear that Wu and Chu disbanded once Chao Cuo died?"
entries.literal: The emperor asked, "On the road from the army, did you hear that Chao Cuo was dead—did Wu and Chu stand down?"

entries.zh: 鄧公曰：「吳為反數十歲矣，發怒削地，以誅錯為名，其意不在錯也。
entries.en: Deng Gong said, "Wu has nursed rebellion for decades; losing counties enraged them, but Chao Cuo's death was never their true aim.
entries.literal: Deng Gong said, "Wu has intended rebellion for several decades; angered by the paring of its territory, it took executing Cuo as its name, but its intent was not on Cuo.

entries.zh: 且臣恐天下之士拑口不敢復言矣。」
entries.en: I fear as well that honest men across the realm will seal their lips and never dare counsel you again.
entries.literal: Moreover your servant fears that the gentlemen of the realm will clamp their mouths and not dare speak again.

entries.zh: 上曰：「何哉？」
entries.en: "How so?" asked the emperor.
entries.literal: The emperor said, "Why so?"

entries.zh: 鄧公曰：「夫晁錯患諸侯強大不可制，故請削之，以尊京師，萬世之利也。
entries.en: Deng Gong said, "Chao Cuo pared the kingdoms because they threatened the capital—that was a policy for the ages;
entries.literal: Deng Gong said, "Chao Cuo feared the feudal lords' strength could not be controlled; therefore he requested to pare them, to honor the capital region—a profit for myriad ages.

entries.zh: 計劃始行，卒受大戮，內杜忠臣之口，外為諸侯報仇，臣竊為陛下不取也。」
entries.en: the blade had barely fallen on his plan when you struck off his head—silencing loyal counsel abroad while handing the rebels a victory at home. That was a mistake, Son of Heaven."
entries.literal: His plan had barely begun when he suddenly suffered great execution—inwardly silencing loyal ministers' mouths, outwardly giving the feudal lords their revenge—your servant privately thinks Your Majesty should not have taken this course."

entries.zh: 於是景帝喟然長息，曰：「公言善。
entries.en: Emperor Jing exhaled long and said, "You speak truth.
entries.literal: Thereupon Emperor Jing drew a long sigh and said, "Your lordship's words are good.

entries.zh: 吾亦恨之！」
entries.en: I regret it now myself."
entries.literal: I too regret it!"

entries.zh: 乃拜鄧公為城陽中尉。
entries.en: He named Deng Gong metropolitan commandant of Chengyang.
entries.literal: Thereupon Deng Gong was appointed commandant of the capital for Chengyang.

entries.zh: 時，賈誼已死，對策者百餘人，唯錯為高第，繇是遷中大夫。
entries.en: Jia Yi was in the grave; of a hundred examinees only Chao Cuo took top rank and rose to grandee of the palace.
entries.literal: At that time Jia Yi was already dead; of those who answered the policy question more than a hundred, only Cuo ranked highest, and from this he was promoted to grandee of the palace.

entries.zh: 錯又言宜削諸侯事，及法令可更定者，書凡三十篇。
entries.en: He also urged stripping the kingdoms and rewriting the code—thirty memorials in all.
entries.literal: Cuo again spoke that it was fitting to pare the feudal lords' territory and on statutes that could be altered and fixed; the writings in all came to thirty chapters.

entries.zh: 孝文雖不盡聽，然奇其材。
entries.en: Wen did not adopt every plan but admired the man.
entries.literal: Emperor Wen did not wholly heed him, yet marveled at his talent.

entries.zh: 當是時，太子善錯計策，爰盎諸大功臣多不好錯。
entries.en: The crown prince loved his schemes; Yuan Ang and the old guard detested him.
entries.literal: At that time the heir apparent favored Cuo's stratagems, while Yuan Ang and many great meritorious subjects disliked Cuo.

entries.zh: 遷為御史大夫，請諸侯之罪過，削其支郡。
entries.en: Raised to imperial counselor, he listed each king's offenses and moved to confiscate outlying counties.
entries.literal: He was promoted to imperial counselor and requested the feudal lords' faults and crimes, cutting away their collateral commanderies.

entries.zh: 奏上，上令公卿、列侯、宗室雜議，莫敢難，獨竇嬰爭之，繇此與錯有隙。
entries.en: The throne sent the proposal to a joint council; only Dou Ying objected—there the feud between them began.
entries.literal: When the memorial went up, the emperor ordered dukes, ministers, marquises, and imperial kin to debate jointly; none dared oppose except Dou Ying, who contended—therefrom he and Cuo bore a rift.

entries.zh: 錯所更令三十章，諸侯□嘩。
entries.en: The thirty new clauses set the kingdoms in an uproar—the damaged graph likely describes their outcry.
entries.literal: Of the thirty chapters of altered orders that Cuo made, the feudal lords were in an uproar (text damaged).

entries.zh: 錯父聞之，從穎川來，謂錯曰：「上初即位，公為政用事，侵削諸侯，疏人骨肉，口讓多怨，公何為也？」
entries.en: Chao Cuo's father rode from Yingchuan and said, "The new emperor trusts you, yet you strip the kings and set brother against brother—the whole realm will curse your name. Why?"
entries.literal: When Cuo's father heard of it, he came from Yingchuan and said to Cuo, "The emperor has just taken the throne; you handle affairs and wield power, encroaching on and paring the feudal lords, estranging men's flesh and bone; many resentments will follow your tongue—what are you doing?"

entries.zh: 錯曰：「固也。
entries.en: Chao Cuo replied, "It has to be done.
entries.literal: Cuo said, "It must be so.

entries.zh: 不如此，天子不尊，宗廟不安。」
entries.en: Without this the throne stays weak and the altars tremble."
entries.literal: If not thus, the Son of Heaven will not be honored, the ancestral temples will not be secure."

entries.zh: 父曰：「劉氏安矣，而晁氏危，吾去公歸矣！」
entries.en: "The Lius will thrive," he said, "but our clan is finished—I am going home."
entries.literal: The father said, "The house of Liu will be secure, but the house of Chao is in peril—I leave you and go home!"

entries.zh: 遂飲藥死，曰「吾不忍見禍逮身。」
entries.en: Thereupon he drank poison and died, saying, "I cannot bear to see disaster reach my person."
entries.literal: Thereupon he drank poison and died, saying, "I cannot bear to see disaster reach my person."

entries.zh: 鄧公，成固人也，多奇計。
entries.en: Deng Gong came from Chenggu and was full of stratagems.
entries.literal: Deng Gong was a man of Chenggu, with many marvelous stratagems.

entries.zh: 建元年中，上招賢良，公卿言鄧先。
entries.en: When Emperor Wu called for Worthy and Good men in the Jianyuan era, the high ministers recommended Deng Gong first.
entries.literal: In the Jianyuan era, the emperor summoned Worthy and Good men; the dukes and ministers recommended Deng first.

entries.zh: 鄧先時免，起家為九卿。
entries.en: Deng Gong had previously been dismissed, but he was now called from private life to serve as one of the Nine Ministers.
entries.literal: Deng had previously been dismissed; he was now appointed from private life as one of the Nine Ministers.

entries.zh: 一年，復謝病免歸。
entries.en: A year later he begged off ill and went home.
entries.literal: After one year he again pleaded illness, resigned, and returned home.

entries.zh: 其子章，以修黃、老言顯諸公間。
entries.en: His son Zhang won fame at court for expounding Huang-Lao doctrine.
entries.literal: His son Zhang, by cultivating Huang-Lao teaching, became conspicuous among the great men.

entries.zh: 卷四十九 爰盎晁錯傳第十九
entries.en: Volume 49: The Biographies of Yuan Ang and Chao Cuo, number nineteen.
entries.literal: Scroll 49: Biography 19 of Yuan Ang and Chao Cuo.

entries.zh: 張釋之字季，南陽堵陽人也。
entries.en: Zhang Shizhi, whose courtesy name was Ji, came from Duyang in Nanyang.
entries.literal: Zhang Shizhi, courtesy name Ji, was a native of Duyang in Nanyang commandery.

entries.zh: 與兄仲同居，以貲為騎郎，事文帝，十年不得調，亡所知名。
entries.en: He lived with his older brother Zhong, bought his way into the post of mounted attendant, and attended Emperor Wen; for ten years he was never moved to a new post and remained entirely unknown.
entries.literal: He dwelt together with his elder brother Zhong; by paying a fee he became a mounted attendant; he served Emperor Wen for ten years without being transferred or promoted, and had no reputation whatever.

entries.zh: 釋之曰：「久宦減仲之產，不遂。」
entries.en: Shizhi said, "My long service as an official has eaten away at Zhong's estate; nothing has come of it."
entries.literal: Shizhi said, "Long serving as an official has reduced Zhong's property; it has not succeeded."

entries.zh: 欲免歸。
entries.en: He wanted to resign and go home.
entries.literal: He wished to resign and return home.

entries.zh: 中郎將爰盎知其賢，惜其去，乃請徙釋之補謁者。
entries.en: Yuan Ang, general of the gentlemen-at-arms, knew Shizhi was capable and hated to lose him, so he asked that Shizhi be reassigned to serve as an usher.
entries.literal: The general of gentlemen-at-arms Yuan Ang knew he was worthy, regretted that he would leave, and therefore asked to have Shizhi transferred to fill a vacancy as usher.

entries.zh: 釋之既朝畢，因前言便宜事。
entries.en: After court was dismissed, Shizhi stepped forward and spoke of policies that would benefit the state.
entries.literal: When Shizhi had finished his court audience, he took the opportunity to speak first of what was expedient.

entries.zh: 文帝曰：「卑之，毋甚高論，令今可行也。」
entries.en: Emperor Wen said, "Keep it practical; spare me lofty theory—tell me what can actually be done today."
entries.literal: The emperor said, "Keep it modest; do not launch into lofty theories; let what you say be feasible in the present."

entries.zh: 於是釋之言秦、漢之間事，秦所以失，漢所以興者。
entries.en: Shizhi then traced events from Qin through to Han, explaining how Qin had lost the empire and how Han had gained it.
entries.literal: Thereupon Shizhi spoke of affairs between Qin and Han—why Qin lost the realm and why Han rose.

entries.zh: 文帝稱善，拜釋之為謁者僕射。
entries.en: The emperor approved, and Shizhi was appointed chief usher (pushe).
entries.literal: The emperor praised him and appointed Shizhi chief usher.

entries.zh: 頃之，太子與梁王共車入朝，不下司馬門，於是釋之追止太子、梁王毋入殿門。
entries.en: Soon after, the crown prince and the king of Liang rode together into the palace precincts without alighting at the Sima Gate; Shizhi overtook them and barred them from the inner hall until they complied.
entries.literal: Before long, the heir apparent and the king of Liang shared a carriage into court; they did not dismount at the Sima gate. Shizhi therefore ran after them and stopped the heir apparent and the king of Liang from entering the hall gate.

entries.zh: 遂劾不下公門不敬，奏之。
entries.en: He then filed a charge of disrespect for not dismounting at the outer gate and submitted it to the throne.
entries.literal: He thereupon impeached them for failing to dismount at the public gate as an act of disrespect and memorialized it.

entries.zh: 薄太后聞之，文帝免冠謝曰：「教兒子不謹。」
entries.en: When Empress Dowager Bo learned of it, Emperor Wen doffed his cap and apologized: "I was remiss in teaching my sons."
entries.literal: When Empress Dowager Bo heard of it, Emperor Wen removed his cap and apologized, saying, "I failed to instruct my sons with strictness."

entries.zh: 薄太后使使承詔赦太子、梁王，然後得入。
entries.en: The empress dowager sent messengers with an edict pardoning the crown prince and the king of Liang, after which they were allowed in.
entries.literal: Empress Dowager Bo sent an envoy bearing an edict pardoning the crown prince and the king of Liang; only then could they enter.

entries.zh: 文帝繇是奇釋之，拜為中大夫。
entries.en: Emperor Wen was struck by Shizhi from that day on and promoted him to grand counsellor of the palace.
entries.literal: From this Emperor Wen thought Shizhi extraordinary and appointed him grand counsellor of the palace.

entries.zh: 文帝崩，景帝立，釋之恐，稱疾。
entries.en: When Wen died and Jing succeeded, Shizhi grew fearful and pleaded illness.
entries.literal: When Emperor Wen died and Emperor Jing took the throne, Shizhi was afraid and pleaded illness.

entries.zh: 欲免去，懼大誅至；
entries.en: He wanted to resign yet dreaded a sweeping punishment;
entries.literal: He wished to resign and leave but feared execution on a great scale would come;

entries.zh: 欲見，則未知何如。
entries.en: he thought of facing the new emperor but could not tell how he would be received.
entries.literal: he wished to appear but did not know how it would go.

entries.zh: 用王生計，卒見謝，景帝不過也。
entries.en: Wang Sheng's advice won out: he went in to apologize, and Emperor Jing did not press the old grudge too far.
entries.literal: Following Wang Sheng's plan he finally went in to apologize, and Emperor Jing did not fault him beyond measure.

entries.zh: 十年，景帝立，以唐為楚相。
entries.en: In the tenth year, after Emperor Jing took the throne, Feng Tang was appointed Chancellor of Chu.
entries.literal: In the tenth year, when Emperor Jing ascended, Tang was made Chancellor of Chu.

entries.zh: 武帝即位，求賢良，舉唐。
entries.en: When Emperor Wu came to the throne he called for worthies and recommended Feng Tang.
entries.literal: When Emperor Wu took the throne, he sought worthy and excellent men and recommended Tang.

entries.zh: 唐時年九十餘，不能為官，乃以子遂為郎。
entries.en: Feng Tang was then more than ninety and unfit for office, so his son Sui was made a court gentleman.
entries.literal: Tang was then over ninety and could not serve in office, so his son Sui was made a gentleman-at-court.

entries.zh: 遂字王孫，亦奇士。
entries.en: Sui, whose courtesy name was Wangsun, was also an extraordinary man.
entries.literal: Sui, courtesy name Wangsun, was also a remarkable man.

entries.zh: 魏尚，槐里人也。
entries.en: Wei Shang was a native of Huaili.
entries.literal: Wei Shang was a native of Huaili.

entries.zh: 汲黯字長孺，濮陽人也。
entries.en: Ji An, whose courtesy name was Zhangru, came from Puyang.
entries.literal: Ji An, courtesy name Zhangru, was a native of Puyang.

entries.zh: 其先有寵於古之衛君也。
entries.en: His forebears had enjoyed favor with the ancient lord of Wei.
entries.literal: His forebears had enjoyed favor with the ancient lord of Wei.

entries.zh: 至黯十世，世為卿大夫。
entries.en: For ten generations before him the family had filled ministerial posts.
entries.literal: Down to An, for ten generations they had been ministers and grandees.

entries.zh: 以父任，孝景時為太子洗馬，以嚴見憚。
entries.en: Recommended on his father's record, he served Emperor Jing as groom to the crown prince and was dreaded for his uncompromising sternness.
entries.literal: By his father's privilege, under Emperor Jing he became groom of the heir apparent and was feared for his severity.

entries.zh: 釋之事景帝歲餘，為淮南相，猶尚以前過也。
entries.en: After a little more than a year serving Jing, Shizhi was made chancellor of Huainan, still on account of the earlier offense.
entries.literal: Shizhi served Emperor Jing for over a year; he was made chancellor of Huainan, still on account of the earlier offense.

entries.zh: 年老病卒。
entries.en: He died in old age of natural causes.
entries.literal: He died of old age and illness.

entries.zh: 其子摯，字長公，官至大夫，免。
entries.en: His son Zhi, courtesy name Zhangong, reached the rank of grandee before being dismissed.
entries.literal: His son Zhi, courtesy name Zhangong, rose to the rank of grandee but was dismissed.

entries.zh: 以不能取容當世，故終身不仕。
entries.en: Unable to trim his sails to the times, he never held office again.
entries.literal: Because he could not accommodate himself to the age he never served in office all his life.

entries.zh: 其後人有盜高廟座前玉環，得，文帝怒，下廷尉治。
entries.en: Later someone stole a jade ring from the dais in Gaozu's temple; when he was caught Emperor Wen, in a rage, sent him to the commandant of justice.
entries.literal: Later someone stole a jade ring from before the seat in Gaozu's temple; he was caught and Emperor Wen, furious, handed him to the commandant of justice for trial.

entries.zh: 案盜宗廟服御物者為奏，當棄市。
entries.en: Shizhi judged theft of imperial ritual gear from the ancestral shrines and recommended execution in the marketplace.
entries.literal: When the case of one who stole ritual objects from the ancestral temple was reported, the matched penalty was public execution in the market.

entries.zh: 上大怒曰：「人亡道，乃盜先帝器！
entries.en: The emperor thundered, "The man is utterly depraved—he stole an object of the late emperor!
entries.literal: The emperor said in great anger, "That man lacks the way; he stole the late emperor's vessel!

entries.zh: 吾屬廷尉者，欲致之族，而君以法奏之，非吾所以共承宗廟意也。」
entries.en: I sent him to you expecting the extermination of his clan; instead you cite the statutes. That is not how I meant to uphold the shrines of our house."
entries.literal: I handed him to the commandant of justice wishing to have his kin exterminated; yet you memorialized according to the law—that is not how I meant to share in sustaining the ancestral temple."

entries.zh: 釋之免冠頓首謝曰：「法如是足也。
entries.en: Shizhi doffed his cap and kowtowed: "The law already prescribes the utmost for this offense.
entries.literal: Shizhi removed his cap and knocked his head in apology, saying, "According to the law this is sufficient punishment.

entries.zh: 且罪等，然以逆順為基。
entries.en: When crimes are of the same grade, one still weighs whether the act was calculated rebellion or mere disorder.
entries.literal: Moreover when crimes are equal, the judgment takes orderly versus rebellious conduct as its basis.

entries.zh: 今盜宗廟器而族之，有如萬分一，假令愚民取長陵一□土，陛下且何以加其法乎？」
entries.en: If stealing vessels from the ancestral temple now brings clan extermination, then suppose, in one chance out of ten thousand, some ignorant commoner took a handful of earth from Changling. What penalty would Your Majesty add then?"
entries.literal: Now to exterminate a whole clan for stealing temple vessels—if there were one chance in ten thousand, suppose common folk took one handful of earth from Changling—how would Your Majesty add to the law then?"

entries.zh: 文帝與太后言之，乃許廷尉當。
entries.en: The emperor took the matter to the empress dowager and then accepted the commandant's sentence.
entries.literal: The emperor spoke of it with the empress dowager and then approved the commandant's verdict.

entries.zh: 是時，中尉條侯周亞夫與梁相山都侯王恬啟見釋之持議平，乃結為親友。
entries.en: At the time Commandant Zhou Yafu of the Tiao marquisate and Wang Tianqi, marquis of Shandu and minister of Liang, saw how fairly Shizhi decided cases and became his close friends.
entries.literal: At that time Commandant Zhou Yafu of the Tiao marquisate and Wang Tianqi, marquis of Shandu and minister of Liang, saw that Shizhi held opinions fairly; they therefore formed friendly ties with him.

entries.zh: 張廷尉繇此天下稱之。
entries.en: From then on Commandant Zhang was honored across the empire.
entries.literal: Commandant Zhang was praised throughout the realm for this.

entries.zh: 張湯以更定律令為廷尉，黯質責湯於上前，曰：「公為正卿，上不能褒先帝之功業，下不能化天下之邪心，安國富民，使囹圄空虛，何空取高皇帝約束紛更之為？
entries.en: When Zhang Tang rewrote the code and became commandant of justice, Ji An cornered him in open court: "As chief minister you neither celebrate the founder's legacy nor reform public morals, bring peace to the realm, fill the granaries, nor clear the jails—why do you busy yourself tearing apart the statutes Gaozu left behind?
entries.literal: Zhang Tang, having revised statutes and ordinances, became commandant of justice; An confronted and rebuked Tang before the sovereign, saying, "You are chief minister; above you cannot extol the late emperor's achievements, below you cannot transform the wicked hearts of the world, settle the state and enrich the people, or empty the prisons—why do you vainly take Gaozu's established rules and alter them in confusion?

entries.zh: 而公以此無種矣！」
entries.en: And for this you will leave no posterity!"
entries.literal: And for this you will leave no posterity!"

entries.zh: 黯時與湯論議，湯辯常在文深小苛，黯憤發，罵曰：「天下謂刀筆吏不可為公卿，果然。
entries.en: In policy debates Zhang Tang always hid behind legal hair-splitting; Ji An lost his temper and swore, "They say a clerk should never rise to high office—how true.
entries.literal: When An debated policy with Tang, Tang's argumentation always lay in twisted wording and petty harshness; An flared with anger and cursed, saying, "The world says brush-and-knife clerks must not become dukes and ministers—it is indeed so.

entries.zh: 必湯也，令天下重足而立，仄目而視矣！」
entries.en: If it must be Tang, he will make all under heaven stand with feet together and look sideways!"
entries.literal: If it must be Tang, he will make all under heaven stand with feet together and look sideways!"

entries.zh: 武帝即位，黯為謁者。
entries.en: When Wu succeeded, Ji An was appointed an usher.
entries.literal: When Emperor Wu took the throne, An became an usher.

entries.zh: 東粵相攻，上使黯往視之。
entries.en: When the Eastern Yue principalities turned on each other, the emperor dispatched Ji An to look into it.
entries.literal: The Eastern Yue states attacked one another; the sovereign sent An to inspect.

entries.zh: 至吳而還，報曰：「粵人相攻，固其俗，不足以辱天子使者。」
entries.en: He got only as far as Wu and sent word back: "Let the Yue fight among themselves—it is their habit and hardly merits an imperial envoy."
entries.literal: He turned back at Wu and reported, "The Yue people fighting one another is their custom; it is not worth troubling an envoy of the Son of Heaven."

entries.zh: 河內失火，燒千餘家，上使黯往視之。
entries.en: When fire ravaged a thousand homes in Henei, the emperor sent him again.
entries.literal: A fire in Henei burned more than a thousand households; the sovereign sent An to inspect.

entries.zh: 還報曰：「家人失火，屋比延燒，不足憂。
entries.en: He returned and reported, "It was an ordinary house fire that spread along adjoining roofs; there is nothing to worry about.
entries.literal: He returned and reported, "A common household fire spread along adjoining roofs; there is nothing to worry about.

entries.zh: 臣過河內，河內貧人傷水旱萬餘家，或父子相食，臣謹以便宜，持節發河內倉粟以振貧民。
entries.en: But on my way through Henei I found tens of thousands starving from flood and drought, some families reduced to cannibalism; I used my commission to open the government granaries and feed them.
entries.literal: Passing through Henei I saw more than ten thousand poor harmed by flood and drought, some fathers and sons eating one another; I dared, as expedient, to take the staff and open the Henei granaries to relieve the poor.

entries.zh: 請歸節，伏矯制罪。」
entries.en: I beg to return the staff and accept punishment for counterfeiting an imperial order."
entries.literal: I beg to return the staff and submit to the offense of counterfeiting an imperial order."

entries.zh: 上賢而釋之，遷為滎陽令。
entries.en: The emperor judged him loyal, forgave the offense, and named him magistrate of Xingyang.
entries.literal: The sovereign thought him worthy and released him, promoting him to magistrate of Xingyang.

entries.zh: 黯恥為令，稱疾歸田里。
entries.en: Ji An found a county post beneath him, feigned illness, and went home to his fields.
entries.literal: An was ashamed to be a magistrate and pleaded illness, returning to his village fields.

entries.zh: 上聞，乃召為中大夫。
entries.en: When word reached the throne, Wu recalled him as grand counsellor of the palace.
entries.literal: When the sovereign heard of it, he summoned him to be grand counsellor of the palace.

entries.zh: 以數切諫，不得久留內，遷為東海太守。
entries.en: His blunt memorials made him unwelcome at court, so he was shifted to governor of Donghai.
entries.literal: Because he remonstrated sharply and repeatedly, he could not long remain inside and was transferred to governor of the Eastern Sea.

entries.zh: 黯多病，病且滿三月，上常賜告者數，終不愈。
entries.en: Ji An was chronically sick; as three months neared, the emperor kept extending his sick leave, but he did not mend.
entries.literal: An was often ill; his illness neared three months; the sovereign repeatedly granted him leave to recover, yet he never got better.

entries.zh: 最後，嚴助為請告。
entries.en: At last Yan Zhu begged the throne on his behalf.
entries.literal: Finally Yan Zhu spoke for him requesting leave.

entries.zh: 上曰：「汲黯何如人也？」
entries.en: Wu asked, "What kind of man is Ji An really?"
entries.literal: The sovereign said, "What sort of man is Ji An?"

entries.zh: 曰：「使黯任職居官，亡以愈人，然至其輔少主守成，雖自謂賁、育弗能奪也。」
entries.en: Yan Zhu replied: "Set him to routine administration and he seems ordinary; but charge him with guarding a young heir and the legacy of the house—even Ben and Yu could not shake his resolve."
entries.literal: [Yan Zhu] said, "If you put An in office to handle affairs, he will not surpass others; yet when it comes to supporting a young ruler and guarding what is established, even men who call themselves Ben and Yu could not budge him."

entries.zh: 上曰：「然。
entries.en: The emperor said, "So.
entries.literal: The sovereign said, "So.

entries.zh: 古有社稷之臣，至如汲黯，近之矣！」
entries.en: In antiquity there were ministers for the altars of soil and grain; as for Ji An, he approaches that!"
entries.literal: In antiquity there were ministers for the altars of soil and grain; as for Ji An, he approaches that!"

entries.zh: 是時，漢方征匈奴，招懷四夷。
entries.en: The Han was then deep in the Xiongnu wars and courting the border tribes.
entries.literal: At that time Han was just campaigning against the Xiongnu and winning over the four Yi.

entries.zh: 黯務少事，間常言與胡和親，毋起兵。
entries.en: Ji An pushed for less government and urged marriage alliances with the steppe instead of new campaigns.
entries.literal: An strove for few affairs and often spoke of peace and kinship with the Hu, not raising troops.

entries.zh: 上方鄉儒術，尊公孫弘，及事益多，吏民巧。
entries.en: The emperor meanwhile embraced Confucianism, elevated Gongsun Hong, and as business multiplied, officials and people grew expert at evasion.
entries.literal: The sovereign was turning toward Confucian learning, honored Gongsun Hong, and as affairs grew more numerous, clerks and commoners grew crafty.

entries.zh: 上分別文法，湯等數奏決讞以幸。
entries.en: Wu delighted in legal exegesis; Zhang Tang and his circle fed him case after case to curry favor.
entries.literal: The sovereign distinguished textual niceties in the law; Tang and others repeatedly memorialized verdicts to win favor.

entries.zh: 而黯常毀儒，面觸弘等徒懷詐飾智以阿人主取容，而刀筆之吏專深文巧詆，陷人於罔，以自為功。
entries.en: Ji An, meanwhile, trashed the Ru scholars and accused Hong to his face of faking wisdom to please the throne, while clerks twisted the code to frame the innocent and pad their résumés.
entries.literal: But An often disparaged Confucians; to the face he attacked Hong and the rest for harboring deceit and displaying cleverness to fawn on the ruler and win accommodation, while brush-and-knife clerks specialized in twisted texts and clever slanders, trapping people in nets to make their own merit.

entries.zh: 上愈益貴弘、湯，弘、湯心疾黯，雖上亦不說也，欲誅之以事。
entries.en: Wu prized Hong and Tang all the more; they loathed Ji An, and the emperor himself cooled—yet all three looked for a charge that would let them kill him.
entries.literal: The sovereign came more and more to esteem Hong and Tang; Hong and Tang inwardly hated An—though the sovereign too was displeased—and wished to execute him on some pretext.

entries.zh: 弘為丞相，乃言上曰：「右內史界部中多貴人宗室，難治，非素重臣弗能任，請徙黯。」
entries.en: Once Gongsun Hong became chancellor, he told the emperor, "The district under the right metropolitan superintendent contains many nobles and imperial clansmen and is difficult to govern. Only a minister of established weight can bear the charge. I request that Ji An be transferred there."
entries.literal: Hong being chancellor, then spoke to the sovereign, saying, "The territory of the right metropolitan superintendent has many nobles and imperial clansmen; it is hard to govern; unless it is a minister of long-standing weight he cannot bear the burden—I beg to transfer An."

entries.zh: 為右內史數歲，官事不廢。
entries.en: Ji An held the post for years without letting administration slide.
entries.literal: As right metropolitan superintendent for several years, official business was not neglected.

entries.zh: 始黯列九卿矣，而公孫弘、張湯為小吏。
entries.en: Ji An had been a nine-minister man when Hong and Tang were still clerks.
entries.literal: At first An ranked with the nine ministers while Gongsun Hong and Zhang Tang were petty clerks.

entries.zh: 及弘、湯稍貴，與黯同位，黯又非毀弘、湯。
entries.en: When they rose to his level, he still spoke of them with contempt.
entries.literal: When Hong and Tang gradually grew noble and shared rank with An, An again condemned and disparaged Hong and Tang.

entries.zh: 已而弘至丞相，封侯，湯御史大夫，黯時丞史皆與同列，或尊用過之。
entries.en: Soon Hong was chancellor and a marquis, Tang imperial counsellor, while Ji An's old subordinates passed him in rank.
entries.literal: In time Hong reached chancellor and was enfeoffed as marquis; Tang became imperial counsellor; at that time An's assistants and clerks were of the same rank, some honored and employed above him.

entries.zh: 黯褊心，不能無少望，見上，言曰：「陛下用群臣如積薪耳，後來者居上。」
entries.en: Bitterness ate at him; he told the emperor, "You stack your ministers like firewood—the last logs tossed on end up on top."
entries.literal: An's heart was narrow; he could not but harbor some resentment; seeing the sovereign he said, "Your Majesty employs the ministers like stacking firewood—the later arrivals sit on top."

entries.zh: 黯罷，上曰：「人果不可以無學，觀汲黯之言，日益甚矣。」
entries.en: After Ji An left, Wu remarked, "A man really must read his books—listen to Ji An now; he grows cruder by the day."
entries.literal: When An withdrew the sovereign said, "Indeed a man cannot lack learning; observe Ji An's words—they grow daily more extreme!"

entries.zh: 鄭當時字莊，陳人也。
entries.en: Zheng Dangshi, courtesy name Zhuang, came from Chen commandery.
entries.literal: Zheng Dangshi, courtesy name Zhuang, was a native of Chen.

entries.zh: 其先鄭君嘗事項籍，籍死而屬漢。
entries.en: His forebear Lord Zheng had served Xiang Yu; when Yu died he transferred his allegiance to Han.
entries.literal: His ancestor Lord Zheng had once served Xiang Yu; when Yu died he attached to Han.

entries.zh: 高祖令諸故項籍臣名籍，鄭君獨不奉詔。
entries.en: Gaozu ordered Xiang Yu's old retainers to refer to him by his personal name as a sign of submission; Lord Zheng alone refused the edict.
entries.literal: Gaozu ordered all former ministers of Xiang Yu to call Yu by his personal name; Lord Zheng alone did not comply with the edict.

entries.zh: 詔盡拜名籍者為大夫，而逐鄭君。
entries.en: Those who obeyed were made grandees; Lord Zheng was banished.
entries.literal: The edict appointed all who named Yu as grandees and expelled Lord Zheng.

entries.zh: 鄭君死孝文時。
entries.en: Lord Zheng died during the reign of Emperor Wen.
entries.literal: Lord Zheng died in Emperor Xiaowen's time.

entries.zh: 當時以任俠自喜，脫張羽於厄，聲聞梁、楚間。
entries.en: Zheng Zhuang made a name as a knight-errant, once snatching Zhang Yu from mortal danger; his fame ran through Liang and Chu.
entries.literal: Dangshi prided himself on knight-errantry and rescued Zhang Yu from peril; his reputation spread between Liang and Chu.

entries.zh: 孝景時，為太子舍人。
entries.en: Under Emperor Jing he served as a gentleman-attendant to the crown prince.
entries.literal: Under Emperor Jing he was attendant to the heir apparent.

entries.zh: 每五日洗沐，常置驛馬長安諸郊，請謝賓客，夜以繼日，至明旦，常恐不遍。
entries.en: On each five-day leave he posted relay horses around Chang'an and spent nights and dawns hosting every guest he could, terrified of missing anyone.
entries.literal: Every five days on bath-leave he always stationed relay horses in the outskirts of Chang'an, inviting and thanking guests, night succeeding day until the next dawn, always fearing not to reach everyone.

entries.zh: 當時好黃、老言，其慕長者，如恐不稱。
entries.en: He studied Huang-Lao texts and courted venerable men as though he could never honor them enough.
entries.literal: Dangshi loved Huang-Lao discourse; in admiring senior worthies he seemed to fear not matching them.

entries.zh: 自見年少官薄，然其知友皆大父行，天下有名之士也。
entries.en: Though young and low in rank, he befriended men a generation older—the most celebrated names of the day.
entries.literal: Though he saw himself as young and of thin rank, his intimate friends were all of his grandfather's generation, famous gentlemen of the empire.

entries.zh: 武帝即位，當時稍遷為魯中尉，濟南太守，江都相，至九卿為右內史。
entries.en: When Emperor Wu came to the throne, Zheng Dangshi rose step by step to commandant of Lu, governor of Jinan, and chancellor of Jiangdu, and finally among the Nine Ministers became right interior secretary.
entries.literal: When Emperor Wu took the throne, Dangshi was gradually promoted to commandant of Lu, governor of Jinan, and chancellor of Jiangdu, and at the Nine Ministers level became right interior secretary.

entries.zh: 以武安魏其時議，貶秩為詹事，遷為大司農。
entries.en: Caught up in the Wu'an–Weiqi factional strife, he was demoted to chamberlain of the heir apparent and then moved to grand minister of agriculture.
entries.literal: Because of the factional disputes of Wu'an and Weiqi, his rank was reduced to chamberlain of the heir apparent, and he was transferred to grand minister of agriculture.

entries.zh: 當時為大吏，戒門下：「客至，亡貴賤亡留門下者。」
entries.en: As a high official he warned his retainers: "When guests come, high or low, let none be kept waiting at the door."
entries.literal: When Dangshi was a senior official he instructed his household staff: "When guests arrive, whether noble or base, do not detain them with the door staff."

entries.zh: 執賓主之禮，以其貴下人。
entries.en: He received them with full courtesy and let his own rank bow to theirs.
entries.literal: He observed host-guest ritual and with his nobility humbled himself to others.

entries.zh: 性廉，又不治產，卬奉賜給諸公。
entries.en: He was honest, kept no landed fortune, and poured every stipend and gift into helping friends.
entries.literal: By nature incorrupt and again not managing estates, he used salary and gifts to supply gentlemen.

entries.zh: 然其饋遺人，不過具器食。
entries.en: His own presents to others never rose above a simple meal in plain ware.
entries.literal: Yet what he sent as gifts to others did not exceed ordinary vessels and food.

entries.zh: 每朝，候上間說，未嘗不言天下長者。
entries.en: Whenever he caught the emperor's ear he spoke of worthy men across the realm.
entries.literal: At each court session he waited for the sovereign's spare moments in speaking and never failed to mention senior worthies of the empire.

entries.zh: 其推轂士及官屬丞史，誠有味其言也。
entries.en: The way he pushed chariots for scholars and for his own deputies had real conviction.
entries.literal: In recommending gentlemen and official subordinates, assistants and clerks, there was truly savor in what he said.

entries.zh: 常引以為賢於己。
entries.en: He always praised them as better men than he was.
entries.literal: He constantly cited them as worthier than himself.

entries.zh: 未嘗名吏，與官屬言，若恐傷之。
entries.en: He never barked a clerk's name; with subordinates he spoke as though afraid to bruise them.
entries.literal: He never called clerks by name; when speaking with subordinates it was as if he feared to wound them.

entries.zh: 聞人之善言，進之上，唯恐後。
entries.en: Good words about others he relayed to the throne the same day, anxious not to lag.
entries.literal: When he heard others' good words he advanced them to the sovereign, fearing only to be too late.

entries.zh: 山東諸公為此翕然稱鄭莊。
entries.en: For this the great families east of the mountains honored him as Zheng Zhuang.
entries.literal: The great lords east of the mountains for this unanimously praised Zheng Zhuang.

entries.zh: 使視決河，自請治行五日。
entries.en: Dispatched to inspect a Yellow River break, he asked five days to pack.
entries.literal: Sent to inspect the river breach, he himself requested five days to arrange his traveling gear.

entries.zh: 上曰：「吾聞鄭莊行，千里不繼糧，治行者何也？」
entries.en: The emperor said, "I have heard that when Zheng Zhuang travels he needs no successive supplies for a thousand li—what is this about arranging traveling gear?"
entries.literal: The sovereign said, "I have heard that when Zheng Zhuang travels he needs no successive supplies for a thousand li—what is this about arranging traveling gear?"

entries.zh: 然當時以朝，常趨和承意，不敢甚斥臧否。
entries.en: In open court, though, he hurried to agree with the emperor and never risked a hard verdict on right and wrong.
entries.literal: Yet Dangshi at court always hurried to harmonize and carry out the sovereign's intent, not daring sharply to judge right and wrong.

entries.zh: 漢征匈奴，招四夷，天下費多，財用益屈。
entries.en: Han's wars against the Xiongnu and its courtship of the border peoples bled the treasury dry.
entries.literal: Han campaigned against the Xiongnu and summoned the four Yi; expenses in the empire were many and fiscal resources grew ever strained.

entries.zh: 當時為大司農，任人賓客僦，入多逋負。
entries.en: As grand minister of agriculture, he entrusted men with the work and his retainers engaged in hire-contracts; much of the revenue fell into arrears.
entries.literal: Dangshi was grand minister of agriculture; in letting people employ guests for hire-rent, income had many arrears.

entries.zh: 司馬安為淮陽太守，發其事，當時在此陷罪，贖為庶人。
entries.en: Sima An, then governor of Huaiyang, exposed the scheme; Zheng Dangshi paid a ransom and was reduced to commoner.
entries.literal: Sima An as governor of Huaiyang exposed the matter; Dangshi on this account fell into crime and ransomed himself to commoner status.

entries.zh: 頃之，守長史。
entries.en: Soon he was serving as chief clerk.
entries.literal: Before long he was acting chief clerk.

entries.zh: 遷汝南太守，數歲，以官卒。
entries.en: He rose to governor of Runan and died in that post a few years later.
entries.literal: He was promoted governor of Runan; after several years he died in office.

entries.zh: 昆弟以當時故，至二千石者六七人。
entries.en: Six or seven of his kinsmen reached the two-thousand-picul rank on his coattails.
entries.literal: Cousins because of Dangshi reached two thousand piculs—six or seven persons.

entries.zh: 卷五十 張馮汲鄭傳第二十
entries.en: Volume 50: The Biographies of Zhang, Feng, Ji, and Zheng (No. 20).
entries.literal: Volume 50, twentieth: Biographies of Zhang, Feng, Ji, and Zheng

entries.zh: 嬰銳為救夫，嬰夫人諫曰：「灌將軍得罪丞相，與太后家迕，寧可救邪？」
entries.en: Dou Ying was bent on saving Guan Fu. His wife warned him, "Guan Fu has insulted the chancellor and defied the Tian family—can you save him?"
entries.literal: Ying was keen to save Fu; Ying's wife remonstrated, saying, "General Guan has offended the chancellor and crossed the empress dowager's house—can he possibly be saved?"

entries.zh: 嬰曰：「侯自我得之，自我捐之，無所恨。
entries.en: Dou Ying said, "I won my title with my own merit; I may lose it the same way—I have no regrets.
entries.literal: Ying said, "The marquisate I won for myself I may cast away for myself; I have no regret.

entries.zh: 且終不令灌仲孺獨死，嬰獨生。」
entries.en: Nor will I let Guan Zhongru die while I alone survive."
entries.literal: Moreover in the end I will not allow Guan Zhongru to die alone while I, Ying, live."

entries.zh: 乃匿其家，竊出上書。
entries.en: He slipped past his household, stole out, and filed a memorial with the throne.
entries.literal: Thereupon he hid it from his family, stole out, and submitted a memorial.

entries.zh: 立召人，具告言灌夫醉飽事，不足誅。
entries.en: He had Guan Fu brought in at once and laid out the whole drunken-scene story, arguing it did not merit death.
entries.literal: He immediately summoned a man in and fully reported Guan Fu's drunken surfeit affair, saying it did not merit execution.

entries.zh: 上然之，賜嬰食，曰：「東朝廷辯之。」
entries.en: The emperor assented, fed Dou Ying, and said, "Argue it out in the eastern court."
entries.literal: The emperor agreed, gave Ying a meal, and said, "Debate it in the eastern court."

entries.zh: 嬰東朝，盛推夫善，言其醉飽得過，乃丞相以它事誣罪之。
entries.en: At the eastern court Dou Ying praised Guan Fu to the skies, blamed the brawl on drink, and called Tian Fen's charges a frame-up.
entries.literal: Ying went to the eastern court and greatly praised Fu's goodness, saying his offense was drunken surfeit, and that the chancellor had falsely accused him on other matters.

entries.zh: 蚡盛毀夫所為橫恣，罪逆不道。
entries.en: Tian Fen blackened Guan Fu as a bully whose crimes knew no law.
entries.literal: Fen greatly slandered Fu's conduct as violent and arbitrary, criminal and contrary to the Way.

entries.zh: 嬰度無可奈何，因言蚡短。
entries.en: Seeing he was losing, Dou Ying turned to Tian Fen's own faults.
entries.literal: Ying, estimating there was nothing to be done, therefore spoke of Fen's shortcomings.

entries.zh: 蚡曰：「天下幸而安樂無事，蚡得為肺附，所好音樂、狗馬、田宅，所愛倡優、巧匠之屬，不如魏其、灌夫日夜招聚天下豪傑壯士與論議，腹誹而心謗，卬視天，俯畫地，辟睨兩官間，幸天下有變，而欲有大功。
entries.en: Tian Fen said, "While the empire enjoys peace, I, as the emperor's uncle, care for music, hounds, horses, and mansions—singers, actors, and craftsmen. I am nothing like Dou Ying and Guan Fu, who recruit ruffians day and night, nurse private grudges, scan heaven and earth, and leer toward both palaces, praying for turmoil so they can seize glory.
