entries.en: Subordinates too puffed up the riches of the west: the grander the tale, the likelier the staff of office; smaller boasts won deputy posts—so liars and riffraff rushed to copy one another.
entries.literal: Their clerks and soldiers also repeatedly again greatly exaggerated what foreign states possessed; those whose words were large were given credentials, those whose words were small became deputies; therefore those who falsely spoke and were without conduct all vied to imitate one another.

entries.zh: 其使皆私縣官齎物，欲賤市以私其利。
entries.en: Envoys skimmed the imperial gifts they carried in train, planning to buy cheap on the side and pocket the difference.
entries.literal: Their envoys all privately embezzled the state goods they carried in train, wishing to buy cheap and privatize the profit.

entries.zh: 外國亦厭漢使人人有言輕重，度漢兵遠，不能至，而禁其食物，以苦漢使。
entries.en: Western courts tired of Han's endless envoys, judged the armies too distant to help, and starved the missions to break them.
entries.literal: The foreign states also wearied of Han envoys, each boasting according to his rank; they reckoned Han troops were far and could not arrive, and cut off their food, thereby distressing Han envoys.

entries.zh: 漢使乏絕，責怨，至相攻擊。
entries.en: Stranded missions turned on one another, blaming and even fighting among themselves.
entries.literal: Han envoys were exhausted and cut off, blamed and resented one another, and reached the point of attacking one another.

entries.zh: 樓蘭、姑師小國，當空道，攻劫漢使王恢等尤甚。
entries.en: The petty kingdoms of Loulan and Jushi straddled the caravan road and preyed worst of all on missions such as Wang Hui's.
entries.literal: Loulan and Jushi, small states, stood athwart the open road and attacked and robbed Han envoys such as Wang Hui especially severely.

entries.zh: 而匈奴奇兵又時時遮擊之。
entries.en: Xiongnu raiding parties joined in, picking off stragglers at will.
entries.literal: Moreover Xiongnu irregular troops also from time to time intercepted and struck them.

entries.zh: 使者爭言外國利害，皆有城邑，兵弱易擊。
entries.en: Returning envoys competed to insist that every western state had cities, feeble armies, and was ripe for the taking.
entries.literal: The envoys vied in speaking of foreign states' profits and harms, that all had walled towns, weak troops, and were easy to strike.

entries.zh: 於是天子遣從票侯破奴將屬國騎及郡兵數萬以擊胡，胡皆去。
entries.en: The emperor sent Marquis Congpiao Punu at the head of tens of thousands of allied horsemen and local levies; the nomads melted away.
entries.literal: Thereupon the Son of Heaven sent Marquis Congpiao Punu leading dependent-state cavalry and commandery troops numbering several tens of thousands to strike the Hu, and the Hu all departed.

entries.zh: 明年，擊破姑師，虜樓蘭王。
entries.en: The following year Jushi was crushed and the king of Loulan taken prisoner.
entries.literal: The next year they smashed Jushi and captured the king of Loulan.

entries.zh: 酒泉列亭障至玉門矣。
entries.en: Signal towers and walls now ran from Jiuquan clear to the Jade Gate.
entries.literal: From Jiuquan watchtowers and barriers were laid in a line to Jade Gate.

entries.zh: 而大宛諸國發使隨漢使來，觀漢廣大，以大鳥卵及犛靬眩人獻於漢，天子大悅。
entries.en: Dayuan and its neighbors sent retinues back with Han missions to see the empire for themselves, bringing ostrich eggs and conjurers from Lijian; the emperor was delighted.
entries.literal: And Dayuan and the various states sent envoys following Han envoys to come, observing Han's vastness, and with large birds' eggs and illusionists from Lijian presented them to Han; the Son of Heaven was greatly pleased.

entries.zh: 而漢使窮河源，其山多玉石，採來，天子案古圖書，名河所出山曰崑崙雲。
entries.en: Han scouts tracked the Yellow River to its source, where jade-strewn peaks yielded specimens for the throne; comparing old maps, the court declared those heights Kunlun.
entries.literal: And Han envoys traced the river's source to its end; that mountain had much jade and stone; they gathered and brought them; the Son of Heaven examined ancient charts and documents and named the mountain whence the river issues Kunlun, it is said.

entries.zh: 其夏，漢亡浞野之兵二萬餘於匈奴，公卿議者皆願罷宛軍，專力攻胡。
entries.en: That summer Han lost twenty thousand men under Zhuoye marquis to the Xiongnu; ministers urged abandoning the Ferghana campaign to hit the nomads alone.
entries.literal: That summer Han lost Zhuoye's troops, over twenty thousand men, to the Xiongnu; those who deliberated among the dukes and ministers all wished to halt the Dayuan army and concentrate force on attacking the Hu.

entries.zh: 天子業出兵誅宛，宛小國而不能下，則大夏之屬漸輕漢，而宛善馬絕不來，烏孫、輪台易苦漢使，為外國笑。
entries.en: The emperor had already committed the host: if Han could not crush so small a kingdom, Daxia and the rest would lose respect, Ferghana's horses would never flow east, Wusun and Luntai would bully every envoy, and the western courts would mock the empire.
entries.literal: The Son of Heaven having already sent out troops to punish Dayuan—if a small state of Dayuan cannot be taken, then Daxia and the like will gradually despise Han, and Dayuan's fine horses will absolutely not come, Wusun and Luntai will easily distress Han envoys, and it will be laughed at by foreign states.

entries.zh: 乃案言伐宛尤不便者鄧光等。
entries.en: He had men such as Deng Guang arrested for arguing most loudly against the invasion.
entries.literal: Thereupon he investigated and prosecuted Deng Guang and others who had said attacking Dayuan was especially inconvenient.

entries.zh: 赦囚徒扞寇盜，發惡少年及邊騎，歲余而出敦煌六萬人，負私從者不與。
entries.en: Convicts fit for frontier duty, street toughs, and border horse were mobilized; after a year of preparation sixty thousand men crossed from Dunhuang, private followers not counted.
entries.literal: He pardoned convicts fit to repel raiders and bandits, raised rowdy youths and frontier cavalry, and after more than a year sixty thousand men marched out of Dunhuang, not counting those who followed on private account.

entries.zh: 牛十萬，馬三萬匹，驢、橐駝以萬數齎糧，兵弩甚設。
entries.en: The train included a hundred thousand oxen, thirty thousand horses, and tens of thousands of donkeys and camels for grain, with crossbows and weapons in full supply.
entries.literal: Cattle one hundred thousand, horses thirty thousand head, donkeys and camels in myriads to carry grain in train, arms and crossbows very fully provided.

entries.zh: 天下騷動，轉相奉伐宛，五十餘校尉。
entries.en: The realm seethed as relays of supply fed more than fifty colonels on the Ferghana expedition.
entries.literal: All under heaven was stirred; relaying one another they supplied the attack on Dayuan—over fifty colonels.

entries.zh: 宛城中無井，汲城外流水，於是遣水工徙其城下水空以穴其城。
entries.en: Ferghana's capital had no wells and drew water from a stream outside; Han sent engineers to divert the flow underground and undermine the walls.
entries.literal: Dayuan's city had no wells within; it drew flowing water outside the walls; thereupon he sent water engineers to divert the water below the city hollow so as to tunnel the city.

entries.zh: 益發戍甲卒十八萬酒泉、張掖北，置居延、休屠以衛酒泉。
entries.en: Another hundred eighty thousand armored men were posted north of Jiuquan and Zhangye, with Juyan and Xiutu garrisons shielding Jiuquan.
entries.literal: He further raised garrison armored soldiers one hundred eighty thousand north of Jiuquan and Zhangye, established Juyan and Xiutu to guard Jiuquan.

entries.zh: 而發天下七科適，及載糒給貳師，轉車人徒相連屬至敦煌。
entries.en: The seven classes liable for corvée were called up, dried rations were loaded for Ershi, and wagon trains of laborers stretched all the way to Dunhuang.
entries.literal: And he raised the empire's seven categories of transport levy, and loaded dried grain to supply Ershi; transport carts and men followed one another in succession to Dunhuang.

entries.zh: 而拜習馬者二人為執驅馬校尉，備破宛擇取其善馬雲。
entries.en: Two expert horsemen were named colonels of the led horse, ready to pick the best stock once Ferghana fell.
entries.literal: And he appointed two men skilled with horses as colonels of the led horse, preparing for when Dayuan was broken to select and take its fine horses, it is said.

entries.zh: 騫孫猛，字子游，有俊才，元帝時為光祿大夫，使匈奴，給事中，為石顯所譖。
entries.en: Zhang Qian's grandson Meng, styled Ziyou, was a brilliant man who rose to grand counsellor under Emperor Yuan, served on the Xiongnu embassy staff, sat in the inner court, and fell to Shi Xian's slander.
entries.literal: Qian's grandson Meng, courtesy name Ziyou, had outstanding talent; in Yuandi's time he was grand counsellor of the palace, was sent to the Xiongnu, was attendant within the palace, and was slandered by Shi Xian.

entries.zh: 自殺。
entries.en: He took his own life.
entries.literal: He killed himself.

entries.zh: 卷六十一 張騫李廣利傳第三十一
entries.en: Volume 61: Biography 31—Zhang Qian and Li Guangli.
entries.literal: Volume 61: Biography Thirty-first, Zhang Qian and Li Guangli.

entries.zh: 自司馬氏去周適晉，分散，或在衛，或在趙，或在秦。
entries.en: After the Simas left Zhou for Jin the line split among Wei, Zhao, and Qin.
entries.literal: From the time the Sima clan left Zhou for Jin, they scattered; some were in Wei, some in Zhao, some in Qin.

entries.zh: 其在衛者，相中山。
entries.en: The Wei branch produced a chancellor of Zhongshan.
entries.literal: Those who were in Wei became chancellor of Zhongshan.

entries.zh: 在趙者，以傳劍論顯，蒯聵其後也。
entries.en: The Zhao line rose on fencing theory; Kuai Kui was of that stock.
entries.literal: Those in Zhao became eminent through treatises on sword transmission; Kuai Kui was their descendant.

entries.zh: 在秦者錯，與張儀爭論，於是惠王使錯將兵伐蜀，遂拔，因而守之。
entries.en: In Qin, Cuo crossed swords in debate with Zhang Yi; King Hui sent him to conquer Shu, which he held thereafter.
entries.literal: The one in Qin was Cuo; he debated with Zhang Yi; thereupon King Hui sent Cuo to lead troops to attack Shu, then took it, and thereupon guarded it.

entries.zh: 錯孫蘄，事武安君白起。
entries.en: Cuo's grandson Qi served Lord Wu'an, Bai Qi.
entries.literal: Cuo's grandson was Qi; he served Lord Wu'an Bai Qi.

entries.zh: 而少梁更名夏陽。
entries.en: Shaoliang was later renamed Xiayang.
entries.literal: And Shaoliang was renamed Xiayang.

entries.zh: 蘄與武安君坑趙長平軍，還而與之俱賜死杜郵，葬於華池。
entries.en: Qi helped Bai Qi slaughter the Zhao army at Changping; on the march home both were ordered to commit suicide at Duyou and were buried at Huachi.
entries.literal: Qi together with Lord Wu'an buried alive Zhao's army at Changping; returning, together with him he was ordered to die at Duyou and was buried at Huachi.

entries.zh: 蘄孫昌，為秦王鐵官。
entries.en: Qi's grandson Chang ran the royal foundries for the king of Qin.
entries.literal: Qi's grandson was Chang; he was Qin's king's ironworks officer.

entries.zh: 當始皇之時，蒯聵玄孫卬為武信君將而徇朝歌。
entries.en: Under the First Emperor, Ang—fourth-generation descendant of Kuai Kui—served Lord Wuxin as a general and reduced Zhaoge.
entries.literal: In First Emperor's time Kuai Kui's great-great-grandson Ang was general under Lord Wuxin and campaigned to Zhaoge.

entries.zh: 諸侯之相王，王卬於殷。
entries.en: When the lords began proclaiming kings, Ang was enthroned in the Yin region.
entries.literal: When the feudal lords set one another up as kings, they made Ang king in Yin.

entries.zh: 漢之伐楚，卬歸漢，以其地為河內郡。
entries.en: When Han struck Chu, Ang came over, and his lands were organized as Henei commandery.
entries.literal: In Han's attack on Chu, Ang submitted to Han; his territory became Henei commandery.

entries.zh: 昌生毋懌，毋懌為漢市長。
entries.en: Chang's son Wu Yi became market commissioner under Han.
entries.literal: Chang begat Wu Yi; Wu Yi was Han's market chief.

entries.zh: 毋懌生喜，喜為五大夫，卒，皆葬高門。
entries.en: Wu Yi's son Xi held fifth-rank grandee rank; father and son lie buried at Gaomen.
entries.literal: Wu Yi begat Xi; Xi was a fifth-rank grandee; when he died, both were buried at Gaomen.

entries.zh: 喜生談，談為太史公。
entries.en: Xi fathered Tan, who became grand scribe.
entries.literal: Xi begat Tan; Tan was the grand scribe.

entries.zh: 卷六十二 司馬遷傳第三十二
entries.en: Volume 62: Biography 32—Sima Qian.
entries.literal: Volume 62: Biographies the Thirty-second, Sima Qian.

entries.zh: 嚴助，會稽吳人，嚴夫子子也，或言族家子也。
entries.en: Yan Zhu came from Wu in Kuaiji commandery, the son of the scholar Master Yan—or, some say, of another branch of the Yan clan.
entries.literal: Yan Zhu was a man of Wu in Kuaiji, son of Master Yan the Confucian, or some say a clansman's son.

entries.zh: 郡舉賢良，對策百餘人，武帝善助對，由是獨擢助為中大夫。
entries.en: When the commandery nominated him as worthy and good, he joined more than a hundred men in the palace examination; the emperor singled out his policy essay and raised him alone to the rank of palace grandee.
entries.literal: The commandery recommended him as worthy and good; over a hundred men answered policy questions; Emperor Wu approved Yan Zhu's answer; on this account alone he promoted Zhu to palace grandee.

entries.zh: 後得朱買臣、吾丘壽王、司馬相如、主父偃、徐樂嚴安、東方朔、枚皋、膠倉、終軍、嚴蔥奇等，並在左右。
entries.en: He soon gathered Zhu Maichen, Wuqiu Shouwang, Sima Xiangru, Zhufu Yan, Xu Le, Yan An, Dongfang Shuo, Mei Gao, Jiao Cang, Zhong Jun, Yan Congqi, and the rest in his inner circle.
entries.literal: Afterwards he obtained Zhu Maichen, Wuqiu Shouwang, Sima Xiangru, Zhufu Yan, Xu Le, Yan An, Dongfang Shuo, Mei Gao, Jiao Cang, Zhong Jun, Yan Congqi, and others, all at his left and right.

entries.zh: 是時，征伐四夷，開置邊郡，軍旅數發，內改制度，朝廷多事，婁舉賢良文學之士。
entries.en: Those were years of constant war on the frontiers, new commanderies carved from barbarian land, armies marching again and again, and sweeping reforms at home. The court was swamped with business and kept summoning men of learning.
entries.literal: At that time, campaigning against the four barbarians, opening and establishing border commanderies, the army repeatedly issued, inwardly reforming the system, the court had many affairs, repeatedly raising worthy and literary scholars.

entries.zh: 公孫弘起徒步，數年至丞相，開東閣，延賢人與謀議，朝覲奏事，因言國家便宜。
entries.en: Gongsun Hong had risen from commoner to chancellor in a few years; he opened the eastern hall to scholars, drew them into counsel, and used each audience to speak plainly of what served the realm.
entries.literal: Gongsun Hong rose from walking on foot; within several years he reached prime minister, opened the east reception hall, extended worthies to deliberate with him, at court audience memorialized affairs, and thereby spoke the state's conveniences.

entries.zh: 上令助等與大臣辯論，中外相應以義理之文，大臣數詘。
entries.en: The emperor set Zhu and his fellows to argue policy with the elder statesmen; memorials flew between palace and ministry until the old guard more than once lost the debate.
entries.literal: The Emperor ordered Zhu and others to debate with great ministers; inner and outer mutually responded with writings of principle and pattern; the great ministers repeatedly were defeated.

entries.zh: 其尤親幸者，東方朔、枚皋、嚴助、吾丘壽王、司馬相如。
entries.en: Those he favored most were Dongfang Shuo, Mei Gao, Yan Zhu, Wuqiu Shouwang, and Sima Xiangru.
entries.literal: Those especially intimate and favored were Dongfang Shuo, Mei Gao, Yan Zhu, Wuqiu Shouwang, Sima Xiangru.

entries.zh: 相如常稱疾避事。
entries.en: Sima Xiangru habitually pleaded illness to dodge court duty.
entries.literal: Xiangru often claimed illness to avoid affairs.

entries.zh: 朔、皋不根持論，上頗俳優畜之。
entries.en: Shuo and Mei Gao traded in wit rather than weighty argument, so the emperor treated them much like court entertainers.
entries.literal: Shuo and Gao did not root their arguments; the Emperor somewhat kept them as jesters.

entries.zh: 唯助與壽王見任用，而助最先進。
entries.en: Only Yan Zhu and Wuqiu Shouwang were given real responsibility, Zhu having won his trust earliest.
entries.literal: Only Zhu and Shouwang were seen and employed, and Zhu was advanced first.

entries.zh: 建元三年，閩越舉兵圍東甌，東甌告急於漢。
entries.en: In the third year of Jianyuan, Minyue marched against Dong'ou, and Dong'ou sent an urgent plea to the Han court.
entries.literal: In the third year of Jianyuan, Minyue raised troops and besieged Dong'ou; Dong'ou reported emergency to Han.

entries.zh: 時武帝年未二十，以問太尉田蚡。
entries.en: The emperor was not yet twenty and put the question to Grand Commandant Tian Fen.
entries.literal: At that time Emperor Wu was not yet twenty; he asked Grand Commandant Tian Fen.

entries.zh: 蚡以為越人相攻擊，其常事，又數反覆，不足煩中國往救也，自秦時棄不屬。
entries.en: Fen replied that border Yue feuds were nothing new, that their loyalties shifted with the wind, and that the court had rightly left them outside the realm since Qin days.
entries.literal: Fen thought that Yue people attacking one another was their constant affair, and that they had repeatedly turned back and forth; it was not worth troubling the central states to go rescue them—they had been abandoned and not made subject since Qin times.

entries.zh: 於是助詰蚡曰：「特患力不能救，德不能覆；
entries.en: Yan Zhu turned on him: "You speak as if power and grace were lacking;
entries.literal: Thereupon Zhu pressed Fen, saying: 'We only fear that strength cannot rescue or virtue cannot shelter;

entries.zh: 誠能，何故棄之？且秦舉咸陽而棄之，何但越也！今小國以窮困來告急，天子不振，尚安所訴，又何以子萬國乎？」
entries.en: if they are not lacking, why cast a vassal away? Qin seized Xianyang and still let lands slip—need we speak only of Yue? A small state begs in peril; if the Son of Heaven will not stir, to whom can it cry, and how will the myriad states call him their father?"
entries.literal: if we truly could, why abandon them? Moreover Qin took Xianyang and then abandoned it—how much more so Yue! Now a small state comes in distress to report emergency; if the Son of Heaven does not rouse himself, where else may they appeal, and how may he be father to the myriad states?'

entries.zh: 上曰：「太尉不足與計。吾新即位，不欲出虎符發兵郡國。」
entries.en: "The Grand Commandant is not the man for this counsel. I have just taken the throne and do not wish to issue the tiger tally and call out the commanderies."
entries.literal: The Emperor said: 'The Grand Commandant is not worth consulting on this. I have newly ascended; I do not wish to issue the tiger tally and mobilize the commanderies and kingdoms.'

entries.zh: 迺遣助以節發兵會稽。
entries.en: He therefore dispatched Yan Zhu with imperial credentials to raise troops in Kuaiji.
entries.literal: Then he sent Zhu with credentials to mobilize troops at Kuaiji.

entries.zh: 會稽守欲距法，不為發。
entries.en: The governor of Kuaiji tried to refuse on legal grounds and would not release the troops.
entries.literal: The Kuaiji administrator wished to resist on legal grounds and would not mobilize.

entries.zh: 助迺斬一司馬，諭意指，遂發兵浮海救東甌。
entries.en: Zhu executed a major, proclaimed the emperor's will, and put an army to sea for Dong'ou.
entries.literal: Zhu then beheaded a major, made the imperial intent known, and thereupon mobilized troops by sea to rescue Dong'ou.

entries.zh: 未至，閩越引兵罷。
entries.en: Before the fleet arrived, Minyue had already broken off the siege.
entries.literal: Before he arrived, Minyue withdrew its troops and ceased.

entries.zh: 及汾陰得寶鼎，武帝嘉之，薦見宗廟，臧於甘泉宮。
entries.en: When the sacred tripod came to light at Fenyin, Emperor Wu displayed it at the shrines and lodged it in Sweet Springs Palace.
entries.literal: When at Fenyin they obtained the precious tripod, Emperor Wu praised it, presented it at the ancestral temple, stored it at Sweet Springs Palace.

entries.zh: 群臣皆上壽賀曰：「陛下得周鼎。」
entries.en: The assembled ministers all raised longevity congratulations, saying: 'Your Majesty obtained Zhou's tripod.'
entries.literal: The assembled ministers all raised longevity congratulations, saying: 'Your Majesty obtained Zhou's tripod.'

entries.zh: 壽王獨曰非周鼎。
entries.en: Wuqiu Shouwang alone said it was not the tripod of Zhou.
entries.literal: Shouwang alone said it was not Zhou's tripod.

entries.zh: 上聞之，召而問之，曰：「今朕得周鼎，群臣皆以為然，壽王獨以為非，何也？
entries.en: The emperor called him in and demanded, "The court calls this the Zhou tripod; you alone deny it—why?
entries.literal: The Superior heard it, summoned and questioned him, saying: 'Now We have obtained Zhou's tripod; the assembled ministers all think it correct; Shouwang alone thinks it not—why?

entries.zh: 有說則可，無說則死。」
entries.en: Convince me or die."
entries.literal: If there is explanation then it is acceptable; without explanation then death.'

entries.zh: 壽王對曰：「臣安敢無說！
entries.en: Shouwang bowed: "How should I dare come without an argument!
entries.literal: Shouwang replied, saying: 'Your servant how dare lack explanation!

entries.zh: 臣聞周德始乎後稷，長於公劉，大於大王，成於文、武，顯於周公，德澤上昭，天下漏泉，無所不通。
entries.en: The virtue of Zhou began with Hou Ji, swelled through Duke Liu and the Great King, ripened under Wen and Wu, and shone through the Duke of Zhou until grace soaked the realm like water from a spring.
entries.literal: Your servant has heard Zhou's virtue began with Hou Ji, grew with Duke Liu, enlarged with Great King, completed with Wen and Wu, displayed with the Duke of Zhou—virtue's moisture rose brilliant above, all under Heaven leaked like a spring, nothing not penetrated.
